lessons.title: What HCI Is and Why It Matters
lessons.content:
Think about your grandmother trying to send money to you with a mobile wallet app. The money is in the account, the network is fine and the app has no bugs. Still, she calls you three times: which button is Send Money, what is this field asking for, did the money go or not? Nothing is broken in the code, yet the system has failed her. The problem sits in the space between a person and a machine. That space has a name, and a whole field of study: Human Computer Interaction, or HCI.

What HCI is: Human Computer Interaction is the study and practice of designing, building and evaluating interactive computing systems so that people can use them well. The three words in the name are the three parts of the subject. The human is the person with a body, senses, memory, feelings, goals and limits. The computer is any interactive system, from a laptop to a phone, an ATM, a ticket kiosk, a car dashboard or a smart watch. The interaction is the conversation between them: the person does something, the system responds, the person reads the response and decides what to do next.

A simple loop: Every interaction follows a loop. You have a goal, for example 'buy a train ticket to Chattogram'. You translate the goal into actions: open the app, choose the station, pick a date, tap Purchase. The system changes its state and shows you something: a seat map, a price, an error, a ticket. You look at the result, compare it with your goal and decide the next step. HCI asks one question at every point of this loop: how easy is it for a real person to know what to do, do it, and understand what happened? We will study this loop in detail later with Don Norman's seven stages of action.

Why HCI is its own subject: You might think a good programmer automatically builds good interfaces. Sadly, no. Programmers know how the system works inside, so everything looks obvious to them. A user only sees the outside. This gap between the builder's view and the user's view is the reason HCI exists. The field borrows from computer science (how to build), cognitive psychology (how people perceive, remember and decide), design (how to communicate with form, layout and colour), sociology and anthropology (how people work in groups and cultures) and ergonomics (how bodies fit tools). An HCI person sits at the meeting point of all of these.

HCI, UI and UX: These three terms get mixed up, so let us separate them. The user interface (UI) is the part of the system the user sees, hears or touches: screens, buttons, menus, sounds, vibrations. User experience (UX) is wider: it is the whole experience of using a product, including how it feels, whether it is trusted, how support works and what happens when something goes wrong. HCI is the academic and research field that studies people and interactive technology; it produced many of the methods UI and UX designers use every day, like usability testing, task analysis and heuristic evaluation. Roughly: HCI is the science, UX is the practice of the whole experience, UI is the visible surface.

A short history, the early days: In the 1940s and 1950s computers were huge machines operated by specialists with switches and punched cards. Nobody worried about ordinary users because there were none. In 1963 Ivan Sutherland built Sketchpad, a program where you could draw directly on a screen with a light pen and move shapes around. It is often called the ancestor of graphical interfaces. In 1968 Douglas Engelbart gave a famous demonstration, later nicknamed the 'mother of all demos', showing a mouse, windows, hypertext links and shared editing, decades before most people owned a computer.

A short history, the personal computer: In the 1970s researchers at Xerox PARC built the Alto, a computer with a graphical screen, windows, icons and a mouse. These ideas reached ordinary buyers through the Apple Macintosh in 1984 and later Microsoft Windows. The style became known as WIMP: windows, icons, menus and a pointer. Around the same time HCI became a formal research field. The ACM's special interest group on computer-human interaction (SIGCHI) began holding the CHI conference in the early 1980s, and in 1983 Card, Moran and Newell published The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction, which gave the field models for predicting how long tasks take.

A short history, the web and the phone: In the 1990s the World Wide Web put interfaces in front of millions of people who had never been trained on any software. Suddenly a confusing website simply lost its visitors to a competitor one click away. In 2007 the iPhone made multi-touch the normal way to use a phone, and smartphones became the first computer for billions of people, including most people in Bangladesh. Today HCI also covers voice assistants, smart watches, virtual reality and AI chat interfaces. Each new device repeats the same old question: does it fit the human?

Why it matters, the cost of bad design: Bad interaction design is expensive. Users make errors, need more training, call support, give up halfway or never come back. In business terms, a checkout page that confuses people directly loses sales. In safety-critical systems the cost can be lives. Investigations of accidents in aviation, medicine and power plants have repeatedly found that confusing displays and controls contributed to human error. A famous example is the Three Mile Island nuclear accident in the United States in 1979, where the control room design made it hard for operators to understand what was really happening.

Why it matters, people are not the problem: When something goes wrong, people often say 'user error'. HCI teaches a different attitude. If many people make the same mistake, the design is probably at fault. A door that everyone pushes when it should be pulled is a design problem, not a problem with everyone. This attitude is the heart of the subject: design for real people as they are, with limited memory, divided attention, tired eyes and busy lives, not for an imaginary perfect user.

Why it matters, it pays back: Good HCI is not decoration added at the end. Fixing a usability problem on a paper sketch costs almost nothing; fixing the same problem after the app is coded, released and used by a million people costs a lot of time and money. That is why HCI methods are used early and often: research the users first, sketch and test cheaply, then build. You will see this idea, called user-centred design, again and again in this course.

What good interaction feels like: When interaction design works, you hardly notice it. You open a ride-sharing app, it already knows your location, you type a destination, see the price, tap once and watch the car approach on the map. You never think about menus or fields. Good design makes the right action obvious, gives clear feedback, forgives mistakes and speaks the user's language. Bad design makes you think about the tool instead of your task.

The main questions of HCI: Most of the subject can be summarised in a few questions. Who are the users and what are their goals? What tasks do they do, where, and with what devices? What do they already know and expect? What design will let them reach their goals effectively, efficiently and with satisfaction? How do we check, with evidence, that the design really works? The first questions lead to user research and task analysis, the middle ones to design and prototyping, and the last one to evaluation.

A tiny worked example: Suppose a hospital app asks patients to enter their date of birth in a single text box with no hint. Out of 100 test users, 30 type 12/05/1990, 25 type 1990-05-12, 20 type 12 May 1990, and the rest write something else. The system accepts only one format, so most entries fail. A developer may blame the users. An HCI view says: the design did not tell people the expected format and did not accept natural variations. A better design shows three small fields labelled day, month and year, or a date picker, and the failure rate drops sharply. Nobody changed the users; we changed the interface.

Real-life example 1, a train ticket website: Imagine a busy Eid travel season. Thousands of people try to buy train tickets online at the same moment. If the purchase flow has too many steps, the session times out while a person is still typing their national ID number, and they lose the seat they selected. HCI thinking would look at the flow step by step: which fields are really necessary, can saved passenger details be reused, does the timer clearly show how much time is left, and is the error message after a timeout helpful? Small interaction changes like these decide whether millions of people feel the service works for them.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet for everyone: Mobile financial services in Bangladesh are used by students in Dhaka and by farmers and day labourers in villages, some of whom read little. The same service must work for both groups. That is why such services often support both a smartphone app with icons and Bangla labels and a simple USSD menu on a basic phone, where you dial a short code and choose numbered options. An HCI designer would study both groups, test with real people, and design clear confirmation screens so nobody sends money to the wrong number. Our running example in this course, a fictional appointment app called DaktarDekhao, faces the same challenge: a young person and an elderly villager must both be able to book a doctor's serial.

Who does HCI work: In industry you will meet UX researchers who study users, interaction designers who plan flows and behaviour, UI or visual designers who craft the screens, UX writers who choose the words, accessibility specialists, and front-end and mobile developers who build it all. Researchers in universities study new interaction techniques and how people use technology in society. Even if you become a backend engineer, HCI helps you design APIs, error messages, command line tools and admin dashboards that other people can actually use.

Course map: This course follows the same order as a real design project. First the human: perception, memory, attention and mental models. Then the computer: input and output devices and interaction styles. Then the core principles from Don Norman: affordances, signifiers, mapping, constraints, feedback, conceptual models, the gulfs, and human error. Then usability and UX goals and the user-centred design process: user research, personas, task analysis, ideation, sketching, prototyping, information architecture and visual design. Then evaluation: heuristic evaluation, cognitive walkthrough, usability testing and the SUS questionnaire, plus predictive models like Fitts' law, Hick's law and the keystroke-level model. We finish with accessibility, designing for Bangladesh, ethics and dark patterns, and emerging interfaces.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A frequent mistake is to treat HCI as 'making things pretty'. Visual design is one part, but HCI is mostly about whether people can achieve their goals. Another mistake is designing for yourself: you are not the user, because you know the system too well. A third is to confuse UI and UX, or to think usability can be added at the end. Exams often ask you to define HCI and explain its multidisciplinary nature, to list milestones such as Sketchpad, Engelbart's demo, the Xerox Alto and the Macintosh, to distinguish UI, UX and HCI, and to explain with an example why bad interface design is costly.

Recap: HCI studies the human, the computer and the interaction loop between them. It exists because builders and users see systems differently. It draws on computer science, psychology, design and social sciences. It grew from Sketchpad and the mouse to WIMP, the web, touch phones and voice. Bad design costs money, time and sometimes lives, and repeated user mistakes usually point to design problems. Good HCI is done early, with real users, and checked with evidence. In the next lesson we start with the first part of the triangle: how the human perceives the screen.
key_points: HCI is the study and practice of designing, building and evaluating interactive systems so people can use them well.
Every interaction is a loop: goal, action, system response, perceiving and judging the result.
HCI is multidisciplinary: computer science, cognitive psychology, design, sociology and ergonomics.
UI is the visible surface, UX is the whole experience, HCI is the research field behind both.
Milestones: Sketchpad (1963), Engelbart's demo (1968), Xerox Alto, Macintosh (1984), the web, iPhone multi-touch (2007).
If many users make the same mistake, the design is probably at fault, not the users.
Fixing problems early on sketches is far cheaper than fixing them after release.
lessons.tip: Start a 'bad design diary' this week. Every time a door, form, app or machine confuses you, write one line about what confused you and why. By the end of the course you will be able to name the exact principle each one broke.
lessons.task: Pick one app you use daily, such as a mobile wallet or a ride-sharing app. Write down your goal, then every action you take and every response the screen gives until the goal is done. Mark one step where a new user, like an elderly relative, might get stuck, and suggest a small change.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes Human Computer Interaction?
options: The study and practice of designing and evaluating interactive systems so people can use them well
The study of how computers communicate with each other over a network
The art of choosing beautiful colours and fonts for websites
The process of writing bug-free code for user interfaces
quiz.explain: HCI covers the human, the computer and the interaction between them, with design and evaluation for real people. Colours are only a small part, and networking is a different subject.

quiz.q: Who built Sketchpad in 1963, often called an ancestor of graphical interfaces?
quiz.explain: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad let users draw on the screen with a light pen. Engelbart is famous for the 1968 mouse demonstration.

quiz.q: Forty out of fifty users press the wrong button on the same screen. What does the HCI view suggest?
options: The users need more training before using the app
The users were careless and the result can be ignored
The design is probably at fault and should be improved
The app should show a warning to type more carefully
quiz.explain: When many people make the same mistake, the cause is usually the design, not the people. HCI fixes the interface instead of blaming users.

quiz.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: UX is only the screens, UI is the whole experience
HCI is a programming language for interfaces
UI and UX mean exactly the same thing
UI is the visible surface, UX is the whole experience of using the product
quiz.explain: UI covers what you see, hear and touch. UX is wider, including feelings, trust and support. HCI is the research field behind both.

quiz.q: Why do HCI methods emphasise testing sketches and prototypes early?
options: Because fixing a usability problem early costs far less than fixing it after release
Because users cannot understand finished apps
Because programmers are not allowed to see sketches
Because early testing replaces all later testing
quiz.explain: A problem found on paper costs almost nothing to fix; the same problem after coding and release costs much more. Testing continues later too.

lessons.title: The Human I: Perception
lessons.content:
Open any busy shopping app during a sale. Red banners flash, prices jump out in bold, a small grey line at the bottom says 'delivery charge applies'. Within one second your eyes have already decided what to look at first, what belongs together and what to ignore. You did not choose this consciously. Your visual system did it for you, using rules that are millions of years old. A designer who knows these rules can guide your eyes to the right place. A designer who ignores them can hide important information without even meaning to. This lesson is about those rules: how humans perceive.

The human as an information processor: A simple model used in HCI treats a person a bit like a computer with input, processing and output. Input comes through the senses: mostly vision, then hearing and touch. Processing happens in memory and thinking, which we study in the next lesson. Output goes through the body: hands, fingers, voice, eyes. This model is a simplification, because people also have feelings, habits and culture, but it is a useful start. For screen-based systems, vision is by far the most important input channel, so we begin there.

How vision works, in brief: Light enters the eye through the lens and lands on the retina at the back. The retina has two kinds of light-sensitive cells. Rods work in dim light and do not see colour. Cones need more light and give us colour and fine detail. Humans normally have three types of cones, sensitive to short, medium and long wavelengths, roughly blue, green and red. The brain combines their signals to produce every colour we see. The signals travel through the optic nerve to the brain, which does most of the real work of turning patches of light into objects, words and faces.

Sharp only in the centre: Here is a surprising fact. Your eye sees sharp detail only in a tiny central area of the retina called the fovea, covering about the size of your thumbnail held at arm's length. Everything else, the periphery, is blurry and weak in colour, but very good at noticing movement. You feel that you see the whole screen sharply because your eyes jump around several times a second. These jumps are called saccades, and the short pauses between them, where you actually take in information, are called fixations. Practical lesson: a message shown far from where the user is looking, for example an error at the top of a long form while the user is typing at the bottom, may simply never be seen.

Reading on screens: When we read, we do not scan every letter one by one. We fixate on a word or two, jump, fixate again, and sometimes jump back. Familiar words are recognised by their overall shape. This is why text written in ALL CAPITALS for a long paragraph is slower to read, why very long lines tire the eye, and why short labels in familiar words work best. For Bangla, the shape of conjunct letters and the top line (matra) matter for recognition, so text size and font quality affect reading even more on small phone screens.

Visual acuity and size: Visual acuity is the ability to see fine detail. It falls with distance, poor light, screen glare and age. Many people above forty find small text hard to read without glasses. A design that looks fine on a designer's large monitor may be unreadable for an elderly user holding a budget phone in bright sunshine at a bus stop. So text size, contrast and spacing are not only matters of taste; they decide whether information gets into the user's head at all.

Colour perception: Colour helps us group, highlight and signal meaning. But colour is perceived differently by different people, on different screens, in different light. Also, our eyes are more sensitive to some colours than others; for example, pure blue text on a black background is hard to read because we see blue detail poorly. Colours also change appearance depending on the colours around them. A grey square looks lighter on a black background and darker on a white one, even when it is exactly the same grey.

Colour vision deficiency: Some people have one type of cone missing or working differently. This is usually called colour blindness, though most affected people see many colours and only confuse certain pairs, most often red and green. It affects about 8 percent of men, roughly 1 in 12, and about 0.5 percent of women, roughly 1 in 200, among people of Northern European descent, where it has been studied most; rates in other groups are similar or a bit lower. In a class of 60 boys, you should expect several. Design rule: never use colour as the only way to show information. A form field with an error should get a red border and an icon and a text message, not just a red border.

Preattentive features: Some visual differences are noticed almost instantly, without searching, before conscious attention kicks in. This is called preattentive processing. Strong preattentive features include colour, size, orientation, motion and enclosure. Try it: among twenty grey dots, one red dot pops out at once. Among twenty letter Ls, one letter T takes longer to find, because the difference is in shape details, not in a preattentive feature. Designers use this to make one important thing pop out, like the main 'Book Now' button. The flip side: if you make everything colourful and bold, nothing pops out anymore.

Gestalt principles, the idea: In the early twentieth century German psychologists of the Gestalt school studied how we see whole patterns rather than separate pieces. 'Gestalt' roughly means 'form' or 'whole shape'. They described several principles of grouping: rules the brain uses to decide which things belong together. These principles are extremely useful for screen design, because users group elements automatically, whether the designer planned it or not.

Proximity: Things that are close together are seen as a group. On a form, a label placed close to its field is read as belonging to it. If the label 'Phone' sits exactly halfway between two fields, users are confused about which one it labels. Grouping by spacing is often cleaner than drawing boxes around everything. A simple rule of thumb: space between groups should be clearly larger than space within a group.

Similarity: Things that look alike, in colour, shape, size or style, are seen as related. If all clickable links are blue and underlined, users learn that blue underlined text means 'clickable'. If one plain heading is also blue and underlined, users will try to tap it. Similarity is the basis of consistent visual language: same kind of thing, same look.

Closure and continuity: Closure means our brain fills in gaps to see complete shapes. A circle drawn with small gaps is still seen as a circle, and many logos and icons rely on this. Continuity means our eyes follow smooth lines and curves; elements arranged on a line or curve are seen as related and in sequence. A row of step indicators connected by a line, like a 'Cart, Address, Payment, Done' progress bar, uses continuity to say 'these are steps in order'.

Figure-ground: We automatically separate what we see into a figure, the object we focus on, and a ground, the background behind it. A pop-up dialog with the page behind it dimmed uses figure-ground: the dialog becomes the figure, the rest becomes ground. If figure and ground have weak contrast, or if the background is a busy photo, text becomes hard to separate and read.

Common region, common fate and symmetry: Common region means elements inside the same boundary, like a card or a box, are seen as a group, even if they are not very close. Card-based layouts in shopping and news apps use this. Common fate means elements that move together are seen as a group; when you drag a selection of several files and they all move together, you see them as one unit. Symmetry means symmetrical shapes are seen as a single object and feel stable and orderly.

A small worked example: Imagine a DaktarDekhao booking screen showing five doctors. In version A, each doctor's name, specialty, fee and a 'Book' button are spread evenly across the screen with equal spacing everywhere. Users in a test tapped the wrong doctor's Book button 4 times out of 20 tries, because the button was equally close to two names. In version B, each doctor is placed on a separate card (common region), the name, specialty and fee are close together (proximity), every Book button has the same colour and shape (similarity), and the cards have clear gaps between them. With the same five doctors and the same users, the confusion disappears. Nothing changed except grouping.

Hearing as a channel: Hearing is our second main channel. Sound is useful because it reaches us even when we are not looking, which is why alarms, ringtones and notification sounds exist. Humans hear roughly from 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz, and the upper limit drops with age. Sound has problems too: it disturbs others, cannot be heard in noise or by deaf users, and disappears once played. So important information should not rely on sound alone. Sound works best as a backup signal: a short beep confirming a payment, together with a visible message.

Touch as a channel: Touch gives information about pressure, texture, vibration and temperature. Phones use haptic feedback, small vibrations, to confirm a key press or warn about an error. Touch also matters for output from the human: fingers have limited precision, which is why tiny buttons cause mistakes. Blind users depend heavily on touch and hearing, for example using screen readers that speak what is under their finger. We study input devices and accessibility in later lessons.

Perception is shaped by expectation: What we see depends partly on what we expect to see. If a user expects the 'Next' button at the bottom right because every other app puts it there, they may not notice a 'Next' button placed at the top left. Experience, culture and context set these expectations. This links perception to memory and mental models, our topic in the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, a bus ticket counter display: Many bus terminals show departure information on a screen. If every line uses the same white text, the passenger must read each line to find their bus. If the destination is in larger text, delayed buses are marked with both a colour and the word 'Delayed', and each operator's buses are grouped with a little space between groups, a passenger can find their bus in seconds. Size and colour give preattentive pop-out; proximity gives grouping; text plus colour helps colour-blind passengers.

Real-life example 2, a medicine label: Two medicine boxes from the same company often look almost identical, same colour, same layout, only a small number changes, like 500 mg versus 250 mg. Similarity tells the brain they are the same thing. A tired pharmacist at the end of a long day can pick the wrong one. Good packaging and good pharmacy software break similarity on purpose for dangerous differences, using different colours, bigger strength numbers and a warning icon.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often list Gestalt principles without being able to point to them on a real screen; always practise with examples. Another mistake is using colour as the only signal, which fails colour-blind users and people with poor screens. A third is assuming users see everything on the screen; they see only where they fixate. Exams often ask you to explain the human as an information processor, describe rods, cones and the fovea briefly, define preattentive processing, and explain four or five Gestalt principles with interface examples.

Recap: Vision is the main input channel for screens. We see sharply only in the small fovea and move our eyes in saccades and fixations, so information far from the focus may be missed. Colour perception varies, and about 1 in 12 men has a colour vision deficiency, so colour must never be the only signal. Preattentive features like colour, size and motion make things pop out instantly. Gestalt principles, proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, figure-ground, common region, common fate and symmetry, explain how users group what they see. Hearing and touch are useful backup channels. Next, we follow the information inside the head: memory, attention and mental models.
key_points: A simple HCI model treats the human as an information processor: senses as input, memory and thinking as processing, body and voice as output.
Sharp vision exists only in the fovea; eyes move in saccades and fixations, so messages far from the user's focus can be missed.
About 1 in 12 men has a colour vision deficiency, so colour must never be the only way to show information.
Preattentive features such as colour, size, orientation and motion pop out instantly without searching.
Gestalt principles: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, figure-ground, common region, common fate and symmetry.
Users group screen elements automatically, so spacing and visual style must match the intended grouping.
Hearing and touch are good backup channels but should not carry critical information alone.
lessons.tip: Take screenshots of three apps you use and draw boxes on them to show the groups you see. Then name the Gestalt principle that created each group. This turns a list of terms into something you can spot in two seconds in an exam.
lessons.task: Find a screen or poster where colour alone carries meaning, such as a red and green status chart. Convert a screenshot to greyscale with your phone's photo editor. Can you still understand it? Write one change that would make it work without colour.

quiz.q: Why might a user never notice an error message shown at the top of a long form while they type at the bottom?
options: Because error messages are always ignored by users
Because sharp vision covers only a small central area and they are fixating elsewhere
Because the top of a screen is outside the human visual field
quiz.explain: We see detail only in the fovea, around where we fixate. A message far from the focus point may simply not be seen.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of men have some form of colour vision deficiency?
quiz.explain: About 8 percent of men, roughly 1 in 12, have a colour vision deficiency, which is why colour should never be the only signal.

quiz.q: A label sits exactly halfway between two input fields and users are unsure which field it belongs to. Which Gestalt principle is being violated?
quiz.explain: Proximity says close things are grouped. The label must be clearly closer to its own field than to any other.

quiz.q: Among twenty grey dots, one red dot is found instantly without searching. What is this called?
quiz.explain: Colour is a preattentive feature: differences in it are detected almost instantly before focused attention.

quiz.q: When several selected files move together as you drag them, you see them as one group. Which principle is this?
quiz.explain: Common fate: elements that move together are perceived as a group.

lessons.title: The Human II: Memory, Attention and Thinking
lessons.content:
Your friend reads out an OTP code on the phone: 4, 8, 2, 9, 1, 7. You repeat it in your head while switching to the app, and then a notification pops up: 'Your parcel has been delivered'. You look at it for one second, come back to the OTP box, and the code is gone from your mind. You did nothing wrong. You just met the limits of human working memory and attention. Every interface asks the user to remember, notice and think. This lesson is about how much people can actually do, and how design can help instead of overload.

The big picture of memory: A classic model, proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin in 1968, describes memory as three stores. Sensory memory holds raw impressions from the senses for a very short time. Short-term memory, today usually called working memory, holds the few things we are actively thinking about. Long-term memory holds knowledge and skills for days, years or a lifetime. Information flows from the senses into working memory if we pay attention to it, and from working memory into long-term memory if we rehearse it, understand it or connect it to what we already know. Modern psychology adds detail, but this three-store picture is still a useful way to think about design.

Sensory memory: Each sense has a tiny buffer. Iconic memory holds a visual image for a fraction of a second. Echoic memory holds sounds for a few seconds, which is why you can sometimes 'replay' what someone just said when you were not listening. Most of this information is lost immediately unless attention picks it out. For design, the lesson is that a message flashed briefly on screen, like a toast notification that disappears after one second, may be gone before the user has attended to it.

Working memory and its limit: Working memory is where we hold and manipulate information right now: the OTP code, the price you are comparing, the step you are on. It is small and fragile. In 1956 George Miller wrote a famous paper titled 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two', observing that people could hold about seven items, give or take two, in immediate memory. Later research, for example by Nelson Cowan in 2001, suggests the true limit for unrelated items is closer to about four chunks when people cannot rehearse. Either way, the key message is the same: working memory is very limited.

How fast it fades: Without rehearsal, items in working memory fade quickly, typically within around 15 to 30 seconds, and they are easily knocked out by distraction, like the parcel notification. Experiments in the late 1950s by Peterson and Peterson showed that when people were stopped from rehearsing, recall of a few letters dropped sharply within about 18 seconds. Interference is often the bigger enemy: new information pushes out old information.

Working memory has parts: Baddeley and Hitch proposed in 1974 that working memory is not one box. A phonological loop holds sounds and words, like repeating a number to yourself. A visuospatial sketchpad holds images and positions, like remembering where a button was. A central executive directs attention between them. A later addition was the episodic buffer, which links these to long-term memory. One practical consequence: two tasks using the same part interfere more. Listening to a voice prompt while reading text is harder than listening while looking at a map.

Chunking: Chunking means grouping small items into bigger meaningful units, so each unit takes one slot. The eleven-digit mobile number 01712345678 is hard to hold as eleven separate digits. Written as 01712-345678, it becomes two or three chunks. Experts chunk better because they know patterns: a chess master sees a whole opening, a beginner sees sixteen separate pieces. In design, chunking appears everywhere: card numbers in groups of four, OTPs split into boxes, long forms split into steps, menus grouped into sections.

Long-term memory: Long-term memory has huge capacity. Psychologists separate explicit memory, things you can state, from implicit memory, things you can do. Explicit memory includes episodic memory, memories of events like your first day at university, and semantic memory, facts and meanings like 'a floppy-disk icon means save'. Implicit memory includes procedural memory, skills like typing or riding a bicycle, which become automatic with practice. Expert users rely heavily on procedural memory: their thumbs know where the 'Send' button is without looking, which is why moving buttons around in an update annoys them so much.

Forgetting and retrieval: We forget mainly because memories interfere with each other and because we cannot find the right cue to retrieve them, not only because they decay. Information that is meaningful, organised and connected to existing knowledge is easier to retrieve. That is why a password like 'k8#Pz!q2' is hard to remember while a long but meaningful passphrase is easier, and why consistent labels across an app help: one learned meaning keeps working everywhere.

Recognition versus recall: This is one of the most important ideas in HCI. Recall means producing information from memory with few cues, like typing a command name from memory. Recognition means picking the right item when you see it, like choosing a command from a menu. Recognition is much easier than recall. This is why graphical menus made computers usable by ordinary people, why autocomplete helps, and why showing recently used items saves effort. Nielsen's heuristics, which we study later, include 'recognition rather than recall' for this reason.

Attention: Attention is the ability to focus mental resources on some information while ignoring the rest. Selective attention lets you follow one conversation in a noisy room; psychologists call this the cocktail party effect, and they noticed that you still catch your own name from across the room. Divided attention means doing two things at once, which works only when at least one task is highly practised and the tasks use different resources. Sustained attention is keeping focus over time, which gets harder when people are tired or the task is boring, like monitoring a security camera for hours.

When attention misses things: Two striking effects show how much we miss. Inattentional blindness means failing to see something clearly visible because attention is elsewhere. In a well-known 1999 study by Simons and Chabris, people counting basketball passes in a video often failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. Change blindness means failing to notice a change, especially when it happens during a blink, a page reload or a screen transition. In interfaces, a value that silently changes after a page refresh, like a price or a selected date, may go unnoticed.

Cognitive load: Cognitive load is the amount of mental effort a task demands from working memory. Researchers like John Sweller separate intrinsic load, which comes from the task itself, like comparing two loan offers, from extraneous load, which comes from poor presentation, like making users remember a code from one screen to type on another. Designers cannot remove intrinsic load, but they can cut extraneous load: show information where it is needed, use defaults, break tasks into steps, and avoid unnecessary choices.

Mental models: A mental model is a person's internal explanation of how something works. The idea goes back to the psychologist Kenneth Craik in 1943. Users build mental models from experience, from what the interface shows them and from similar systems. Models are often incomplete or even wrong, yet people still act on them. Many people press a lift call button many times believing it makes the lift come faster. Many people turn a room thermostat or air-conditioner remote to the extreme setting hoping it will cool faster, when most systems cool at the same rate and simply stop at a different temperature. The behaviour is reasonable given the user's model; the model is just wrong.

Why mental models matter for design: When the user's model matches how the system really works, people predict results correctly, make fewer errors and recover easily. When the models clash, people are surprised and frustrated. A classic example is 'save': many new users believe what they see on screen is already safe, while the system keeps changes only in memory until saved. Modern apps that save automatically are designed to match the user's model instead of fighting it. In lesson 7 we will meet Don Norman's terms for this: the designer's model, the user's model and the system image.

Thinking, problem solving and decisions: People are not perfectly logical. We use shortcuts called heuristics, which are usually helpful but sometimes lead to biases. We tend to accept default options, so defaults are powerful and must be chosen carefully. Too many choices can make decisions slower and more stressful. We judge by what is easiest to recall, so a vivid recent experience can outweigh real statistics. Designers should support decision making by showing the important comparison side by side, rather than making users remember and compute.

A worked example, the OTP screen: Look again at our opening story and redesign it. Problem 1: the user must hold six digits in working memory while switching apps, which is heavy extraneous load. Fix: on Android and iOS, apps can offer to auto-fill an SMS code, so no memory is needed. Problem 2: the code is shown as one long string. Fix: show it as two chunks, 482 917, and use six separate input boxes so the user can see their progress. Problem 3: a notification interrupts during entry. The app cannot stop all notifications, but it can keep what the user already typed and give a clear 'Resend code' option with a visible countdown, so a lost code is not a disaster. Each change reduces memory load or protects against attention slips.

Real-life example 1, a cash-in at a mobile wallet agent: A customer at a small agent shop in a market wants to deposit 2,000 taka. The agent reads the number from a scrap of paper, types it, then types the amount, while three other customers talk to him. If the app shows the entered number in large chunked digits and asks for confirmation with the account name before sending, the agent can catch an error without remembering anything. Recognition (seeing the name) beats recall (remembering the number).

Real-life example 2, the DaktarDekhao booking flow: Early sketches asked patients to note down a doctor's code on one screen and type it on the payment screen. Elderly users forgot the code or swapped digits. The redesign carried the chosen doctor's name, photo and time forward to every later screen, so nothing needed to be remembered. Errors dropped and the task became shorter. This is the 'reduce short-term memory load' principle in action.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Many students say 'menus must have at most seven items because of Miller's law'. That is a misuse: Miller's number is about holding items in memory, but a visible menu uses recognition, not memory. Another mistake is confusing selective and divided attention, or recognition and recall. Exams often ask you to draw the three-store memory model, explain chunking with an example, compare recognition and recall, define cognitive load or mental models, and give design guidelines that follow from memory limits.

Recap: Memory has sensory, working and long-term stores. Working memory is tiny, about seven items in Miller's classic estimate and closer to four chunks in later research, and fades in seconds when interrupted. Chunking, recognition, defaults and showing information where it is needed all reduce load. Attention is selective and easily captured; inattentional and change blindness show how much we miss. Users act on mental models, which may be wrong, so designs should match or gently correct them. Next we turn from the human to the machine side: input and output devices.
key_points: The three-store model: sensory memory, short-term or working memory, and long-term memory.
Working memory is very limited: Miller's 7 plus or minus 2 (1956), and about 4 chunks in later work such as Cowan's (2001).
Chunking groups items into meaningful units, like writing 01712-345678 instead of eleven separate digits.
Recognition is much easier than recall, which is why menus, autocomplete and recent items help.
Attention can be selective, divided or sustained; inattentional blindness and change blindness show what we miss.
Extraneous cognitive load comes from poor design and can be reduced; intrinsic load comes from the task itself.
Users act on mental models, which may be incomplete or wrong; good design matches or corrects them.
lessons.tip: When you study any interface, ask one question per screen: what does this screen force me to remember? Every answer is a design flaw you can name in an exam: memory load, recall instead of recognition, or missing chunking.
lessons.task: Ask three friends to remember a random 11-digit number you read once without grouping, and another 11-digit number read in chunks like 01712-345678. Ask them to write both after 20 seconds of chatting. Count the correct digits and see whether chunking helped.

quiz.q: Which change best reduces working memory load on an OTP entry screen?
options: Letting the app auto-fill the code from the SMS
Making the code longer for security
Showing the code for only one second
Asking the user to type the code twice
quiz.explain: Auto-fill removes the need to hold the digits in working memory while switching apps.

quiz.q: Choosing a command from a visible menu instead of typing its name relies mainly on what?
quiz.explain: Seeing the option and picking it is recognition, which is much easier than recalling a name from memory.

quiz.q: What did Cowan's later work suggest about the limit of working memory for unrelated items?
options: It is unlimited if the person is motivated
quiz.explain: Miller's classic estimate was about seven plus or minus two, but later research suggests closer to four chunks when rehearsal is prevented.

quiz.q: People counting basketball passes fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit. What is this called?
quiz.explain: Inattentional blindness is missing something clearly visible because attention is focused elsewhere.

quiz.q: A user turns the AC remote to its lowest temperature to make the room cool faster. What does this show?
options: Good use of a preattentive feature
A mental model that does not match how the system works
quiz.explain: The user's internal model says a lower setting cools faster; most systems cool at the same rate and just stop at a different temperature.

lessons.title: The Computer Side: Input and Output Devices
lessons.content:
Imagine giving the same task, 'send 500 taka to your mother', to three people. One sits at a desktop computer with a keyboard and mouse. One stands on a moving bus holding a touchscreen phone with one hand. One has an old keypad phone and dials a short code. The goal is identical, but the way each person tells the computer what they want, and the way the computer answers, is completely different. Those channels are the input and output devices, the computer side of the HCI triangle. A design that ignores the device ends up fighting the user's hands and eyes.

What input and output mean here: An input device turns human actions, like key presses, finger movements, speech or body movement, into signals the computer can process. An output device turns the computer's state into something a human can perceive: light on a screen, sound, vibration or print on paper. Every interaction loop passes through both. In the previous lessons we saw the human's channels; now we look at the machine's matching channels and how well they fit.

Direct and indirect input: A useful distinction is between direct and indirect input. With direct input you act exactly where the result appears: you touch a button on a touchscreen, or draw with a stylus on the screen. With indirect input your hand moves in one place and the effect appears elsewhere: you move a mouse on the desk and a pointer moves on the screen. Direct input is easy to learn because it feels natural. Indirect input can be more precise and less tiring, because your hand rests on the desk and does not cover what you are looking at.

The keyboard: The keyboard is still the main way to enter text on computers. The common QWERTY layout comes from typewriters designed in the 1870s, and has stayed mainly because millions of people already know it, not because it is the fastest possible layout; alternatives like Dvorak exist but never replaced it. This is a good HCI lesson in itself: once a design is learned by many people, the cost of switching can outweigh small improvements. Keyboards are fast for skilled typists, support shortcuts like Ctrl+C, and give physical feedback with each key press.

Typing Bangla: Typing Bangla raises extra design questions, because the script has more letters than a keyboard has keys, plus vowel signs and conjuncts. Two broad approaches exist. Fixed layouts map each key to Bangla characters directly; Bijoy, developed by Mustafa Jabbar and first released in 1988, is a well-known example used widely in offices and printing. Phonetic methods let you type Bangla sounds with English letters, so typing 'ami' produces আমি; Avro Keyboard, a free tool released in 2003, popularised this approach. Fixed layouts are fast once learned but take training; phonetic input is easy for anyone who already types English. On phones, many virtual keyboards offer both styles. A designer who knows this will never assume that all users type Bangla the same way.

The mouse and other pointing devices: The mouse was developed in the 1960s by Douglas Engelbart's team and became common with graphical interfaces. It is an indirect, relative pointing device: it reports movement, not absolute position. Systems use control-display gain, meaning how far the pointer moves for a given hand movement, often with acceleration so a fast flick crosses the screen and a slow movement allows precise placement. Touchpads on laptops, trackballs and pointing sticks are relatives of the mouse. How long it takes to hit a target with a pointer is predicted by Fitts' law, which we will calculate in lesson 23.

Touchscreens: Most phones use capacitive touchscreens, which sense the small electrical change caused by a finger. Older devices and some kiosks use resistive screens, which detect pressure and work with any object, even a fingernail or a gloved finger. Touch is direct and supports gestures like tap, long press, swipe, pinch and drag. But touch has weaknesses. Your finger covers what you are touching, there is no hover state to preview a button, and there is little physical feedback. Most important is the fat finger problem: a fingertip is much bigger than a mouse pointer's hot spot, so small targets placed close together lead to wrong taps.

Target sizes: Because of the fat finger problem, platform guidelines set minimum touch target sizes. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines recommend at least 44 by 44 points. Google's Material Design recommends at least 48 by 48 density-independent pixels (dp). The web accessibility standard WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for its AA level, with exceptions. The visible icon can be smaller than the touch area, as long as the tappable region is large enough and not overlapping its neighbours.

Pixels, density and dp: Screens are made of pixels, and phones differ greatly in how many pixels they pack per inch. A button 48 pixels wide would look big on an old low-density phone and tiny on a modern sharp one. To solve this, Android measures layouts in density-independent pixels: 1 dp equals 1 physical pixel on a 160 dpi screen, so on a 480 dpi screen 1 dp equals 3 pixels. A 48 dp target therefore becomes 48 x 3 = 144 physical pixels there, roughly the same physical size as before. iOS uses points in a similar way, with 1 point mapping to 2 or 3 pixels on most current iPhones. Designers should think in these units, not raw pixels.

The stylus: A stylus or pen gives much finer control than a finger, which makes it useful for drawing, handwriting and signing, for example at a parcel delivery terminal. Active pens can detect pressure and tilt. Handwriting recognition turns pen strokes into text, which can help users who are more comfortable writing than typing.

Voice input: Speech recognition lets people speak commands or dictate text. It is hands-free and eyes-free, which helps drivers, people with motor impairments and people who find typing hard, including users with low literacy. Its weaknesses are noise, privacy in public places, accents and mixed-language speech, and the fact that users often do not know what commands the system understands. Voice interfaces are covered further in the last lesson.

Camera and sensors: Modern phones are full of sensors that act as input. The camera reads QR codes for payments and can scan documents. The accelerometer and gyroscope detect tilt and motion, so the screen rotates when you turn the phone. GPS gives location, so a ride app knows where to pick you up. The proximity sensor turns off the screen when you hold the phone to your ear, preventing cheek taps. Fingerprint and face sensors provide quick authentication. Each sensor can remove a step from a task, but also raises privacy questions, which we discuss in the ethics lesson.

Keypad phones: Many people still use basic feature phones with a 12-key numeric keypad. Text entry uses multi-tap, pressing a key several times to cycle through letters, which is slow. Interaction is often through USSD menus: you dial a code such as one beginning with an asterisk and ending with a hash, and choose numbered options on a tiny text screen. Designing for these devices means very short menus, numbered choices, and no reliance on graphics.

Output: displays: The screen is the main output channel. Important properties are size, resolution (number of pixels, like 1080 by 2400), pixel density, brightness, contrast and refresh rate. LCD screens use a backlight shining through liquid crystals; OLED screens light each pixel individually, giving deep blacks, and dark themes can save some battery on them. E-ink screens, used in e-readers, are easy to read in sunlight and use power only when the image changes, but refresh slowly. In practice, a design must work on a large office monitor and on a small, dim budget phone in bright sunlight.

Output: sound and haptics: Sound output includes beeps, alert tones and synthesised speech. Text-to-speech lets screen readers read the interface aloud for blind users and can help people who struggle to read. Haptic output means vibrations: a short buzz on a key press, a different pattern for an error, a long vibration for an incoming call. Haptics are private and work in noisy places, which is why a payment terminal or phone uses them to confirm actions.

Output: paper and other channels: Printers still matter. Small thermal printers produce receipts at shops and ticket counters, and their narrow width and limited fonts constrain what can be shown; Bangla text on receipts needs a printer or printing method that supports the script. Other output channels include LEDs on devices, like the light on a router showing internet status, and the physical movement of machines such as an ATM pushing out cash.

Worked example, one form on three devices: Consider the DaktarDekhao form asking for the patient's phone number. On a desktop, a normal text field works; the user types with the keyboard. On a phone, the field should open the numeric keypad automatically, which on the web is done by setting the input type to tel, so the user does not hunt for digits on a letter keyboard. The 'Next' button should be at least 48 dp tall and placed where the thumb reaches easily. On a keypad phone through USSD, the system should ask for the number in one short prompt and confirm it back before continuing. Same data, three device-appropriate designs.

Real-life example 1, ATM and kiosks: An ATM combines a physical keypad, often a touchscreen or side buttons, a card slot, a cash dispenser, a receipt printer and sometimes a speaker and headphone jack for blind users. Users stand, are often in a hurry and may be nervous about security. Big buttons, few steps and clear audio and visual feedback are essential. The physical slots should be clearly marked so people know where the card and cash go, which leads straight to Norman's ideas in lesson 6.

Real-life example 2, a rider app outdoors: A delivery rider in Dhaka uses a phone mounted on a motorbike or held in one hand, in rain or bright sun, often wearing a helmet. Typing is nearly impossible while moving. Good design for this context uses large high-contrast buttons, location from GPS instead of manual address entry, voice or vibration alerts for new orders, and very few taps to confirm pickup and delivery. The device and context shape the design as much as the user's goals do.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A common mistake is designing only on a large desktop monitor and testing with a mouse, then shipping to phones where the targets are too small and hover effects do not exist. Another is using raw pixels instead of dp or points. A third is forgetting basic phones and low-end devices. Exams often ask you to classify input devices (text entry, pointing, direct versus indirect), compare touch and mouse, explain the fat finger problem and target sizes, and describe output devices and their properties with examples.

Recap: Input devices turn human actions into signals; output devices turn system state into light, sound, vibration or print. Direct input like touch is natural but imprecise; indirect input like the mouse is precise but must be learned. QWERTY survives through habit, and Bangla input comes in fixed layouts like Bijoy and phonetic tools like Avro. Touch targets need around 44 points on iOS, 48 dp on Android and at least 24 CSS pixels under WCAG 2.2 AA. Displays differ in size, density and brightness, and sensors can remove steps from tasks. Always design for the actual device and context. Next we look at the different styles of conversation between people and computers.
key_points: Input devices turn human actions into signals; output devices turn system state into something people can perceive.
Direct input (touch, stylus on screen) feels natural; indirect input (mouse, touchpad) is often more precise and less tiring.
Bangla can be typed with fixed layouts such as Bijoy or phonetic methods such as Avro; users differ, so do not assume one method.
The fat finger problem makes small, close targets error-prone on touchscreens.
Minimum targets: about 44 x 44 pt (Apple), 48 x 48 dp (Material), at least 24 x 24 CSS px (WCAG 2.2 AA).
Android dp: 1 dp = 1 px at 160 dpi, so 48 dp = 144 px on a 480 dpi screen.
Sensors such as GPS, camera and accelerometer can remove steps, and keypad phones need short numbered USSD menus.
lessons.tip: Whenever you sketch a screen, write the device and context in the corner: 'phone, one hand, outdoors' or 'desktop, office, keyboard'. It forces you to check target sizes, input type and readability before anyone else points them out.
lessons.task: Open three apps on your phone and measure the smallest button you often tap by comparing it with your fingertip. Note any place where you have tapped the wrong thing. Then check whether the number fields in those apps open the numeric keypad automatically.

quiz.q: On a 480 dpi Android screen, how many physical pixels wide is a 48 dp touch target?
quiz.explain: 1 dp is 1 px at 160 dpi. At 480 dpi the factor is 480 / 160 = 3, so 48 dp x 3 = 144 px.

quiz.q: Why is a mouse called an indirect pointing device?
options: Because it only works with wires
Because the hand moves in one place and the effect appears on the screen elsewhere
Because it is slower than a keyboard
quiz.explain: With indirect input the hand and the result are in different places, unlike touch where you act exactly on the target.

quiz.q: What is the fat finger problem?
options: Fingertips are much larger than a pointer hot spot, so small close targets cause wrong taps
Touchscreens stop working with dry fingers
Users type too fast on physical keyboards
Phones become warm when used for long
quiz.explain: A fingertip covers a large area and hides the target, so tiny buttons placed close together lead to errors.

quiz.q: Typing 'ami' with English letters and getting আমি on screen is an example of which input approach?
quiz.explain: Phonetic input, popularised by tools like Avro, converts the sounds typed with English letters into Bangla script.

quiz.q: Which design suits a basic keypad phone using a USSD service?
options: Large image buttons with swipe gestures
Short menus with numbered options on a text screen
quiz.explain: USSD on feature phones shows plain text menus; users reply by pressing a number, so menus must be short and numbered.

lessons.title: Interaction Styles and Paradigms
lessons.content:
Think of the different ways you can order food. You can tell a waiter in your own words, 'one plate of kacchi, less oil, and a borhani'. You can point at pictures on a menu card. You can fill in a paper order slip with tick boxes. Or, at some restaurants, you can pick dishes on a tablet and drag them into a basket. The goal is the same, but the style of the conversation differs, and each style suits different customers and situations. Computers offer the same choice. The basic ways people and computers talk to each other are called interaction styles, and the big historical shifts in how we think about computing are called interaction paradigms.

What an interaction style is: An interaction style is a general way for a user to tell the system what to do and to receive its responses. Textbooks usually list command language, menu selection, form fill-in, direct manipulation, natural language, and question-and-answer, with touch and gesture as modern additions. Real systems mix several styles. The skill is to know the strengths and weaknesses of each, so you can choose the right one for each user and task. The previous course on System Analysis and Design touched these briefly; here we look at each one more closely.

Command language: In a command language, the user types instructions in a defined syntax, and the system executes them. Examples are the Linux shell, where 'cp report.txt backup/' copies a file, the Windows command prompt, and the search operators people type into search engines. Strengths: commands are fast and powerful for experts, can be combined, repeated, saved into scripts and run on many files at once. Weaknesses: they rely on recall, not recognition. A new user facing a blinking cursor has no idea what is possible, and a small typing mistake gives an error. Good command interfaces reduce this with consistent naming, built-in help, tab completion and helpful error messages that suggest the right command.

Menu selection: In menu selection the system shows a list of options and the user picks one. Because options are visible, menus rely on recognition and are easy for beginners. Types include pull-down menus at the top of a window, pop-up or context menus that appear on right-click or long press, cascading menus with sub-menus, and toolbars and ribbons of icons. Menus can also be numbered, as in USSD services on basic phones and in telephone banking ('press 1 for balance'). Weaknesses: deep menus hide options several levels down, and experts find clicking through menus slow. The standard fix is to offer keyboard shortcuts shown next to menu items, so menus also teach the faster path.

Menu depth versus breadth: A design decision every menu faces is whether to show many options on one level (broad and shallow) or few options on many levels (narrow and deep). Suppose a service has 64 functions. With 8 options per level, users reach any function in 2 steps, since 8 x 8 = 64. With only 2 options per level they would need 6 steps, since 2 to the power 6 is 64. Research on menus generally found that broader, shallower menus are faster and cause fewer navigation errors, as long as options are well grouped and labelled. Very deep menus make users lose their way. We return to this in the information architecture lesson.

Form fill-in: Form fill-in presents labelled fields for the user to complete, much like a paper form. It suits data entry, like registering for an account, booking a ticket or filling in a patient's details. Users see all required information at once and can move between fields. Good forms use clear labels, sensible order, the right input controls (date pickers, drop-downs, radio buttons) and inline validation. Weaknesses: long forms are tiring, and users must understand the meaning of each field. Splitting a long form into steps with a progress indicator, a pattern often called a wizard, keeps each step small.

Direct manipulation: Ben Shneiderman introduced the term direct manipulation in the early 1980s to describe interfaces where users act on visible objects instead of typing commands. He described three main features. First, continuous visible representation of the objects of interest: you can see the files, the map, the photo. Second, physical actions instead of complex syntax: drag, tap, pinch, rather than typed commands. Third, rapid, incremental, reversible actions whose effect is immediately visible: you drag the slider and the volume changes right away, and you can drag it back. Early examples he discussed include video games and the VisiCalc spreadsheet; modern examples are dragging files to a folder, resizing a photo with two fingers, and moving a pin on a map.

Why direct manipulation works, and its limits: Direct manipulation is easy to learn, because actions resemble the physical world; errors are easy to see and undo; and users feel in control. But it has limits. Repetitive tasks on many objects, like renaming 500 photos, are slow by hand where a command or script would do it in seconds. Some actions have no obvious visual form, like 'find all invoices over 10,000 taka from last March'. Direct manipulation also depends on good visuals and enough screen space, and can be hard for blind users unless carefully made accessible.

WIMP and the desktop metaphor: WIMP stands for windows, icons, menus and pointer. It combines direct manipulation with menus and forms, and has been the main style for personal computers since the 1980s. WIMP interfaces use the desktop metaphor: files, folders, a trash can and a desktop, borrowed from the office. Metaphors help beginners transfer what they know from the real world, but can also mislead when the computer behaves differently, for example when 'deleting' a file only moves it to a recycle bin that can still be restored.

Touch and gestures: On phones and tablets, the dominant style is touch-based direct manipulation with gestures: tap to select, long press for more options, swipe to scroll or dismiss, pinch to zoom, drag to move. Touch is very direct, but gestures have a discoverability problem: nothing on the screen tells you that swiping a message left reveals a delete button. Designers therefore usually provide a visible alternative for any important gesture, and use common gestures that users already know from other apps.

Natural language and conversational interfaces: In a natural language interface, users type or speak ordinary sentences: 'remind me to pay the electricity bill on Sunday'. Chatbots and voice assistants use this style. It needs no special syntax and suits occasional users and people who cannot easily use screens. But natural language is ambiguous, users do not know what the system can do, and errors in understanding are frustrating. Modern AI language models have made conversational interfaces much more capable, but the same design questions remain: how does the user know what to ask, how does the system show what it understood, and how are mistakes corrected?

Question-and-answer: In a question-and-answer style the system leads the dialogue, asking one question at a time: 'Which district are you in?', 'Which hospital?', 'Which doctor?'. This is easy for first-time users, because they only answer what is asked. Setup wizards and many USSD flows work this way. It is slow and rigid for experts, who would prefer to jump directly to what they want.

Comparing styles with a small example: Consider the task 'find last month's bills and email them to the accountant'. With a command language an expert might type one line using a search command and a mail command, taking a few seconds, but a beginner could not do it at all. With menus and forms a beginner could open the search form, choose 'last month' from a drop-down, select the results and click 'Email', taking perhaps a minute. With direct manipulation the user could drag the bills onto the accountant's contact. With natural language the user might say 'email last month's bills to Rahim bhai', fastest of all if the system understands correctly, and confusing if it picks the wrong Rahim. Each style trades learnability, speed, power and error risk differently.

Interaction paradigms through history: A paradigm is a broad model of how computing is done, shaping all the interfaces of its time. In the batch processing era, users handed decks of punched cards to operators and collected printed results hours later; there was almost no interaction. Time-sharing in the 1960s let many users share one computer through terminals, giving the first real-time conversations with machines, mostly by command language. Personal computing put a whole computer on one person's desk, and with WIMP made it usable without training.

Paradigms, the web, mobile and beyond: Networking and the World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee around 1989 to 1991, made hypertext the everyday paradigm: click a link and go somewhere else. Mobile computing put computers in pockets and changed the context: small screens, touch, interruptions, location awareness. In 1991 Mark Weiser of Xerox PARC described ubiquitous computing, a vision of computing woven invisibly into everyday objects and environments, so that people use it without thinking of 'a computer'. Smart homes, wearables and sensors in cities move in that direction. Each new paradigm keeps older styles alive; you still use menus and forms inside a mobile app.

Choosing a style: When choosing, consider the users and tasks. For novices and occasional users, prefer recognition-based styles: menus, forms, direct manipulation, question-and-answer. For frequent expert users, add accelerators: shortcuts, commands, search, gestures. For data entry, use forms. For spatial or visual tasks, like editing photos or maps, use direct manipulation. For users who cannot read well or cannot look at a screen, consider voice with careful design. Most good systems are layered: an easy path for beginners and faster paths that experts can grow into.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet: A typical mobile wallet in Bangladesh shows several styles at once. The app home screen uses large icon menus like Send Money, Cash Out and Pay Bill. The send flow is form fill-in: number, amount, reference. Choosing a contact from a list is recognition. Scanning a merchant's QR code is a kind of direct physical action with the camera. Confirming with a press-and-hold button is direct manipulation that also prevents accidental taps. And the USSD service on a basic phone is a pure numbered menu and question-and-answer dialogue.

Real-life example 2, DaktarDekhao for two users: For a first-time village user, DaktarDekhao could lead with question-and-answer: choose district, choose hospital, choose department, choose time, each on its own screen with large buttons and Bangla labels. For a returning user or a hospital receptionist booking dozens of patients a day, the same app could offer a search box and a 'repeat last booking' shortcut. One system, two styles, matched to two kinds of users.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A common mistake is to think one style is always best, for example 'command lines are outdated'. Developers and system administrators still rely on them because they are powerful. Another is to forget the discoverability of gestures. A third is confusing interaction styles with paradigms: a style is a way of conversing, a paradigm is a broad era or model of computing. Exams often ask you to list interaction styles with advantages and disadvantages, explain Shneiderman's direct manipulation principles, compare menus with command language, explain WIMP, and describe paradigms such as batch, time-sharing, WIMP, the web and ubiquitous computing.

Recap: Interaction styles are basic ways of conversing with a system: command language (fast for experts, relies on recall), menus (recognition, easy for beginners), form fill-in (structured data entry), direct manipulation (visible objects, physical actions, reversible immediate feedback), natural language (no syntax, but ambiguous), question-and-answer (guided, slow for experts), and touch and gestures (direct, but hard to discover). Paradigms moved from batch to time-sharing, personal computing and WIMP, the web, mobile and ubiquitous computing. Good systems mix styles for different users. Next we meet Don Norman's principles that make any style understandable: affordances, signifiers, mapping and constraints.
key_points: Interaction styles: command language, menus, form fill-in, direct manipulation, natural language, question-and-answer, touch and gestures.
Command language is fast and powerful for experts but relies on recall; menus rely on recognition and suit beginners.
Broad, shallow menus are usually faster than narrow, deep ones: 64 functions need 2 levels at 8 options but 6 levels at 2 options.
Shneiderman's direct manipulation: visible objects, physical actions instead of syntax, rapid incremental reversible actions with immediate feedback.
WIMP means windows, icons, menus and pointer, often built on the desktop metaphor.
Gestures are direct but hard to discover, so important gestures need a visible alternative.
Paradigms: batch, time-sharing, personal computing and WIMP, the web, mobile, ubiquitous computing (Weiser, 1991).
lessons.tip: Make a small table with the interaction styles as rows and four columns: learnability, speed for experts, error risk, best use. Fill it with one example app per row. One table like this answers most exam questions on this topic.
lessons.task: Choose one app you use, such as a mobile wallet or a ride-sharing app, and find at least four different interaction styles inside it. For each, write the screen where it appears and one reason the designers chose that style there.

quiz.q: Which interaction style relies most on recall rather than recognition?
quiz.explain: In a command language the user must remember command names and syntax; menus and forms show the options, so they rely on recognition.

quiz.q: A service has 64 functions. With 8 options at each menu level, how many levels does a user go through to reach any function?
quiz.explain: 8 x 8 = 64, so two levels are enough. With only 2 options per level it would take 6 levels, because 2 to the power 6 is 64.

quiz.q: Which is one of Shneiderman's features of direct manipulation?
options: Users type commands in an exact syntax
Rapid, incremental, reversible actions with immediately visible effects
The system asks one question at a time
All options are hidden until the user asks for help
quiz.explain: Direct manipulation shows objects continuously, uses physical actions instead of syntax, and gives rapid, reversible, visible results.

quiz.q: What is the main usability weakness of gesture-based interaction such as swiping a message to reveal Delete?
options: Gestures are always slower than typing
Gestures are hard to discover because nothing on screen shows them
Gestures only work on desktop computers
quiz.explain: Gestures are invisible, so users may never find them unless there is a visible alternative or a hint.

quiz.q: Who described ubiquitous computing in 1991 as computing woven invisibly into everyday objects?
quiz.explain: Mark Weiser of Xerox PARC described ubiquitous computing in 1991. Berners-Lee invented the web; Shneiderman coined direct manipulation.

lessons.title: Norman's Design Principles I: Affordances, Signifiers, Mapping and Constraints
lessons.content:
Walk into almost any office building in Dhaka and you will find a glass door with a big metal handle on both sides. You grab the handle and pull. Nothing happens. You push, and it opens. A minute later someone else does exactly the same thing. The door is not broken, and the people are not stupid. The handle simply tells your hands 'pull me' on a door that needs a push. Doors like this are so common that designers call them 'Norman doors', after Don Norman, the cognitive scientist who made them famous. In this lesson we learn the vocabulary Norman gave us to explain why some things are easy to use and others are not.

Who Don Norman is: Don Norman is a cognitive scientist and designer who worked at universities and at Apple, and who helped make the term 'user experience' popular. His book The Design of Everyday Things, first published in 1988 under the title The Psychology of Everyday Things and revised in 2013, is one of the most read books in HCI. Its message is simple: when people struggle with everyday objects, the fault is usually in the design. Norman described a few principles that good design follows. This lesson covers discoverability, affordances, signifiers, mapping and constraints. The next lesson covers feedback, conceptual models and the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Discoverability and understanding: Norman says two of the most important qualities of a design are discoverability and understanding. Discoverability means: can a person figure out what actions are possible and where and how to perform them? Understanding means: can they figure out what the product means, how it is supposed to be used, and what all the controls and settings do? A remote control with forty identical tiny buttons fails discoverability. A washing machine with a dial that says 'Program 7' fails understanding. The principles below are the tools that create discoverability and understanding.

Affordances, the idea: The word 'affordance' was coined by the psychologist James J. Gibson. Norman brought it into design. An affordance is a relationship between the properties of an object and the abilities of the person using it, which determines how the object could possibly be used. A chair affords sitting for an adult. A flat plate on a door affords pushing. A small ball affords throwing for a child, but a heavy stone ball may not afford throwing for that same child. Notice that the affordance depends on both: the object and the person. A high shelf affords reaching for a tall adult but not for a small child.

Affordances, real and perceived: An affordance can exist without anybody noticing it. A hidden swipe gesture on a phone affords deleting a message, but if nothing shows it, people never discover it. That is why designers care about perceived affordances, the possibilities a person actually notices. Norman pointed out that on screens, most of what designers call affordances are really perceived: a flat picture of a button does not physically afford pressing any more than the rest of the glass does. The whole screen affords touching everywhere. What matters is what tells the person where to touch. That brings us to signifiers.

Signifiers: In the 2013 edition Norman added the term signifier to fix the confusion. A signifier is any mark, sound or perceivable signal that communicates where the action should take place and what it is. The affordance is the possibility; the signifier is the clue. A flat metal plate on a door signals 'push here'. A vertical bar handle signals 'pull'. A sign saying PUSH is also a signifier, though a sign is often a sign that the design failed. On screens, signifiers include the shape and shadow of a button, an underlined blue link, a text field with a blinking cursor, a small grey handle at the top of a bottom sheet hinting it can be dragged, and three dots that suggest a hidden menu.

Signifiers on screens, a worked check: Take a login screen with two lines of plain text, 'Forgot password' and 'Terms of service', in the same colour as the rest of the text. Both are actually links, but nothing signals that they can be tapped. Users will not tap them, or will tap randomly to test. Now style them in a link colour, maybe underlined, and keep that style consistent across the app. You have not changed what the screen affords; you added signifiers. A good test: if you remove the text labels from your screen, can a person still tell which things are tappable? Flat design trends that removed shadows, borders and button shapes sometimes hurt usability because they removed signifiers along with the decoration.

False signifiers: Signifiers can also lie. A Norman door's pull handle on a push door is a false signifier.
