On screens, underlining text that is not a link, styling a plain label like a button, or making an advertisement look like a download button are false signifiers. The last one is not an accident but a deceptive pattern, which we discuss in the ethics lesson. Accidental or not, a false signal teaches users to distrust the interface.

Mapping: Mapping is the relationship between controls and their results. Good mapping makes the relationship obvious from the layout. The classic example is a stove with four burners in a square and four knobs in a straight line. Which knob controls which burner? People have to read labels or guess, and they often guess wrong. If the knobs are arranged in the same square pattern as the burners, the mapping is natural: the top-left knob controls the top-left burner. Natural mapping uses spatial analogy, so the layout of the controls copies the layout of the things they control.

Mapping, more examples: In a car, turning the steering wheel clockwise turns the car right: a natural mapping. A volume slider where up or right means louder matches the cultural idea that 'more' is up. A lift panel where the button for the top floor is at the top matches the building. In a classroom with six ceiling fans and a row of six identical switches by the door, nobody knows which switch runs which fan, so people flip switches until the right one starts. A small sketch of the room above the switches, or arranging switches to match the fan positions, fixes it. On screens, mapping appears when a list's sort arrow points the way the list is sorted, or when a map's zoom gesture moves outward to enlarge.

Mapping and culture: Some mappings depend on culture. In many cultures time flows from left to right, so a timeline or a progress bar fills from left to right. In languages written right to left, such as Arabic, interfaces are often mirrored. Bangla and English both read left to right, so standard left-to-right layouts suit Bangladeshi users. Colour mapping also depends on culture and context: red usually means stop or danger, and green means go or success, but in stock market apps in some countries the colours are reversed. When in doubt, test with your actual users.

Constraints, the idea: Constraints limit the possible actions, so the wrong ones become hard or impossible. They guide people toward the right action without instructions. Norman lists four kinds: physical, cultural, semantic and logical. His famous example is a toy motorcycle made of a few Lego pieces. Even people who have never seen it can usually assemble it correctly on the first try, because constraints rule out most wrong placements.

Physical constraints: A physical constraint uses shape and size. A USB-C plug fits only into a USB-C port. A SIM card has a cut corner so it goes in only one way. The old USB-A plug fit only one way but looked almost symmetric, so people often tried it upside down first; the physical constraint worked, but the signifier was weak. On screens, physical constraints become disabled buttons, sliders that cannot go beyond their limits, and date pickers that do not allow February 30.

Cultural constraints: Cultural constraints come from learned conventions. In Bangladesh people know a red traffic light means stop, that in a queue you stand behind the last person, and that a phone's green button answers a call. On screens, conventions such as a magnifying glass for search, a cross in the top corner for close, and the logo at the top left leading to the home page are cultural constraints. Breaking a convention without a strong reason forces users to relearn, so designers usually follow platform conventions.

Semantic constraints: Semantic constraints come from the meaning of the situation. In the Lego motorcycle, the rider must face forward because riders face forward, and the windshield must be in front of the rider because its purpose is to protect the rider's face. On screens, an amount field for sending money should accept only numbers and a phone number field should accept only digits, because of what the fields mean. A date-of-birth field should not accept tomorrow's date.

Logical constraints: Logical constraints use reasoning. If you have assembled everything and one piece is left with one empty spot, logic says it goes there. Natural mapping is often a logical constraint: if the knobs are laid out like the burners, logic tells you which is which. On screens, a step indicator that says 'Step 2 of 4' lets users reason how much is left. A form that shows the next field only after the previous one is filled leaves only one logical place to act.

Real-life example 1, DaktarDekhao's booking button: In the first version of our fictional appointment app, the booking screen showed a list of doctors as plain text with a tiny grey 'Book' word on the right. In testing, older users scrolled up and down, unsure what to tap. The team applied Norman's ideas. Signifier: each doctor became a card with a clear coloured 'Book serial' button. Mapping: the available time slots were shown in the order of the day, morning on the left to evening on the right, matching how people think about the day. Constraints: full slots were greyed out and could not be selected, and the date picker allowed only days when the doctor sits. Booking errors dropped and nobody needed to call the helpline to ask which word to tap.

Real-life example 2, a Dhaka lift panel: Many lifts in Dhaka buildings have the floor buttons arranged in two columns, numbered in an order that does not match the building, plus 'open' and 'close' symbols that look alike. People press the wrong one when someone is running toward the lift. Applying mapping, floor buttons should be ordered bottom to top like the floors. Applying signifiers, the door-open button can be made larger, a different colour and placed apart from door-close. Applying constraints, the door could refuse to close when the sensor detects a person. Same principles, physical world.

Putting them together: The principles work as a team. Affordances say what is possible. Signifiers tell people where and how to act. Mapping makes the link between control and result obvious. Constraints prevent wrong actions. When all four are right, people do not need instructions. When they are wrong, designers add labels, signs and manuals, which are patches over a weak design. Norman's advice: if a simple object needs a sign, the design probably failed.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often mix up affordance and signifier. Remember: the affordance is the possible action, the signifier is the clue that shows it. Another mistake is to think mapping is only about physical knobs; it applies to every layout where controls relate to results. Some think constraints annoy users; good constraints feel invisible because they only block mistakes. Exams often ask: define affordance, perceived affordance and signifier with examples; explain natural mapping with the stove example; list and explain the four types of constraints with examples; analyse a 'Norman door' or a given screen using these principles.

Recap: Norman's book showed that difficulties with everyday things are usually design failures. Discoverability and understanding are the goals. Affordances, a term from Gibson, are the possible actions given an object and a person. Signifiers are the signals that show where and how to act, and on screens they carry most of the weight. Mapping links controls to results, best when spatially natural. Constraints, physical, cultural, semantic and logical, block wrong actions. Next lesson: what happens after the action, with feedback, conceptual models and the two gulfs.
key_points: Don Norman's The Design of Everyday Things (1988, revised 2013) argues that struggles with everyday things are usually design failures.
Discoverability means people can find what actions are possible; understanding means they know what things mean and do.
An affordance (term from J. J. Gibson) is a relationship between an object and a person that determines possible uses.
A signifier is a perceivable signal showing where and how to act; on screens, signifiers do most of the work.
Natural mapping copies the layout of what is controlled, like stove knobs arranged like the burners.
Constraints limit wrong actions: physical (shape), cultural (conventions), semantic (meaning), logical (reasoning).
A design that needs a sign or manual for a simple action is usually a weak design.
lessons.tip: Carry Norman's four words in your head when you walk around: affordance, signifier, mapping, constraint. Every door, switch board and app you meet is free practice. Explaining a bad design in these words is exactly what exam questions ask you to do.
lessons.task: Find a switch board in your home or classroom with three or more switches. Draw it, then draw the room showing what each switch controls. Is the mapping natural? Redesign the switch layout or add a small diagram so that a guest could guess correctly on the first try.

quiz.q: A door has a flat metal plate where you would put your hand. What is the plate?
quiz.explain: The plate is a perceivable clue showing where and how to act: push. The door's ability to be pushed is the affordance; the plate signals it.

quiz.q: Four stove knobs are placed in a square matching the four burners. Which principle is applied?
quiz.explain: Natural mapping copies the spatial layout of what is controlled, so the link between knob and burner becomes obvious.

quiz.q: A SIM card has one cut corner so it can go into the tray only one way. What type of constraint is this?
quiz.explain: Shape physically prevents the wrong orientation. That is a physical constraint.

quiz.q: Which statement about affordances and signifiers is correct?
options: An affordance is a possible action; a signifier is the clue that shows where and how to do it
They are two names for the same thing
A signifier is always a written label
quiz.explain: Norman separated them in 2013: the affordance is the possibility, the signifier is the perceivable signal. Signifiers can be shapes, colours, sounds or labels.

quiz.q: Using a magnifying glass icon for search and a cross icon for close relies mainly on which constraint?
quiz.explain: These are learned conventions shared by users, so they are cultural constraints. Breaking them forces people to relearn.

lessons.title: Norman's Design Principles II: Feedback, Conceptual Models and the Two Gulfs
lessons.content:
You press the lift call button on the ground floor. The button does not light up. Did it register? You press it again, then three more times, harder each time. Someone else arrives and presses it too. If the button had simply glowed after the first press, nobody would have pressed it again. That tiny light is feedback, and its absence turns calm people into button-hammering machines. In the last lesson we looked at what helps people act: affordances, signifiers, mapping and constraints. This lesson is about the other half of the loop: how people understand what happened, and how they build a picture of how a system works in the first place.

Feedback, what it is: Feedback is communicating the results of an action back to the person. When you tap a button, it changes colour; when you send a message, a tick appears; when you pay, a confirmation screen shows the amount and the receiver. Feedback answers the questions 'Did the system hear me?' and 'What did it do?'. Without it, people repeat actions, give up too early, or assume something went wrong when it did not. Norman lists feedback as one of the fundamental principles of interaction.

Good feedback is immediate: Feedback must arrive quickly. Even a delay of a tenth of a second can feel like lag. HCI uses three well-known response time limits, described by Jakob Nielsen based on older research. About 0.1 second is the limit for a response to feel instantaneous, as if the user caused it directly, like a button changing colour when pressed. About 1 second is the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted; they notice the delay but keep their focus. About 10 seconds is the limit for keeping attention on the task; beyond that, people start doing other things and need a clear progress indicator.

Using the limits, a worked example: Suppose loading the list of doctors in DaktarDekhao takes 3 seconds on a slow mobile connection. That is beyond 1 second, so the user will notice the wait; the screen should show something immediately, such as a loading animation or placeholder cards, within 0.1 second of the tap. If uploading a prescription photo takes 25 seconds, that is beyond 10 seconds, so the app needs a progress bar showing how much is done, ideally with the option to cancel. A spinner with no information for 25 seconds makes people think the app has frozen, and many will close it.

Good feedback is informative: Feedback should say what happened in words the user understands. 'Error 500' is feedback, but useless. 'Serial booked for Dr. Rahman, Tuesday 10:30 am, serial number 14' is informative: it confirms the action and gives the details the user needs. Feedback should also be specific about failures: 'Payment failed: your balance is 120 taka, the fee is 300 taka' tells the user what to do next.

Good feedback is not too much: Too much feedback is as bad as too little. Norman gives the example of household appliances that beep for everything until people ignore all beeps, including important ones. On phones, an app that sends a notification for every small event trains users to swipe them all away. Feedback should be prioritised: unimportant things gently and briefly, important things clearly, dangerous things impossible to miss. A confirmation dialog for every action is a form of excessive feedback; people learn to tap Yes without reading.

Feedback channels: Feedback can be visual (colour change, tick, progress bar), auditory (the click of a camera, a payment success sound), or haptic (a vibration when you long-press). Combining channels helps in noisy places or when the user is not looking directly at the screen, but each channel should mean something consistent. A short vibration for success and a different pattern for an error lets users know the result even with the phone in a pocket.

Conceptual models: A conceptual model is an explanation, usually highly simplified, of how something works. It does not need to be complete or accurate; it only needs to be useful enough to let people predict what will happen. The folder and file icons on a computer give a conceptual model: documents live in folders, like papers in a cabinet. Of course nothing is physically inside anything, but the model lets people organise and find their work. When a conceptual model is good, people can figure out new actions on their own. When it is wrong or missing, people make predictable mistakes.

The three parts of a conceptual model: Norman describes three related models. The designer's model is the conceptual model in the designer's head, how they intend the system to work. The user's model, or mental model, is what the user believes about how the system works. The system image is everything the user can actually see and experience: the interface, its behaviour, the messages, the manual, the help pages, even the packaging. The key insight is that designers cannot talk to every user directly. The only way the designer's model reaches the user is through the system image. If the system image is unclear or misleading, users build the wrong mental model.

A wrong mental model, the thermostat: Norman's famous example is the room thermostat. Many people believe that setting the thermostat to a very high temperature will heat the room faster, like opening a tap wider. In fact most home thermostats are simple on-off switches: the heater runs at full power until the target temperature is reached, so a higher setting does not heat faster; it only overshoots. The device's system image gives no clue about how it works, so people invent a model. You can see the same thing with lift buttons pressed repeatedly or with people tapping a slow app button again and again, believing it will speed things up.

The seven stages of action: Norman described action as a cycle of seven stages. First comes the goal: what you want to achieve. Then come three stages of execution: plan the action, specify an action sequence, and perform it. Then three stages of evaluation: perceive the state of the world, interpret the perception, and compare the outcome with the goal. Example: goal, 'recharge 50 taka to my mother's phone'. Plan: use my mobile wallet. Specify: open the app, tap Mobile Recharge, enter her number, enter 50, enter PIN. Perform: do the taps. Perceive: the screen shows a green tick and a message. Interpret: it says the recharge to her number succeeded. Compare: yes, the goal is achieved. Many everyday actions run through these stages so quickly that we never notice them.

The gulf of execution: Between a person's goal and the system's controls there may be a gap, which Norman calls the gulf of execution. It is the difficulty of figuring out how to operate the system: what actions are possible, and which one serves my goal? A wide gulf means the user knows what they want but cannot find how to do it. The tools for bridging it are the ones from the last lesson: signifiers show where to act, mapping links controls to results, constraints remove wrong options, and a good conceptual model helps users plan. Asking 'Can the user tell what to do here?' is asking about the gulf of execution.

The gulf of evaluation: On the return path there is another gap, the gulf of evaluation. It is the difficulty of figuring out what state the system is in and whether the goal has been achieved. A wide gulf means the user did something but cannot tell what happened. The tools for bridging it are feedback and a good conceptual model: clear status displays, confirmations, progress indicators, and results shown in the user's terms. Asking 'Can the user tell what happened?' is asking about the gulf of evaluation.

Worked example, the ATM: Let us analyse a cash withdrawal. Goal: get 2,000 taka. Gulf of execution: the old ATM screen shows eight unlabelled side buttons and options like 'Fast Cash' and 'Other Services'. A first-time user from a village does not know whether 2,000 is under Fast Cash or Withdrawal, and the buttons are beside the screen with small arrows, a weak mapping. Bridging it: labels closer to the buttons, plain words like 'Withdraw cash', Bangla language option on the first screen. Gulf of evaluation: after entering the amount, the machine goes silent for several seconds while processing. The user wonders whether it worked and may even walk away. Bridging it: a 'Processing, please wait' message with a moving indicator, a sound when cash is ready, and a clear 'Take your card' message before the cash, so people do not forget their card.

Worked example, mobile recharge: Now a recharge in a wallet app. Execution problem found in testing: the app asks for 'Operator' with logos only; some users could not recognise their own operator logo, and the app could have detected it from the number prefix anyway. Fix: detect the operator automatically, show it with its name, let users change it if needed. Evaluation problem: after entering the PIN, the old app returned silently to the home screen; the balance updated, but users did not notice and some recharged twice. Fix: a clear success screen with amount, number, time and a transaction ID, plus an SMS. Both gulfs narrowed, and double recharges fell.

Real-life example, Bangladesh railway counters to apps: When ticket buying moved from counters to apps, users lost the human clerk who used to explain things and confirm that the ticket was booked. The app's system image must now do that job. A clear seat map acts as a good conceptual model of the coach. A final screen showing train name, coach, seat, date and a downloadable ticket bridges the gulf of evaluation. Anything vague, such as 'Your request has been received' without saying whether a seat was confirmed, leaves people anxious and sends them to the helpline.

How the principles connect: Put both lessons together. Discoverability helps people find possible actions. Affordances, signifiers, mapping and constraints shrink the gulf of execution. Feedback shrinks the gulf of evaluation. The conceptual model, delivered through the system image, supports both: with a good mental model, people can plan actions and interpret results even in situations they have never seen. When you evaluate any design, walk through the seven stages and ask at each one: what could go wrong here?

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often reverse the gulfs. Execution is about doing (from goal to action); evaluation is about understanding results (from system state back to the goal). Another mistake is thinking a mental model must be technically correct; it only needs to support correct predictions. Some think feedback means only error messages; success and progress feedback matter just as much. Exams often ask: list and explain the seven stages of action with an example; define the gulfs of execution and evaluation and how to bridge them; explain designer's model, user's model and system image with a diagram; state the 0.1, 1 and 10 second limits.

Recap: Feedback tells people the result of their actions; it should be immediate, informative, prioritised and not excessive, using the 0.1, 1 and 10 second limits as guides. A conceptual model is a simplified explanation of how something works; the designer's model reaches the user's mental model only through the system image. The seven stages of action are goal, plan, specify, perform, perceive, interpret, compare. The gulf of execution is the gap between intention and possible actions; the gulf of evaluation is the gap between system state and the user's understanding. Next we look at what happens when things go wrong: human error and how to design for it.
key_points: Feedback communicates the result of an action; it should be immediate, informative, prioritised and not overwhelming.
Response time limits: about 0.1 s feels instant, about 1 s keeps the flow of thought, about 10 s is the limit of attention.
A conceptual model is a simplified explanation that lets people predict how a system behaves.
The designer's model reaches the user's mental model only through the system image: interface, behaviour, messages and docs.
Seven stages of action: goal, plan, specify, perform, perceive, interpret, compare.
The gulf of execution is the difficulty of knowing how to act; signifiers, mapping and constraints bridge it.
The gulf of evaluation is the difficulty of knowing what happened; feedback and clear status displays bridge it.
lessons.tip: When you analyse any design, draw the seven stages as a circle and write one possible problem next to each stage. This turns a vague 'it is confusing' into precise, exam-ready answers about the gulf of execution or evaluation.
lessons.task: Time three actions on your phone with a stopwatch app: opening a heavy app, sending a photo, and loading a web page on mobile data. For each, note what feedback appears in the first 0.1 second, and whether the wait goes beyond 1 or 10 seconds. Suggest better feedback for the worst one.

quiz.q: About how long can a response take and still feel instantaneous to the user?
quiz.explain: Around 0.1 second feels instant. Around 1 second keeps the flow of thought; around 10 seconds is the limit of attention.

quiz.q: A user knows exactly what they want but cannot figure out which button does it. Which gulf is wide?
quiz.explain: The gulf of execution is the gap between the user's intention and the actions the system makes available.

quiz.q: In Norman's terms, how does the designer's model reach the user?
options: Through the system image: the interface, behaviour, messages and documentation
Through direct training of every user
quiz.explain: Designers rarely talk to users directly, so the system image is the only channel; if it is unclear, users form wrong mental models.

quiz.q: After paying, the app silently returns to the home screen and users pay twice. What is the best fix?
options: Add more options to the home screen
Show a clear success screen with amount, receiver and transaction ID
Hide the pay button after one use per day
quiz.explain: The problem is a wide gulf of evaluation; informative feedback confirming what happened bridges it.

quiz.q: Which list gives the seven stages of action in the correct order?
options: Plan, goal, perform, specify, interpret, perceive, compare
Goal, perform, plan, specify, compare, perceive, interpret
Goal, plan, specify, perform, perceive, interpret, compare
Perceive, interpret, compare, goal, plan, specify, perform
quiz.explain: Start with the goal, then three execution stages (plan, specify, perform), then three evaluation stages (perceive, interpret, compare).

lessons.title: Human Error and Designing for Error
lessons.content:
Have you ever poured tea into the sugar pot instead of the cup while chatting? Or typed your friend's name in the 'To' box and then sent a message meant for someone else? Or, on autopilot, taken the usual road to university on a Friday when you meant to go to a relative's house? Everybody makes errors, every day. The surprising lesson of HCI is that most of these errors are not caused by stupidity or carelessness. They come from the normal way human minds work, meeting designs that do not account for it. If errors are normal, then designing for error is not an extra feature. It is part of the job.

Why talk about error at all: In the last two lessons we saw how good signifiers, mapping, constraints and feedback make interaction smooth. But no design prevents every error. People are tired, distracted, interrupted and in a hurry. A good designer assumes errors will happen and asks three questions: how can I make errors less likely, how can I make them easy to notice, and how can I make them easy to recover from? Before we can answer, we need a vocabulary for the different kinds of error.

The two big families: Don Norman divides human error into two families: slips and mistakes. A slip happens when a person intends to do one action and ends up doing another. The goal was right, the execution went wrong. Pouring tea into the sugar pot is a slip: you knew you wanted the cup. A mistake happens when the goal or plan itself is wrong. You then carry out the wrong plan perfectly. Taking the wrong medicine because you misread the prescription is a mistake: you did exactly what you planned, but the plan was wrong. In terms of the seven stages of action, slips happen in the lower stages (specifying and performing the action), while mistakes happen in the higher stages (forming the goal and the plan) and in interpreting the results.

Why the difference matters: Slips and mistakes need different design fixes. Slips are common among experts, because experts do things automatically without paying close attention. The fix is usually better constraints, clear feedback and making similar actions look and feel different. Mistakes are more common among novices or in unfamiliar situations, because they come from a wrong understanding. The fix is a better conceptual model, clearer information and helpful explanations. If you treat a mistake like a slip, by adding a 'Are you sure?' dialog, the user will simply confirm the wrong plan.

Action-based slips, capture: Norman lists several kinds of slips. A capture slip happens when a frequently done activity takes over a less familiar one. You plan to stop at the pharmacy on the way home, but you follow your usual route and arrive home without the medicine. On screens, a capture slip happens when two flows share their first steps. If 'Send Money' and 'Cash Out' screens look nearly identical for the first two steps, a user who usually does Send Money may slip into that flow when they intended to cash out. The fix is to make the flows look different as early as possible.

Action-based slips, description-similarity: A description-similarity slip happens when the target of an action is similar to another target. You throw your sweaty shirt into the toilet instead of the laundry basket, because both are open containers in the same room. On screens, two buttons with similar shape and position but very different effects invite this slip: 'Save' and 'Delete' side by side, both grey, both the same size. The fix is to make important targets look different and to place destructive actions away from frequent ones.

Mode errors: A mode error happens when a device behaves differently in different modes and the user does not realise which mode it is in. Typing a password with Caps Lock on is a classic. Typing a long message in Bangla while the keyboard is in English mode, so you get a line of random English letters, is another. Mode errors are common in devices with few buttons and many functions, such as digital watches. Fixes include avoiding modes where possible, making the current mode very visible (a clear 'বাং' or 'EN' indicator), and warning when behaviour is unexpected, like 'Caps Lock is on' near a password field.

Memory-lapse slips: A memory-lapse slip happens when you forget to do something or forget where you were in a sequence, often because of an interruption. You leave your card in the ATM after taking the cash; you forget to attach the file you said was attached. The fix is to reduce the steps that rely on memory, to show the current state clearly, and to design the order of steps so the important one cannot be skipped. Some email apps now warn you if your message mentions an attachment but none is attached. That is designing for a memory lapse.

Rule-based mistakes: Mistakes come in different types too. In a rule-based mistake the person correctly understands the situation but applies the wrong rule, or the rule itself is faulty, or they misjudge which situation they are in. A new user sees a green button and assumes, by a rule from other apps, that green means 'continue', but in this app green means 'add another item'. Designers reduce rule-based mistakes by following conventions and by making the situation clear.

Knowledge-based mistakes and memory-lapse mistakes: A knowledge-based mistake happens when the situation is new and there is no rule to follow, so people reason it out, and their reasoning goes wrong because their mental model is wrong. A first-time user who thinks that pressing 'Back' cancels a payment that was already sent is making a knowledge-based mistake. A memory-lapse mistake happens when forgetting leads to a wrong goal or plan, for example forgetting that you already booked a serial yesterday and booking a second one. Fixes are clear conceptual models, good explanations, and showing relevant history, such as 'You already have a serial on Tuesday'.

Forcing functions: The strongest way to prevent an error is a forcing function: a constraint that makes the wrong action impossible until a step is done. Norman describes three types. An interlock forces operations to take place in the right order: a microwave oven will not run while the door is open. A lock-in keeps an operation active so someone cannot stop it too early: many programs ask whether you want to save before they close. A lockout prevents someone from entering a dangerous place or state: a barrier at the stairway that stops people running past the ground floor exit into the basement during a fire. Many ATMs return the card before giving the cash, so you cannot take the money and forget the card. That is a forcing function against a memory-lapse slip.

Poka-yoke: In Japanese manufacturing the same idea is called poka-yoke, meaning mistake-proofing, associated with the engineer Shigeo Shingo. The SIM tray with a cut corner, the car that will not start unless it is in park or neutral, and the form that will not submit until a required checkbox is ticked are all poka-yoke. In software, disabling the 'Send' button until the amount and number are valid is a gentle form of mistake-proofing.

Undo, the best friend of users: Forcing functions can be annoying if overused, so for most everyday actions the best tool is undo. If an action can be reversed, people can explore without fear. Gmail-style 'Undo send' for a few seconds, a deleted file going to the recycle bin instead of vanishing, or 'Message deleted, Undo' at the bottom of the screen all let users recover from slips quickly. Where undo is impossible, such as a money transfer that has already left the account, the design should place a clear review step before the point of no return.

Confirmations and their overuse: A confirmation dialog asks 'Are you sure?' before an action. It seems safe, but it has a weakness: people confirm automatically. If every action asks for confirmation, users learn to tap Yes without reading, and the dialog no longer protects anything. Confirmations work best when they are rare, reserved for actions that are destructive and hard to undo, and when they repeat the important details: 'Send 5,000 taka to 01711-XXXXXX (Karim)? This cannot be undone.' A confirmation that shows details gives the user a real chance to catch a mistake, not just a habit to click through.

Good error messages: When an error does happen, the message is part of the design. A good error message says what went wrong in plain language, why it happened if useful, and how to fix it. It is polite and never blames the user. It appears near the problem, for example under the field that needs fixing. It keeps the user's work, so they do not have to type everything again. Compare 'Invalid input' with 'The mobile number should have 11 digits starting with 01. You entered 10 digits.' The second tells the user exactly what to do.

The Swiss cheese model: In big systems such as hospitals and airlines, serious accidents rarely have one cause. The psychologist James Reason described the Swiss cheese model: each layer of defence (design, training, procedures, checks) is like a slice of Swiss cheese with holes. Usually the holes do not line up, so an error passing through one hole is stopped by the next slice. An accident happens when holes in many slices line up at the same moment. The lesson for designers: do not rely on a single defence, and do not blame the last person in the chain. Add several layers, such as constraints, feedback, review steps and undo.

Real-life example 1, a medicine dose: Imagine DaktarDekhao adds a feature where doctors type prescriptions. A doctor types '10' in the dose field meaning 1.0 mg, but the decimal point is missed, a classic slip. Designing for error: the dose field shows the unit next to it, the system checks the dose against a normal range for that medicine and shows a warning when it is far above it, and the pharmacist sees the same warning. Three slices of cheese, not one.

Real-life example 2, mobile money to the wrong number: A very common error in Bangladesh is sending money to a wrong number by mistyping one digit. Designs that help include showing the receiver's registered name before the final confirmation, suggesting recent contacts so people do not type the full number, and making the final review screen show the number in large digits. These turn a silent slip into a visible one that the user can catch before it is too late.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often mix up slips and mistakes. Ask: was the goal right? If yes and the action went wrong, it is a slip. If the goal or plan was wrong, it is a mistake. Another error is to think confirmations solve everything; overused, they solve nothing. Exams ask: define slips and mistakes with examples; explain capture, description-similarity and mode errors; explain the three forcing functions (interlock, lock-in, lockout); describe the Swiss cheese model; list properties of good error messages.

Recap: Errors are normal and mostly come from how human minds work. Slips are wrong actions toward a right goal; mistakes are wrong goals or plans. Slip types include capture, description-similarity, mode errors and memory lapses; mistakes can be rule-based, knowledge-based or memory-lapse. Design for error by preventing it (constraints, forcing functions, poka-yoke), making it visible (feedback, review steps) and making recovery easy (undo, good error messages). Use confirmations sparingly and with details. Think in layers, like Swiss cheese, not one perfect wall.
key_points: Errors are normal; design should make them less likely, easy to notice and easy to recover from.
A slip is a wrong action toward a correct goal; a mistake is a wrong goal or plan carried out correctly.
Slip types include capture slips, description-similarity slips, mode errors and memory-lapse slips.
Mistakes can be rule-based, knowledge-based or memory-lapse; they are fixed with better conceptual models and information.
Forcing functions make errors impossible: interlock (order), lock-in (keep active), lockout (block entry).
Undo is the most user-friendly protection; confirmations should be rare and repeat key details.
Reason's Swiss cheese model: accidents happen when holes in several defence layers line up, so build multiple layers.
lessons.tip: When you meet any error, ask yourself one question: was the goal right? That single question sorts slips from mistakes, and from there the correct design fix follows almost automatically.
lessons.task: Look through your phone for one action that cannot be undone (for example deleting a chat, sending money or uninstalling an app). Write how the app protects you: is there a forcing function, a confirmation with details, or undo? Sketch an improved version that would catch a one-digit or wrong-person slip.

quiz.q: You meant to tap Save but tapped Delete, which sits right next to it in the same colour. What kind of error is this?
quiz.explain: The goal was right, the action hit a similar-looking target. That is a description-similarity slip; make the targets look different and separate them.

quiz.q: A user types a whole message while the keyboard is in the wrong language. What is the best design fix?
options: Ask 'Are you sure?' before every message
Make the current mode clearly visible, such as a language indicator
quiz.explain: This is a mode error. Showing the current mode clearly, or avoiding modes, is the standard fix.

quiz.q: A microwave will not start while its door is open. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: An interlock forces operations to happen in the right order: close the door first, then heat.

quiz.q: Why do frequent 'Are you sure?' dialogs often fail to prevent errors?
options: People learn to confirm automatically without reading
They make the app run slower
They are not allowed on mobile phones
They always show too many details
quiz.explain: When confirmations appear for everything, users click Yes by habit. Confirmations should be rare and show important details.

quiz.q: What does James Reason's Swiss cheese model teach designers?
options: Use one strong defence instead of many weak ones
Accidents happen when holes in several defence layers line up, so use multiple layers
Most accidents have exactly one cause
quiz.explain: Each layer has holes; an accident passes through when they align. Several independent layers make that unlikely, and blaming the last person misses the system.

lessons.title: Usability and User Experience
lessons.content:
Imagine two rice cookers in a shop in New Market. Both cook rice perfectly. The first has one switch and one light: press down to cook, it clicks up when the rice is done. The second has a panel of fourteen buttons with English abbreviations and a manual of forty pages. Both are useful, because both cook rice. But one is far more usable. And if the first also looks nice on your kitchen shelf, plays a gentle tune when the rice is ready and has never burned a single pot, people will love it and tell their neighbours. That is the difference between usefulness, usability and user experience, and this lesson makes those words precise.

Why we need precise words: People say 'this app is easy' or 'this app is bad' all the time, but those words are too vague to design with or to test. A design team needs to agree what 'good' means before they start, and they need to measure whether they reached it. HCI gives us definitions and goals that can be turned into numbers, so 'easy to use' becomes something like 'nine out of ten first-time users can book a serial in under three minutes without help'.

The ISO definition of usability: The international standard ISO 9241-11 defines usability as the extent to which a system, product or service can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use. Every phrase matters. Specified users means usability is always for someone: an app usable for a university student may not be usable for an elderly farmer. Specified goals means it is for some task. Context of use means where, with what device, under what conditions: in a quiet office, or on a crowded bus with one hand and weak signal.

Effectiveness: Effectiveness is the accuracy and completeness with which users achieve their goals. Can they actually do the task, and is the result correct? It is usually measured by task completion rate: if 20 users try to book a serial and 17 succeed, the completion rate is 85 percent. Errors also count: a user who books the wrong doctor did not achieve the goal, even though they finished the flow.

Efficiency: Efficiency is about the resources spent to achieve the goal: time, effort, number of steps, mental load. It is often measured as time on task, or as the number of taps or screens needed. Two designs can both be fully effective, but if one needs 12 taps and 90 seconds and the other needs 5 taps and 30 seconds, the second is more efficient. Efficiency matters most for frequent tasks: saving 10 seconds on a task done 100 times a day saves more than 16 minutes daily.

Satisfaction: Satisfaction is the user's comfort with and attitude toward the system: did it feel pleasant, frustrating, trustworthy, stressful? It is subjective, so we measure it by asking users, often with standard questionnaires such as the System Usability Scale, which we will calculate in the usability testing lesson. A system can be effective and efficient yet unsatisfying, for example if it feels cold, rude or untrustworthy.

A small worked comparison: Ten users test two versions of a recharge screen. With version A, 7 users finish correctly, taking on average 80 seconds, and rate it 3 out of 5 for comfort. With version B, 9 users finish correctly in an average of 45 seconds and rate it 4 out of 5. Version B wins on all three measures: effectiveness (90 percent against 70 percent), efficiency (45 against 80 seconds) and satisfaction (4 against 3). Real results are rarely this clean; often one version is faster but causes more errors, and the team must decide which measure matters most for these users.

Nielsen's five quality components: Jakob Nielsen describes usability through five components that are easy to remember. Learnability: how easy is it for users to do basic tasks the first time they meet the design? Efficiency: once users have learned it, how quickly can they perform tasks? Memorability: when users return after a period of not using it, how easily can they re-establish proficiency? Errors: how many errors do users make, how severe are they, and how easily can they recover? Satisfaction: how pleasant is it to use? Notice how learnability and memorability are about time: the first day, and coming back after a month. An app for paying the yearly university fee must be very memorable, because people use it once a year.

Usability goals in textbooks: The popular textbook Interaction Design by Rogers, Sharp and Preece lists six usability goals, close to Nielsen's list: effective to use, efficient to use, safe to use (protecting users from dangerous errors), having good utility (providing the right functions), easy to learn and easy to remember how to use. Each goal can be turned into a question for a design: 'Is it safe? What happens if the user taps Pay twice?' or 'Does it have good utility? Can the user actually cancel a booking, or is that function missing?'

Utility and usability: Nielsen points out that usefulness has two parts. Utility asks whether the design provides the features users need. Usability asks how easy and pleasant those features are to use. A product needs both. A beautiful, easy app that cannot do what users need has usability but no utility. A powerful app full of features that nobody can figure out has utility but poor usability. Both end up unused. In short: useful = utility + usability.

From usability to user experience: Usability focuses on getting tasks done. User experience is broader. ISO 9241-210 describes UX as the user's perceptions and responses that result from the use or anticipated use of a system, product or service. 'Anticipated use' is important: UX starts before you touch the product, with its reputation, its advertisement and the first impression in the app store, and continues after use, with support, updates and memories. UX includes emotions such as trust, pride, fun, frustration and anxiety.

User experience goals: Rogers, Sharp and Preece separate usability goals from user experience goals. Desirable UX goals include satisfying, enjoyable, engaging, pleasurable, exciting, entertaining, helpful, motivating, supportive of creativity, cognitively stimulating, fun and rewarding. Undesirable ones include boring, frustrating, annoying, childish, unpleasant, patronising and making one feel guilty. Some goals conflict with usability goals. A game should be challenging, which is not 'efficient'. A meditation app may slow you down on purpose. So the team must choose which goals matter for this product and these users.

Pragmatic and hedonic qualities: The researcher Marc Hassenzahl describes two kinds of product qualities. Pragmatic quality is about getting things done: is it practical, clear, efficient? Hedonic quality is about the self: is it stimulating, does it let me express who I am, does it feel good? A mobile wallet needs high pragmatic quality first. A photo-editing app for young people also needs high hedonic quality, or they will move to a cooler app even if the old one works fine.

The UX honeycomb: Peter Morville proposed a simple picture called the user experience honeycomb, with seven qualities. Useful: does it meet a real need? Usable: is it easy to use? Desirable: do people want it, through brand, image and emotional design? Findable: can users find the product and find content within it? Accessible: can people with disabilities use it? Credible: do users trust and believe it? Valuable: does it deliver value to the users and to the organisation paying for it? The honeycomb is a handy checklist for discussions, though it is not a measurement tool.

A quick recap of golden rules: In System Analysis and Design you met Shneiderman's eight golden rules: consistency, universal usability, informative feedback, dialogs that yield closure, error prevention, easy reversal, keeping users in control, and reducing short-term memory load. They are practical guidelines that serve the usability goals above: consistency helps learnability and memorability, error prevention and reversal serve safety, and feedback and closure serve satisfaction. We will meet a related list, Nielsen's ten heuristics, in the evaluation part of this course.

Measurable usability requirements: Goals become useful when they become measurable. A usability requirement states a user group, a task, a context and a target. For DaktarDekhao: 'At least 80 percent of first-time users aged 50 and above, using their own Android phone, can book a serial within 3 minutes without help.' 'Returning users can book a repeat serial in under 30 seconds.' 'Fewer than 2 percent of bookings are for the wrong date.' 'The average SUS score in testing is at least 75.' Each statement can be tested and passed or failed. Vague goals like 'user-friendly' cannot.

Trade-offs: Usability goals sometimes pull in different directions. Security wants long passwords and two-step verification; efficiency wants fewer steps. Learnability likes big buttons and simple menus; experts want shortcuts and dense screens. Good design looks for clever answers, such as fingerprint login for both security and speed, or a simple default with hidden shortcuts for experts, and when trade-offs are unavoidable, it decides using the priorities of the main user group.

Real-life example 1, a university result portal: Thousands of students check results on the same day. Effectiveness: can every student find their result with roll number and registration number? Efficiency: can they do it in a few taps even on a slow phone connection? Memorability: students use it twice a year, so the flow must be obvious each time. Satisfaction and UX: a portal that crashes on result day creates stress and anger, no matter how good it is on other days. The context of use, a spike of users on mobile data, is part of usability.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet: For a mobile wallet, the most important goals are effectiveness and safety: money must go to the right person, and errors must be rare and recoverable. Efficiency matters for frequent users who send money daily. Credibility in the honeycomb is huge: if the app looks unprofessional or messages are unclear, people fear losing money and will not trust it. Hedonic qualities like cashback animations may add delight, but they must never hide important information like fees.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A common mistake is to treat usability as a single feeling rather than measurable components. Another is to forget the 'specified users and context' in the ISO definition and claim a product is usable in general. Students also confuse UX with UI, or think UX goals are always compatible with usability goals. Exams often ask: give the ISO 9241-11 definition and explain its three measures; list Nielsen's five components; distinguish usability goals from UX goals with examples; explain utility vs usability; write measurable usability requirements for a given system.

Recap: Usability, by ISO 9241-11, is about specified users achieving specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context. Nielsen describes it with learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction. Usefulness needs both utility and usability. UX is wider, covering perceptions and emotions before, during and after use, with goals like enjoyable or trustworthy, and pragmatic and hedonic qualities. Turn goals into measurable requirements, accept trade-offs wisely, and let the main users decide priorities. Next we look at the process that puts users at the centre of design.
key_points: ISO 9241-11: usability is the extent to which specified users achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
Effectiveness is accuracy and completeness, efficiency is resources spent, satisfaction is comfort and attitude.
Nielsen's five components: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction.
Useful = utility (right features) + usability (easy and pleasant to use).
UX is broader than usability: perceptions and emotions before, during and after use.
Pragmatic quality is about getting things done; hedonic quality is about stimulation and identity.
Good usability goals are measurable: user group, task, context and a numeric target.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write a design goal, try to add a number and a user group to it. 'Easy to use' becomes 'eight of ten first-time users finish in two minutes'. This habit impresses examiners and real clients alike.
lessons.task: Choose one app you use and write five measurable usability requirements for it, one each for learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction. Each must name the user group, the task and a number.

quiz.q: Which three measures appear in the ISO 9241-11 definition of usability?
quiz.explain: ISO 9241-11 defines usability with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction for specified users, goals and context.

quiz.q: An app for paying a yearly fee is used once a year. Which of Nielsen's components is especially important?
quiz.explain: Memorability is how easily returning users can use it again after a long break, critical for rarely used systems.

quiz.q: A beautiful, easy app lacks the one function users need. What does it lack?
quiz.explain: Utility is whether the design provides the needed features. Usefulness requires both utility and usability.

quiz.q: Which is a measurable usability requirement?
options: 80 percent of first-time users aged 50+ can book a serial within 3 minutes without help
quiz.explain: It names the users, task, condition and numeric target, so it can be tested and passed or failed.

quiz.q: Which statement about user experience is correct?
options: UX covers only the visual design of screens
UX includes perceptions and responses before, during and after use, including emotions
UX is the same as the ISO definition of usability
UX goals never conflict with usability goals
quiz.explain: ISO 9241-210 includes anticipated use, and UX covers emotions like trust and fun. Some UX goals, like challenge in games, conflict with efficiency.

lessons.title: The User-Centred Design Process
lessons.content:
Think about how a good tailor in Dhaka makes a shirt. First they take your measurements and ask what the shirt is for: office, wedding or daily wear. They cut the cloth, then call you for a trial fitting with the stitches still loose. You try it on, they notice the shoulders are tight and the sleeves too long, they adjust, and you try again. Only when it fits do they finish the final stitching. Nobody thinks this is wasteful. Yet many software teams do the opposite: they guess what users want, build the whole product, release it, and only then discover it does not fit. User-centred design is the tailor's method applied to interactive systems.

What user-centred design is: User-centred design (UCD), also called human-centred design, is an approach in which the needs, abilities and context of the real users drive every stage of the design, and in which designs are tested with users and improved repeatedly. It is not a single technique; it is a process and a mindset. The opposite is technology-centred or designer-centred design, where the team builds what is technically convenient or what they personally like, and users must adapt.

Why design must be iterative: There are three simple reasons. First, users cannot fully describe what they need until they see something concrete; a sketch triggers comments that an interview never would. Second, designers are not the users and cannot predict how real people will react. Third, every design is full of assumptions, and the only way to find which are wrong is to test. So instead of one long straight line from requirements to release, UCD runs in loops: understand, design, test, learn, and repeat, each loop making the design fit better, just like the tailor's fittings.

Gould and Lewis's three principles: In 1985 John Gould and Clayton Lewis published three principles that still sum up UCD. One, early focus on users and tasks: understand who the users are and what they do, by studying them directly, not by guessing. Two, empirical measurement: early in development, have real users try simulations and prototypes, and observe and measure their performance and reactions. Three, iterative design: when problems are found, fix them, then test again; design, test, measure and redesign in a repeating cycle. Almost every modern process is a variation of these three ideas.

The ISO 9241-210 activities: The international standard ISO 9241-210 describes human-centred design for interactive systems. After planning the process, it has four linked activities. First, understand and specify the context of use: who the users are, their tasks, and their environment. Second, specify the user requirements, including usability goals. Third, produce design solutions that meet the requirements, from early concepts to detailed designs. Fourth, evaluate the designs against the requirements, with users. If the evaluation shows the design does not meet the requirements, the team goes back to whichever earlier activity is needed, and the cycle continues until it does.

ISO principles in plain words: The same standard lists principles behind the activities. The design is based on an explicit understanding of users, tasks and environments. Users are involved throughout design and development, not just at the start. The design is driven and refined by user-centred evaluation. The process is iterative. The design addresses the whole user experience, not just the screens. And the design team includes multidisciplinary skills and perspectives, such as researchers, designers, developers and domain experts.

Design thinking: Another popular way to describe the process is design thinking, made widely known by the design firm IDEO and the Stanford d.school. It is often drawn as five modes. Empathize: learn about users through observation and conversation. Define: turn what you learned into a clear problem statement focused on users' needs. Ideate: generate many possible solutions. Prototype: build quick, cheap versions of the best ideas. Test: try the prototypes with users and learn. The modes are not strictly in order; a test might send you back to empathize or define.

The double diamond: The UK Design Council introduced the double diamond in 2005 to describe the design process. It has four phases shaped like two diamonds side by side. Discover: open up and explore the problem broadly through research. Define: narrow down to a clear problem to solve. Develop: open up again, exploring many possible solutions. Deliver: narrow down, testing and refining until one solution is ready. The diamonds show an important rhythm: diverge (go wide and generate options), then converge (choose and focus). The first diamond is about designing the right thing; the second is about designing the thing right.

Diverging and converging, an example: Suppose the problem is 'patients miss their doctor serial'. Discover: the team visits a district hospital, talks to patients, nurses and the serial clerk, and finds many reasons: patients forget the date, they arrive too early and leave, they cannot read the paper slip, the doctor's timing changes. Define: they choose one focused problem, 'patients do not know when their turn is approaching'. Develop: they brainstorm SMS reminders, a live queue number on a screen, a voice call, a missed-call system. Deliver: they prototype two options, test with ten patients, and choose an SMS with a live queue position because it worked even on basic phones.

Involving users, how much: Users can take part in different ways. In informative involvement, they provide information through interviews and observation. In consultative involvement, they comment on designs made by the team. In participative design, also called co-design, users design together with the team as partners. Participatory design has strong roots in Scandinavia, where workers were involved in designing the systems they would use. More involvement gives better understanding and stronger ownership, but takes more time and requires careful facilitation.

UCD in the software development life cycle: In System Analysis and Design you studied the SDLC, and in Software Engineering you met waterfall and agile models. UCD is not a separate life cycle; it fits into them. In a waterfall project, the risk is that user research happens only at the start and user testing only at the end, when changes are expensive. A better approach is to do research and prototype testing during analysis and early design, so that requirements are validated before coding. In iterative and agile projects, UCD fits more naturally, because the product is built in small increments that can be tested.

Agile UX and dual-track work: In agile teams, a common pattern is dual-track development. One track, discovery, does research, sketches and prototype tests for upcoming features. The other track, delivery, builds and releases features that discovery has already validated. Discovery stays one or two sprints ahead of delivery. Lean UX, described by Jeff Gothelf, pushes the idea further: treat each design as a hypothesis, build the smallest thing that can test it, measure, and learn. The key point is the same as Gould and Lewis: test early, test often, learn from real users.

What each loop produces: It helps to know the outputs of each stage. Understanding the context produces research findings, personas, scenarios, task analyses and journey maps. Specifying requirements produces measurable usability goals and user requirements. Designing produces sketches, wireframes, prototypes, information architecture and visual designs. Evaluating produces lists of usability problems with severity, measured results and recommendations. In the following lessons we study each of these in detail.

A DaktarDekhao story: Let us follow the running example through one loop. Context: researchers visit an upazila health complex and observe patients, many elderly, some with low literacy, most with Android phones shared within the family. Requirements: 80 percent of first-time users aged 50 and above should book a serial in under 3 minutes without help; text must be in Bangla; the app must work on slow 2G or 3G connections. Design: the team sketches three home screen ideas on paper and builds a clickable prototype of the best one. Evaluation: six patients try it; four cannot find the doctor list because it is hidden under an icon with no label. Next loop: the icon gets a Bangla label and moves to the home screen, and the next test shows five of six succeed. The design is not finished, but each loop made it fit better.

Real-life example 1, redesigning a government service form: Many government services in Bangladesh have moved online. A UCD team improving such a form would start by watching citizens fill it in at an information centre, noting which fields cause confusion and which documents people do not have. They would rewrite labels in plain Bangla, cut unnecessary fields, prototype the new form, test it with people of different ages and education, and repeat. The result is fewer rejected applications and fewer trips to the office.

Real-life example 2, a startup's first product: A small startup wants to build an app for small grocery shops to track credit given to customers, the 'baki khata'. Instead of coding for six months, the team visits shops, notices that shopkeepers write in a notebook with one hand while serving customers, and that speed matters more than features. They test a paper prototype with three shopkeepers in a week. The feedback kills two planned features and adds a big 'add baki' button. Weeks of development are saved because they learned before building.

How long one loop takes: A loop does not have to be slow. Early in a project, a loop can take an afternoon: sketch three screens on paper, show them to three people in the canteen, and redraw. Later, a loop may take a sprint of one or two weeks: build a clickable prototype, run a formal test with five or six users, analyse the results and update the design. After release, a loop may use analytics and support complaints collected over a month. The fidelity and cost of each loop grow as the design becomes more certain, which keeps early mistakes cheap.

Common misunderstandings: UCD does not mean doing whatever users say. Users are experts on their own lives and problems, but not necessarily on solutions; designers interpret what they observe. UCD is not only for big companies; even one hallway test with three people is UCD. It is not a one-time phase at the start; it continues through the project. And it does not slow projects down overall; it moves the cost of discovering problems to the cheap early stages.

What exams ask: Typical questions: define user-centred design and contrast it with technology-centred design; state and explain Gould and Lewis's three principles; describe the activities of ISO 9241-210 with a diagram; explain the double diamond and the idea of diverging and converging; describe the five modes of design thinking; explain how UCD can be combined with agile development. Use a short worked example, like the serial-missing problem above, to show the loop in action.

Recap: User-centred design puts real users' needs, abilities and context at the centre and improves designs through repeated testing. Gould and Lewis summarised it as early focus on users and tasks, empirical measurement and iterative design. ISO 9241-210 describes four activities: understand the context, specify requirements, produce design solutions, and evaluate, looping until requirements are met. Design thinking and the double diamond describe the same spirit with diverge-converge rhythms. UCD fits inside waterfall or agile processes, best through early and continuous testing. Next lesson: how to understand users, starting with asking them good questions.
key_points: User-centred design lets real users' needs, abilities and context drive design, with repeated testing and improvement.
Design must be iterative because users react to concrete designs, designers are not users, and assumptions must be tested.
Gould and Lewis (1985): early focus on users and tasks, empirical measurement, iterative design.
ISO 9241-210 activities: understand the context of use, specify user requirements, produce design solutions, evaluate against requirements.
Design thinking modes: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test.
The double diamond (Design Council, 2005): discover, define, develop, deliver, alternating diverging and converging.
In agile teams, dual-track work keeps discovery (research and testing) a step ahead of delivery (building).
lessons.tip: Remember the tailor: measure, cut, fit, adjust, fit again. Whenever an exam asks about any design process model, you can explain it as a version of this loop, and then name the specific phases of the model asked.
lessons.task: Pick a small problem around you, such as students missing class notices. Draw the double diamond on paper and fill it: three things you would research in Discover, one problem statement in Define, at least five ideas in Develop, and how you would test the best one in Deliver.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Gould and Lewis's three principles?
options: Early focus on users and tasks
Complete all coding before involving users
quiz.explain: Gould and Lewis argued for involving users early, measuring with them, and iterating. Waiting until coding is done goes against all three.

quiz.q: In ISO 9241-210, what happens if evaluation shows the design does not meet the requirements?
options: The team iterates back to the needed earlier activity and continues
quiz.explain: The human-centred design activities form a loop; the team returns to understanding, requirements or design as needed until requirements are met.

quiz.q: In the double diamond, what does the first diamond mainly focus on?
options: Designing the right thing: discovering and defining the problem
quiz.explain: Discover and Define explore and then narrow the problem. The second diamond, Develop and Deliver, focuses on designing the thing right.

quiz.q: What is dual-track development in agile UX?
options: Two teams building the same feature in competition
Separate apps for Android and iOS
A discovery track researching and testing ideas ahead of a delivery track that builds validated features
Running tests only after both tracks finish
quiz.explain: Discovery stays a sprint or two ahead, so delivery builds features that have already been checked with users.

quiz.q: Which statement about user-centred design is correct?
options: It means doing exactly what users ask for
It only applies to large companies with labs
It is a one-time phase done before coding
Users are involved throughout, and designers interpret their needs rather than simply following requests
quiz.explain: Users are experts on their problems, not necessarily on solutions; UCD involves them throughout and designers interpret findings.

lessons.title: User Research I: Asking People
lessons.content:
Imagine you want to build an app that helps village patients book a doctor's serial at the district hospital. You sit in a cafe in Dhaka with your friends and decide: patients want online payment, a chat with the doctor and a dark mode. You build all of it. Three months later almost nobody in the village uses it. When you finally visit, you learn the real problem: people did not know which day the specialist doctor sits, and they travel two hours only to find the doctor absent. Nobody asked them. User research is the habit of finding out about real people before deciding what to build. This lesson is about the first family of methods: asking people.

What user research is: User research is the systematic study of the people who will use a product: who they are, what goals they have, what they do now, what problems they face, and in what context. It is not the same as asking people what features they want. People are experts on their own lives and problems, but they are usually not good at designing solutions. Henry Ford is often quoted as saying that customers would have asked for faster horses, though there is no reliable evidence he said it. The point still stands: research should uncover needs and behaviour, and designers then invent the solution.

How this differs from requirements gathering: In System Analysis and Design you learned interviews and questionnaires to collect system requirements: what data to store, what reports to print, what rules to follow. HCI research asks different questions. It looks at the person rather than the system: what are they trying to achieve in their life, what frustrates them, what do they already know, what words do they use, what devices and connections do they have, and when and where will they use our product? The techniques look similar, but the focus moves from 'what should the system do' to 'what is it like to be this user'.

Start with research questions: Good research starts with clear research questions, written before you talk to anyone. For DaktarDekhao they might be: How do patients currently find out when a doctor is available? Who in the family usually arranges a hospital visit? What phones and internet do they have? What makes them trust or distrust a booking? Research questions are for the team, not for participants. From them you write the actual questions you will ask, in plain language. Without research questions, interviews drift into friendly chats that produce nothing useful.

Qualitative and quantitative research: Qualitative research collects rich descriptions: stories, reasons, feelings, behaviour. It answers why and how, usually with a small number of people, such as eight to fifteen interviews. Quantitative research collects numbers: how many, how often, how much. It answers what and how many, usually with many people, such as a survey of three hundred users or analytics from thousands. Neither is better. Qualitative research tells you that elderly patients rely on their children to book; quantitative research tells you whether that is 10 percent of users or 60 percent. Good projects often use both: interviews to discover, a survey to measure.

Interviews, three types: A structured interview uses a fixed list of questions in a fixed order, like a spoken questionnaire. It is easy to compare answers but leaves no room to follow surprises. An unstructured interview is like a guided conversation around a topic, with very few prepared questions. It can uncover unexpected things but is hard to compare and needs a skilled interviewer. A semi-structured interview, the most common in HCI, has a prepared guide of main questions and topics but lets the interviewer change order, skip questions and ask follow-ups. It balances comparability with discovery.

Interviews, asking about real behaviour: The best interview questions ask about specific past experiences, not opinions about the future. 'Would you use an app to book a doctor?' invites a polite yes that means nothing. 'Tell me about the last time someone in your family went to the hospital. How did you decide which day to go?' produces a real story with details: who called whom, how long they waited, what went wrong. People are poor at predicting their own future behaviour but fairly good at describing what actually happened. A useful rule: ask about the past, observe the present, and be careful with the future.

Good questions and leading questions: A leading question pushes the participant toward an answer. 'Don't you find the hospital queue very frustrating?' suggests the expected answer. A neutral version is 'How was your experience of the queue?'. Avoid double-barrelled questions that ask two things at once, such as 'Was the app fast and easy?', because a person may think it was fast but not easy. Avoid jargon; say 'phone screen' not 'interface'. Use open questions that begin with how, what, tell me about, or walk me through, and then follow with probes: 'Why was that?', 'What happened next?', 'Can you show me?'. Silence is also a tool: wait a few seconds after an answer and people often add the most valuable detail.

Running an interview: Introduce yourself and the purpose in simple words, explain how long it will take, and ask for consent to take notes or record. Start with easy warm-up questions about the person's background. Move to the main topics, keep your guide visible but do not read it like an exam. Listen more than you talk; a good ratio is the participant speaking most of the time. End by asking 'Is there anything I should have asked but did not?', thank them, and give any promised compensation. Write a summary within a few hours while memory is fresh. Ideally one person asks and another takes notes.

Surveys: A survey or questionnaire collects answers from many people in a standard form, on paper, by phone or online. It is good for measuring how common something is, comparing groups, and tracking change over time. It is poor at explaining why. Question types include closed questions with fixed choices (single choice, multiple choice), rating scales, ranking questions and a few open text questions. Open questions are valuable but take long to analyse, so use them sparingly. Keep the survey short; every extra question reduces the number of people who finish.

Likert scales: A Likert scale, named after the psychologist Rensis Likert, asks how much a person agrees with a statement, usually on five or seven points, for example strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree. Write statements clearly and about one idea each. Keep the scale direction consistent, and label the points. A small worked example: twenty patients rate 'Booking a serial was easy' and the answers are 2 strongly disagree, 3 disagree, 5 neutral, 7 agree and 3 strongly agree. Ten of twenty, which is 50 percent, agree or strongly agree. Reporting the full distribution is better than only an average, because the five people who disagree may be exactly the elderly users the design is failing.

Sampling: You cannot ask everybody, so you ask a sample. The key question is whether the sample represents the people you care about. An online survey shared on Facebook will reach people who are online, young and comfortable with smartphones, and miss exactly the low-literacy, basic-phone users a hospital booking service must serve. That is sampling bias. Random sampling gives everyone in the population an equal chance; stratified sampling makes sure each important group, such as urban and rural, or young and old, is included in a planned share. For qualitative interviews you usually use purposive sampling: deliberately choosing people who differ in important ways.

Pilot testing: Before sending a survey to three hundred people, try it with three to five. A pilot shows confusing wording, missing answer options, questions in the wrong order, and how long it really takes. In Bangladesh it is also where you discover that a word you translated into formal Bangla is not understood, or that 'monthly income' makes people uncomfortable. Fixing a survey after it is sent is impossible; fixing it after a pilot is easy.

Focus groups: A focus group brings together about six to ten people with a moderator to discuss a topic for an hour or two. It is useful for hearing a range of opinions, the words people use, and how they react to each other's ideas. Its weakness is group dynamics: one confident person can dominate, and others may agree just to fit in. Focus groups tell you what people say in public, not what they do in private, so they should not be used to judge whether an interface is usable. For that we use usability testing.

Research ethics and consent: Research involves real people, so it carries responsibilities. Participants should give informed consent: they understand what the research is for, what will happen, how their data will be used, and that they can stop at any time without penalty. Protect privacy: store notes securely, remove names and phone numbers from reports, and never share recordings without permission. Be careful with vulnerable people, such as patients, children or people who may feel they cannot say no to an educated visitor from the city. Universities often require approval from an ethics committee before research with people. Pay or thank participants fairly for their time.

Biases to watch: Social desirability bias means people give answers that make them look good: they say they read terms and conditions or always check the receiver's number. Acquiescence bias means a tendency to agree with statements, especially toward a person seen as having higher status. Confirmation bias is the researcher's own trap: noticing only answers that support what you already believe. Defences include neutral questions, asking about specific past events, mixing statement directions, having two people analyse notes, and actively looking for evidence that you are wrong.

Real-life example 1, DaktarDekhao interviews: The team interviewed twelve people in a district town: patients, family members who book for elders, a hospital clerk and two doctors. Using semi-structured interviews about the last hospital visit, they found three patterns. Most bookings were made by a son, daughter or neighbour on behalf of an elderly patient. People mainly wanted to know whether the doctor would really be there that day. Many had smartphones but limited data packs. These findings changed the plan: booking for another person became a main feature, doctor availability went on the home screen, and the app was designed to work on slow connections.

Real-life example 2, a campus food survey: A student team wanted to build a canteen pre-order app at their university. Interviews with ten students suggested that long queues at lunch were the main pain. They then ran a short survey with 200 responses, stratified by department and year. It showed that queues mattered mostly between 1 pm and 2 pm and mostly to students with labs right after lunch.
