The final design focused on fast pre-ordering for a pickup time slot rather than a full menu catalogue. Qualitative discovery, then quantitative measurement.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes include asking users to design the solution, asking about the future instead of the past, using leading questions, surveying only easy-to-reach people, skipping the pilot and treating a focus group as a usability test. Exams often ask you to compare qualitative and quantitative research, explain structured, semi-structured and unstructured interviews, identify and rewrite leading or double-barrelled questions, explain Likert scales and sampling, and describe informed consent.

Recap: User research finds out about real users' goals, behaviour, problems and context before design decisions are made. Start with research questions. Use qualitative methods to discover why and quantitative methods to measure how many. Semi-structured interviews about specific past experiences are the workhorse of HCI. Surveys measure at scale but need clear, neutral questions, good sampling and a pilot. Focus groups show opinions, not usability. Always get informed consent, protect privacy and guard against bias. Next lesson: instead of asking people, we watch them.
key_points: User research studies real users' goals, behaviour, problems and context; it uncovers needs, not ready-made feature lists.
Write research questions first; turn them into plain-language questions for participants.
Qualitative research explains why and how with few people; quantitative research measures how many with many people.
Semi-structured interviews about specific past experiences are the most common HCI interview style.
Avoid leading, double-barrelled and jargon questions; use open questions, probes and silence.
Surveys need short, neutral questions, Likert scales used clearly, a representative sample and a pilot test.
Informed consent, privacy and awareness of social desirability, acquiescence and confirmation bias are essential.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write an interview question, check if it starts with 'Would you...'. If it does, rewrite it as 'Tell me about the last time you...'. That one habit will make your research far more honest.
lessons.task: Interview one family member for ten minutes about the last time they paid a bill or bought a ticket using their phone. Use only open questions and at least three probes. Afterwards, write the three most surprising things you learned and one question you asked that was accidentally leading, with a neutral rewrite.

quiz.q: Which interview question is most likely to give reliable information about real behaviour?
options: Would you use an app to book a doctor?
Don't you agree hospital queues are terrible?
Tell me about the last time your family visited the hospital. How did you choose the day?
Do you want online payment and chat in the app?
quiz.explain: Asking about a specific past event gives a real story. Questions about the future invite polite guesses, and the second option is leading.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between qualitative and quantitative research?
options: Qualitative uses computers, quantitative uses paper
Qualitative is always better than quantitative
Qualitative explains why and how with rich detail; quantitative measures how many with numbers
Quantitative is only used in medicine
quiz.explain: Qualitative research discovers reasons and behaviour from fewer people; quantitative research measures size and frequency from many people. Good projects often combine them.

quiz.q: 'Was the app fast and easy to use?' is a poor survey question because it is:
options: Double-barrelled: it asks two things at once
quiz.explain: Someone may find the app fast but not easy. Split it into two questions, one idea each.

quiz.q: An online survey shared only on Facebook will likely miss low-literacy basic-phone users. This problem is called:
quiz.explain: The sample does not represent the population the service must serve. Stratified or purposive sampling, and offline methods, help reach the missing groups.

quiz.q: Why should a focus group not be used to judge whether an interface is usable?
options: It shows what people say in a group, not how they actually use the interface
It is too expensive for any project
It always has only one participant
It is illegal in most countries
quiz.explain: Group dynamics shape opinions, and talking about a design is not the same as using it. Usability testing observes real use.

lessons.title: User Research II: Watching People
lessons.content:
Ask a shopkeeper in Kawran Bazar how he keeps track of what customers owe him, and he will say: 'I write it in my notebook.' Sit beside him for one busy morning, and you will see much more. He writes some debts in the notebook, keeps others in his head for regular customers, scribbles a few on the back of cigarette packets, asks his son to remember the rest, and checks his mobile wallet history to see who paid. None of this came out in the interview, not because he lied, but because people do not notice their own habits. That is why the second family of research methods does not ask. It watches.

Why watching matters: There is a well-known gap between what people say and what people do. When we describe our work, we give a tidy, idealised version. We forget workarounds, sticky notes, small tricks and interruptions, because they feel too ordinary to mention. Yet those are exactly the details a designer needs. Observation shows the real tasks, the real environment, the real tools people combine and the real problems they have learned to live with. A good rule from the last lesson was 'ask about the past, observe the present'. This lesson is about observing the present.

Direct observation: In direct observation the researcher watches people as they do their normal activities, in their normal place, and takes notes. It can be done as a passive 'fly on the wall', where the researcher stays quiet and tries not to influence anything, or as participant observation, where the researcher joins in, for example helping at the pharmacy counter for a day to feel the pressure from inside. Notes should record what happens, when, with what tools, who else is involved, and what goes wrong, separating facts ('she checked the shelf twice') from interpretations ('she seemed unsure of the stock').

The observer effect: People behave differently when they know they are being watched. This is often called the Hawthorne effect, after studies at a factory called the Hawthorne Works in the United States in the 1920s and 1930s, though researchers still debate how strong the original effect was. In practice: people may work more carefully, follow official rules they normally skip, or hide workarounds. Ways to reduce it include observing for longer so people get used to you, being friendly and non-judgemental, explaining that you are studying the system and not judging them, and focusing on what people do repeatedly rather than on the first few minutes.

Indirect observation: In indirect observation you study traces of behaviour instead of watching live. Examples include photos of a workspace, the notebook where the shopkeeper writes debts, screenshots users share, call centre complaint logs, or the paper forms the hospital clerk fills. These artefacts tell stories: a form with handwritten notes in the margin shows fields that are missing; a printed notice taped on a machine shows that the machine's interface failed to explain something.

What to look for: Beginners often watch and see nothing, because everything looks normal. A simple checklist helps. One common checklist is called AEIOU: Activities (what people are doing, step by step), Environments (the place, noise, light, space), Interactions (between people, and between people and things), Objects (the tools, papers, phones and devices in use) and Users (who is present and what roles they play). Also watch for breakdowns: moments of hesitation, repeated actions, errors, questions to a colleague, and workarounds such as a sticky note with a password or a calculator beside a computer that already calculates. Every workaround is a sign that the current design does not fully support the work.

Contextual inquiry, what it is: Contextual inquiry is a field method developed by Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt as part of their Contextual Design approach. It combines observation and interviewing: the researcher goes to the user's real place of work or life, watches them do real tasks, and asks questions while the work happens. A session usually lasts one to two hours with one person. It is one of the most powerful methods in HCI because it captures both what people do and why they do it, in the moment, when memory is not an issue.

The master-apprentice model: The heart of contextual inquiry is a relationship idea. The user is the master and the researcher is the apprentice. An apprentice learning a craft does not hand out a questionnaire; they watch the master work, ask 'why did you do that?', and try to understand the reasoning. This model puts the user in the expert position, which makes people comfortable and makes them explain details they would never mention in an interview room. The researcher does not lecture, demonstrate or suggest solutions.

Four principles of contextual inquiry: Beyer and Holtzblatt describe four principles. Context: go to the place where the work happens and observe ongoing work, not summaries. Partnership: the user and researcher explore the work together, with the user guiding and the researcher asking. Interpretation: the researcher shares their understanding during the session ('So you check the wallet history because customers often say they paid?'), and the user confirms or corrects it, so interpretations are tested on the spot. Focus: the researcher has a clear project focus that guides what to pay attention to, without closing their eyes to surprises.

Running a contextual inquiry: A session typically has four parts. First a short conventional interview: introductions, consent, and an overview of the person's work. Then the transition: explain that now you will watch and they should work as usual and talk about what they are doing. Then the main contextual interview: observe, ask small questions at natural pauses, note artefacts and take photos with permission. Finally a wrap-up: summarise what you learned and let the user correct you. After the session, the team writes up notes the same day.

Ethnography in brief: Ethnography comes from anthropology. It means spending a long time, often weeks or months, living or working among a group to understand their culture and practices from the inside. Full ethnography is rare in product teams because it is slow, but lighter versions, sometimes called rapid or design ethnography, are common: a few days in a village health centre or a garment factory can reveal social rules that shape technology use. For example, who in the household controls the phone, or whether women prefer to ask a female health worker rather than use an app.

Diary studies: Some behaviour is spread over days or weeks and happens when no researcher is present. In a diary study participants record their experiences over a period, for example one entry each time they try to book a doctor or each evening for two weeks. Entries can be written, voice notes, photos or short messages in a chat app. Diary studies capture real moments, changing feelings and rare events. Their weaknesses: people forget to write, entries become shorter over time, and writing is hard for low-literacy participants, so voice notes or photos often work better in Bangladesh. Gentle daily reminders and a short end interview help.

Analytics and logs: Once a product exists, it can watch its own users at scale. Analytics record events such as screens opened, buttons tapped, time spent, errors shown and where people leave. A funnel shows how many users pass each step of a flow. Worked example: in DaktarDekhao's booking flow, 1,000 users open the doctor list, 600 pick a doctor, 450 pick a time slot, but only 180 finish payment. The biggest drop is between slot and payment: 270 of 450, which is 60 percent, leave at that step. Analytics tell you where the problem is and how big it is; they do not tell you why. You then use interviews or usability testing on that step.

Combining methods, triangulation: Each method has blind spots. Interviews capture reasons but not real behaviour; observation captures behaviour but only for a few people; analytics capture many people but not reasons. Triangulation means using more than one method and checking whether they point in the same direction. If interviews say 'payment is confusing', analytics show a 60 percent drop at payment, and observation shows people looking for a cash option, you can be confident.

Making sense of data, affinity diagrams: After research, a team may have hundreds of notes. An affinity diagram turns them into insight. The method is often traced to the Japanese anthropologist Jiro Kawakita, and is also called the KJ method. Steps: write each single observation on its own sticky note or digital card; put all notes on a wall; group notes that feel related, without starting from predefined categories; name each group with a short sentence in the user's voice, such as 'I don't know if the doctor will come'; then group the groups into bigger themes. The result shows patterns across many people instead of memorable single stories.

From findings to insights: A finding is something you observed: 'seven of twelve people booked on behalf of someone else'. An insight explains what it means for design: 'the real user is often a family helper, so booking must handle the patient and the booker as different people'. Good research reports present a few strong insights, each backed by evidence such as quotes, photos and numbers, and each linked to design implications. Insights then feed personas and scenarios, which are the topic of the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, a pharmacy counter: A team designing stock software for small pharmacies did contextual inquiry at three shops. They noticed staff repeatedly asked customers to show the empty medicine strip, because names are hard to spell and many medicines have similar names. Nobody had mentioned it in interviews. The design added search by barcode and by photo of the strip, and showed medicine images in results. One afternoon of watching changed a core feature.

Real-life example 2, a garment worker's phone: Researchers interested in how factory workers use mobile wallets ran a two-week diary study with voice notes, then visited some participants at home. They found that one phone was often shared by several family members, PINs were shared within the family, and money was often sent home to the village right after payday. The resulting design ideas focused on clear transaction histories and safer sharing, not on fancy features. Watching and listening over time revealed the real context.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes are observing only a few minutes, mixing facts and interpretations in notes, teaching users the 'right way' during observation, relying on analytics alone, and presenting single stories instead of patterns. Exams often ask: why observation is needed when interviews exist; the four principles and the master-apprentice model of contextual inquiry; direct versus indirect observation; the Hawthorne effect; strengths and weaknesses of diary studies and analytics; and the steps of building an affinity diagram.

Recap: People cannot fully describe their own behaviour, so we watch. Direct observation shows real work, indirect observation reads its traces. Contextual inquiry combines watching and asking in the user's real context, using the master-apprentice relationship and the principles of context, partnership, interpretation and focus. Ethnography goes deep into culture; diary studies capture behaviour over time; analytics measure behaviour at scale and show where problems are. Triangulate methods, then turn many notes into insights with an affinity diagram. Next: turning those insights into personas, scenarios and journey maps.
key_points: People do not notice their own habits, so observation reveals behaviour that interviews miss.
Direct observation watches work live; indirect observation studies traces such as forms, notes and logs.
The Hawthorne or observer effect: people act differently when watched; longer, friendly observation reduces it.
Contextual inquiry (Beyer and Holtzblatt) uses the master-apprentice model and four principles: context, partnership, interpretation, focus.
Diary studies capture behaviour over days or weeks; voice notes and photos help low-literacy participants.
Analytics and funnels show where and how many users struggle, but not why; triangulate with other methods.
Affinity diagrams (KJ method) group single observations bottom-up into themes that become design insights.
lessons.tip: Keep two columns in your observation notes: 'What I saw' and 'What I think it means'. Mixing them is the most common research mistake, and separating them makes your later analysis far more trustworthy.
lessons.task: Watch a family member or shopkeeper for 20 minutes while they do a routine task with a phone or register, with their permission. Write at least 15 single observations, one per small slip of paper. Then group them on a table into an affinity diagram and name each group in the person's own words.

quiz.q: In contextual inquiry, what is the relationship between user and researcher?
options: Teacher and student, with the researcher teaching
Master and apprentice, with the user as the master
quiz.explain: The user is the expert of their work; the researcher learns like an apprentice by watching and asking why.

quiz.q: Which is an example of indirect observation?
options: Sitting beside a clerk while she serves customers
Joining shop work for a day
Studying the margin notes written on a hospital's paper forms
quiz.explain: Indirect observation studies traces of behaviour, such as artefacts, logs and forms, rather than watching live.

quiz.q: In a funnel, 450 users choose a time slot and 180 finish payment. What share of them drop at payment?
quiz.explain: 450 minus 180 is 270 users who leave; 270 divided by 450 is 0.6, which is 60 percent.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building an affinity diagram?
options: Write each single observation on its own note
Decide the final categories before reading the data
Calculate the average of all answers
quiz.explain: Affinity diagramming is bottom-up: one observation per note, then group related notes, then name and group the groups.

quiz.q: Why should analytics be combined with interviews or testing?
options: Analytics show where and how many users struggle, but not why
quiz.explain: Analytics measure behaviour at scale but cannot explain the reasons; qualitative methods fill that gap. This is triangulation.

lessons.title: Personas, Scenarios and Journeys
lessons.content:
After two weeks of research, the DaktarDekhao team has a wall full of sticky notes, forty pages of interview summaries, a funnel chart and dozens of photos. In the design meeting someone says, 'Users want a fast booking.' Another says, 'No, users are old and need big buttons.' A third says, 'Users are students like us.' Everyone talks about 'the user', but each person imagines someone different, usually someone like themselves. The research is wasted if it cannot be carried into decisions. Personas, scenarios, user stories and journey maps are tools that turn research into shared, concrete pictures of who we design for and what they go through.

The elastic user problem: Alan Cooper, a software designer who popularised personas in his 1999 book The Inmates Are Running the Asylum, pointed out a problem he called the elastic user. When a team says 'the user', the word stretches to fit whatever each person wants to argue. A developer who wants to add a feature imagines a power user; a manager who wants to cut it imagines a beginner. Without a specific, agreed picture of the user, every debate becomes opinion against opinion. A persona fixes the picture.

What a persona is: A persona is a fictional but realistic description of a typical user, built from research data. It has a name, a photo or sketch, a short background, and most importantly goals, behaviours, frustrations, skills and context. It is not a real person, and it is not a demographic summary like 'women aged 25 to 40'. It is a single believable character that represents a pattern found in many real people. Teams then ask, 'Would Rahima understand this screen?' instead of 'Would users understand this?'.

A worked persona for DaktarDekhao: Persona 1, Rahima Begum, 52, lives in a village near a district town, a homemaker who studied up to class five. Goals: see the heart specialist without wasting a day's travel; not depend on others for every visit. Behaviours: uses a basic smartphone mainly for voice calls and watching videos; reads Bangla slowly; asks her son for anything 'complicated'. Frustrations: travelled twice to find the specialist absent; confused by English words on forms. Context: shares a phone data pack with family, weak signal at home. A short quote captures her voice: 'I just want to know the doctor is there before I leave home.'

Goals are the core: The most important part of a persona is its goals, because design is about helping people reach them. Cooper distinguished life goals (what kind of person I want to be), experience goals (how I want to feel, for example not stupid, not anxious) and end goals (what I want to get done, for example book a serial for Tuesday). End goals drive most interface decisions, while experience goals guide tone, reassurance and feedback. Rahima's experience goal 'not feel stupid' tells the team to avoid jargon and to confirm every step clearly.

Building personas from data: Personas come out of research, step by step. First, list the behaviour variables you saw in the data, such as who makes the booking (self or helper), phone skill (low to high), reading comfort in Bangla, and distance from the hospital. Second, place each interviewed person along each variable. Third, look for people who cluster together on several variables at once; a cluster of helpers who are young, phone-confident and book for several relatives is a pattern. Fourth, write one persona per strong pattern, borrowing real quotes and details from the people in that cluster. Finally, check the personas with the research team: does each one feel like people we actually met?

What to avoid in personas: A persona built in a meeting without research is just stereotypes with a name. Common problems are irrelevant details (favourite colour, a long life story) that do not affect design, too many personas so that none is really used, and personas that nobody looks at after the first week. Good personas are based on research patterns, short enough to fit on one page, focused on behaviour and goals, and displayed where the team works.

Primary, secondary and negative personas: A product usually has three to five personas, but one should be the primary persona: the person the main interface is designed for, whose needs must be satisfied. Secondary personas are mostly satisfied by the primary design but need a few additions. A negative persona describes someone the product is deliberately not designed for. For DaktarDekhao, Rahima might be secondary, because the research showed most bookings are made by helpers. Persona 2, Sabbir, 24, Rahima's son, a college student in the district town with a mid-range Android phone, who books for his mother, grandfather and neighbours. If the design works for Sabbir booking for several people, and also lets Rahima check her serial in big Bangla text, both are served. A negative persona might be a private clinic manager wanting full hospital management software.

Empathy maps: An empathy map is a quick visual tool for summarising what we know about a user type. A sheet is divided into four areas: Says (direct quotes), Thinks (what they might be thinking but not saying), Does (actions and behaviours) and Feels (emotions and worries). Often pains and gains are added below. For Rahima: Says 'I'll ask my son'; Thinks 'I might press something wrong and lose money'; Does travels two hours by bus and easy-bike; Feels anxious and tired. Empathy maps are fast to build in a workshop and help a team align before writing full personas.

Scenarios: A scenario is a short story describing a persona using, or trying to use, a product to reach a goal in a specific situation. Stories are powerful because they include context, motivation, time pressure and emotion, which lists of features do not. Mary Beth Rosson and John Carroll, in their scenario-based design approach, distinguish problem scenarios, which describe how people do the task today with its difficulties, and activity scenarios, which describe how the same task could be done with the new design. Later scenarios can add more interface detail.

A problem scenario: On Sunday evening Rahima's chest feels tight again. She asks Sabbir to arrange a visit to the heart specialist. Sabbir calls the hospital number three times; nobody answers. On Monday he asks a neighbour who heard the specialist sits on Tuesdays. Rahima and her husband leave at seven in the morning, reach the hospital at nine, and wait in a long queue for a ticket, only to learn the specialist is at a conference this week. They return home tired and two hundred taka poorer. Notice that this scenario mentions no app at all; it shows the real problem.

An activity scenario: On Sunday evening Sabbir opens DaktarDekhao, switches the patient to 'Amma', and taps Heart. He sees that the specialist sits on Tuesday and Thursday, and that Tuesday shows 'Doctor confirmed present'. He books Tuesday's serial 14, expected time around 10:30, and the app sends an SMS in Bangla to Rahima's phone. On Tuesday morning at seven, before they leave, Rahima receives another SMS: 'Doctor present today, your serial is 14.' This scenario now contains design ideas, such as booking for family members, confirmed presence and SMS to a basic phone, without describing any screen yet.

User stories: In agile teams, needs are often written as user stories: short statements in the form 'As a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some reason]'. For example: 'As a family helper, I want to book serials for several family members from my account so that I don't need separate phones for each.' User stories are smaller than scenarios and are used for planning work. A common checklist for good stories is INVEST, from Bill Wake: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. Stories should come from personas and scenarios, not from guesses.

Acceptance criteria: Each user story needs acceptance criteria: conditions that must be true for the story to be done. A popular format is Given, When, Then. Given a helper has added two patients, when he books a serial, then he must choose which patient the serial is for, and the confirmation SMS goes to that patient's phone number. Acceptance criteria turn fuzzy wishes into testable statements, which helps designers, developers and testers agree.

Customer journey maps: A journey map shows the whole experience of a persona over time, across many touchpoints, not only inside the app. Columns are stages, for example Notice symptoms, Find doctor, Book, Travel, Wait, Consultation, Follow-up. Rows typically include actions (what the person does), touchpoints (where they interact: phone call, app, SMS, hospital counter, bus), thoughts, an emotion curve that rises and falls, pain points, and opportunities. A journey map often reveals that the worst moments are outside the screen, such as uncertainty while travelling, which the app could reduce with an SMS.

Reading a journey map, a worked example: Suppose the team rates Rahima's emotion at each stage from minus 2 (very bad) to plus 2 (very good): Notice symptoms minus 1, Find doctor minus 2, Book minus 1, Travel minus 1, Wait minus 2, Consultation plus 1, Follow-up 0. The two lowest points are Find doctor and Wait. That tells the team where to focus: confirming doctor presence before travel, and giving a live serial status so patients can wait outside or nearby instead of standing for hours. Design effort goes where the curve is lowest.

How the tools fit together: Research produces data. Affinity diagrams find patterns. Personas give the patterns a face and goals. Empathy maps summarise feelings. Problem scenarios describe today's pain; activity scenarios imagine the future. Journey maps show the full experience over time. User stories and acceptance criteria break the future into buildable pieces. Each tool answers a different question, and none of them is useful without real research underneath.

Real-life example, a bus ticket app: A Bangladeshi team building an intercity bus ticket app made a journey map for a persona, a garment worker travelling home for Eid. The map showed that buying the ticket was not the worst moment; the worst was the uncertainty on travel day about whether the bus was delayed and which counter to go to. The team added a trip-day screen with departure counter, a live delay message and a helpline button. Without the journey map, they would have kept polishing the purchase screen.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes are inventing personas without research, writing demographics instead of goals and behaviours, making too many personas, describing scenarios as screen-by-screen instructions too early, and writing user stories that describe a solution instead of a need ('I want a dropdown'). Exams often ask: define a persona and list its contents; explain primary and secondary personas; write a persona and a scenario for a given system; distinguish problem and activity scenarios; write user stories in the standard format with acceptance criteria; draw a journey map with touchpoints and pain points.

Recap: Personas are research-based fictional characters that fix the elastic user problem and keep goals at the centre. Use few personas, one primary, and keep them to one page. Empathy maps summarise says, thinks, does and feels. Scenarios are stories of personas pursuing goals: problem scenarios for today, activity scenarios for the future. User stories (As a, I want, so that) with acceptance criteria (Given, When, Then) break work into testable pieces. Journey maps show the whole experience, emotions and pain points over time. Next: analysing tasks step by step with hierarchical task analysis.
key_points: The elastic user problem: without a specific picture, 'the user' stretches to fit everyone's opinion.
A persona is a fictional but research-based character with goals, behaviours, frustrations and context, not just demographics.
Goals are the core of a persona; end goals drive features, experience goals guide tone and reassurance.
Use few personas: one primary that the main design must satisfy, secondary ones, and optionally a negative persona.
Problem scenarios describe today's difficulties; activity scenarios describe how the new design could help (Rosson and Carroll).
User stories follow 'As a ..., I want ..., so that ...' and need acceptance criteria such as Given, When, Then.
Journey maps show stages, touchpoints, emotions, pain points and opportunities across the whole experience.
lessons.tip: Print your primary persona on one page and stick it above your desk while designing. Before you add any feature, ask out loud: 'Which goal of this persona does this serve?' If you cannot answer, the feature probably does not belong.
lessons.task: Choose a service you know well, such as admission to your university or buying a train ticket. Write a one-page persona for a typical user based on two short conversations with real people, then write one problem scenario and draw a simple journey map with five stages and an emotion curve. Mark the lowest point.

quiz.q: What problem do personas mainly solve, according to Alan Cooper?
options: The elastic user: 'the user' stretches to fit each person's opinion
quiz.explain: A specific, agreed persona stops each team member from imagining a different user that suits their own argument.

quiz.q: Which item belongs most clearly in a good persona?
options: The user's goals and frustrations based on research
A long list of ages and incomes only
quiz.explain: Personas centre on goals, behaviours and frustrations drawn from research, not on features or demographics alone.

quiz.q: A story describing how patients currently travel to the hospital only to find the doctor absent, with no app involved, is a:
quiz.explain: A problem scenario shows how the task is done today and its difficulties. Activity scenarios imagine the new design.

quiz.q: Which is a correctly formed user story?
options: The system shall store patient records in a table
Add a dropdown menu on the booking screen
As a family helper, I want to book for several relatives from one account so that I don't need separate phones
quiz.explain: The standard form is 'As a [user], I want [goal] so that [reason]'. It states a need, not a solution or a system requirement.

quiz.q: In a journey map, the emotion curve is lowest at the 'Wait' stage. What should the team do?
options: Remove the Wait stage from the map
Ignore it because it happens outside the app
Focus design effort on reducing pain at that stage, for example live serial status
Add more colours to the booking screen
quiz.explain: The lowest points of the curve show where the experience hurts most, even outside the screen. Design effort should go there.

lessons.title: Task Analysis and Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA)
lessons.content:
Ask your mother how she makes khichuri and she will say 'just cook rice and dal together'. Watch her actually do it and you will see twenty small steps: washing the rice, soaking the dal, frying onions, adding turmeric, checking the water level, tasting for salt, lowering the flame at the right moment. Some steps happen in a fixed order, some only if something is missing, and some are repeated until it looks right. If you wanted to build a robot cook, the short answer would be useless. You would need the full breakdown. Task analysis is that breakdown, done for the things people do with technology.

What task analysis is: Task analysis is the study of what people do, step by step, to achieve their goals, and what they need to know to do it. It describes the work as it really happens, not as the manual says it happens. In HCI we use it to understand the current way people work before designing, to check a new design against real tasks, to find steps where errors are likely, and to write training material or help. It sits between user research, which tells us who the users are and what they want, and design, which decides what the system should be.

Goals, tasks and actions: Three words are used in a careful way. A goal is the state a person wants to reach, such as 'my brother in Rajshahi has 2,000 taka'. A task is a structured set of activities done to reach the goal, such as 'send money with a mobile wallet'. An action is a single step with no meaningful smaller part for our purposes, such as 'tap the Send Money icon' or 'type the PIN'. The same goal can be reached by different tasks: you could also ask a shop agent to send the money, or give cash to a bus driver. Task analysis usually starts from a goal and asks: what tasks and actions do people use to get there?

Why analyse tasks at all: First, designers who skip task analysis often design for an imagined task. A team may build a beautiful 'transfer' screen without realising that users first check their balance every single time, so the balance should be visible on the transfer screen. Second, a breakdown reveals unnecessary steps, which you can remove. Third, it shows where memory, attention or knowledge is needed, which are the places users fail. Fourth, it gives a shared language: designers, developers and testers can all point at step 3.2 and agree what they mean.

Hierarchical task analysis: The best known method is hierarchical task analysis, or HTA, developed by John Annett and Keith Duncan in the late 1960s, originally for training industrial workers. HTA breaks a goal down into subtasks, then breaks each subtask down further, building a tree. At every level it also writes a plan, which says in what order and under what conditions the subtasks are done. The tree shows what is done; the plans show how the parts fit together. Both are needed. A list of steps without plans cannot express choices or repetitions.

Numbering: HTA uses a simple numbering scheme. The top goal is 0. Its subtasks are 1, 2, 3 and so on. The subtasks of task 2 are 2.1, 2.2, 2.3. The subtasks of 2.3 are 2.3.1, 2.3.2, and so on. The plan for task 0 is called plan 0, the plan for task 2 is plan 2. This numbering lets you refer to any step precisely, and it maps easily onto a tree diagram or a table.

Kinds of plans: Plans come in a few common forms. A fixed sequence says do the steps in order: 'Do 1, then 2, then 3'. A selective plan says choose one depending on a condition: 'If the receiver is in contacts, do 2.1; otherwise do 2.2'. An optional step is done only sometimes: 'Do 4 if you want to add a reference note'. A cyclic plan repeats until a condition is met: 'Repeat 3.1 to 3.2 until the PIN is accepted, at most three times'. Some steps can be done in any order, and plans can say that too: 'Do 1 and 2 in any order, then 3'. Writing plans forces you to notice decisions users must make, and decisions are where design can help or hurt.

Worked HTA, sending money, top level: Let us analyse the goal '0. Send 2,000 taka to my brother with a mobile wallet app'. After observing several users, we write the top level: 1. Open the wallet app and log in. 2. Choose the receiver. 3. Enter the amount. 4. Add a reference (optional). 5. Confirm with PIN. 6. Check the result. Plan 0: Do 1, 2, 3 in order; do 4 if the user wants a note; then do 5 and 6.

Worked HTA, the next level: Now we break down the subtasks. Task 1, open and log in: 1.1 find the app on the home screen, 1.2 tap it, 1.3 enter the login PIN or use fingerprint. Plan 1: do 1.1 to 1.3 in order; if login fails, repeat 1.3. Task 2, choose the receiver: 2.1 tap Send Money, 2.2 pick from recent or saved contacts, 2.3 type the number, 2.4 check the name shown. Plan 2: do 2.1; if the brother is in recent contacts do 2.2, otherwise do 2.3; then do 2.4. Task 5, confirm: 5.1 read the review screen, 5.2 enter the PIN, 5.3 tap and hold to confirm. Plan 5: in order; if the review shows a wrong number or amount, go back to 2 or 3.

Worked HTA, as a table: HTA is often presented as a table with columns for the task number, the task description, the plan, and notes on problems. For our example the row for 2.3 might read: '2.3 Type 11-digit number. Note: one-digit slips are common; the user must remember or copy the number from another app.' The row for 2.4 might say: 'Check name shown. Note: only works if the name appears; users in a hurry skip it.' These notes are the most valuable output. They point directly to design ideas, such as showing recent contacts first and displaying the receiver's name in large text.

The stopping rule: How far down should you go? You could break 'type the PIN' into 'move thumb to digit 4, press, move to digit 7' and so on, but that rarely helps. Annett and Duncan suggested a rule based on probability and cost, often called the P x C rule: stop breaking a task down when the probability of failure multiplied by the cost of failure is acceptably small. In plain words, keep going deeper only where people actually struggle or where a mistake would be expensive. For the money transfer, entering the number deserves detail because a slip sends money to a stranger; tapping the app icon does not.

Using HTA to find problems: Once the tree is built, walk through it and ask at each step: what does the user need to know here, what must they remember, what could go wrong, and how would they notice? In our wallet example, step 2.3 requires remembering 11 digits, step 2.4 relies on the user bothering to check, and step 6 depends on whether the success screen is clear. HTA also lets you compare designs. If version A needs 14 actions and version B needs 9 for the same goal, B is likely faster, although you should still test it, because fewer steps that are confusing can be worse than more steps that are obvious.

HTA for comparing current and new: A useful trick is to make two HTAs: one for the current way (for example, a paper register at a pharmacy) and one for the proposed system. Putting them side by side shows which steps disappear, which new steps the system adds, and where users might feel the new way is slower. If the old paper way needed 5 steps to record a sale and the app needs 12, expect resistance, however modern the app looks.

Task analysis and other methods: HTA works well for tasks with clear steps. Other methods exist for different needs. Cognitive task analysis (CTA) focuses on the thinking inside the task: what knowledge, judgement and decisions experts use, such as how an experienced doctor decides which patient to see first. CTA uses interviews and observation of experts and is harder to do. GOMS, which you will meet in the lesson on predictive models, describes tasks in terms of goals, operators, methods and selection rules, and can predict time. Use cases and user stories, from software engineering, describe system behaviour from the user's side but with less detail about the human's actions.

Where the data comes from: HTA is only as good as the observations behind it. You build it from the research methods of earlier lessons: watching people do the task in their real setting, contextual inquiry, interviews and existing documents such as manuals. Always check your HTA with real users. People often say they do things one way and actually do them another. A cashier may describe a neat procedure but in practice skip the receipt step whenever the queue is long, and your design must handle that reality.

Real-life example 1, DaktarDekhao booking: The team analysed '0. Book a serial for my mother with Dr. Rahman'. HTA showed that elderly users often book for someone else, a step the first design ignored: it assumed the patient was the logged-in user. Plan 2 became: 'If booking for self, use profile; otherwise do 2.2, add patient name and age.' The analysis also showed users check the doctor's sitting days before choosing a date, so the redesign displayed those days directly on the calendar. Both changes came straight from the task tree.

Real-life example 2, a garment factory line: Task analysis was born in industry, and it still fits there. Imagine a garment factory in Gazipur introducing a tablet app for supervisors to record hourly production. An HTA of the paper process showed supervisors walk the line, count pieces per worker, write numbers on a board, and later copy them to a register. The app design that followed let supervisors enter counts while walking, with large number buttons usable while holding a bundle of cloth, and removed the copying step entirely. Without the HTA, the designers might have put a desktop form in a tablet.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A common mistake is listing steps without plans, which hides the choices and repetitions. Another is going too deep everywhere instead of where the P x C rule says it matters. A third is analysing the task as the designer imagines it rather than as users actually do it. Some students confuse goals with tasks; remember the goal is the end state, the task is the way of reaching it. Exams often ask you to draw an HTA for an everyday task such as withdrawing cash from an ATM or booking a ticket, with correct numbering and plans, and to explain the stopping rule and how HTA helps design.

Recap: Task analysis describes what people actually do to reach their goals. Goals are end states, tasks are structured activities, actions are single steps. HTA, from Annett and Duncan, breaks a goal into a numbered tree of subtasks with a plan at each level: fixed sequence, selective, optional, cyclic or any order. Stop decomposing where probability times cost of failure is small. Use the tree to find memory demands, error-prone steps and unnecessary work, and to compare designs. Cognitive task analysis looks at expert thinking; GOMS predicts time. Next we turn the problems we found into ideas.
key_points: Task analysis describes what people actually do, step by step, to reach a goal and what they need to know.
A goal is an end state, a task is a structured set of activities to reach it, an action is a single step.
Hierarchical task analysis (HTA), from Annett and Duncan, breaks a goal into a numbered tree of subtasks (0, 1, 1.1, 1.2...).
Each level has a plan: fixed sequence, selective, optional, cyclic or any order.
The P x C stopping rule: decompose further only where probability times cost of failure is significant.
HTA notes reveal memory demands, error-prone steps and unnecessary work, which become design ideas.
Cognitive task analysis studies expert thinking and decisions; GOMS models tasks to predict time.
lessons.tip: When you draw an HTA in an exam, write the plans clearly under each parent task. Many students draw a perfect tree and lose marks because a tree without plans cannot show order, choices or repetition.
lessons.task: Watch a family member do one real task on their phone, such as paying an electricity bill or recharging. Write an HTA with at least two levels and plans. Add a notes column, mark two steps where errors could happen, and suggest one design change for each.

quiz.q: In HCI terms, 'my brother in Rajshahi has 2,000 taka' is best described as:
quiz.explain: A goal is the end state the person wants. Sending money through an app is a task, and tapping a button is an action.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a plan in HTA?
options: The numbered list of all subtasks
The cost of developing the system
A sketch of the screen layout
It states the order and conditions under which subtasks are done
quiz.explain: Plans express sequence, choices, optional steps and repetition. Without plans a tree cannot show how subtasks fit together.

quiz.q: 'If the receiver is in recent contacts, do 2.2; otherwise do 2.3.' What kind of plan is this?
quiz.explain: A selective plan chooses between subtasks depending on a condition.

quiz.q: According to the P x C stopping rule, when should you stop breaking a task down?
options: When probability of failure times cost of failure is acceptably small
When the tree fills one page
quiz.explain: Annett and Duncan's rule says decompose only where failure is likely or expensive; elsewhere more detail adds little.

quiz.q: Which method focuses mainly on the knowledge, judgement and decisions experts use inside a task?
quiz.explain: Cognitive task analysis studies the thinking part of the work, such as how an experienced doctor prioritises patients.

lessons.title: Ideation and Sketching
lessons.content:
Imagine a group of friends planning a picnic. One person says 'let's go to Ratargul' and everyone immediately starts arguing about the boat fare. Nobody ever considered the other twenty places they could have gone. The first idea grabbed all the attention. Design teams fall into the same trap all the time: someone shows a screen, and the rest of the meeting is spent polishing that one screen. Ideation is the deliberate practice of generating many ideas before choosing, and sketching is the quickest way to make those ideas visible. This lesson is about both.

Where ideation fits: By now we have done user research, built personas, written scenarios and analysed tasks. We know who the users are, what they try to do and where they struggle. The next step in the user-centred design cycle is to produce possible solutions. In the double diamond model this is the start of the second diamond: first we diverge, generating many options, then we converge, choosing the most promising. Ideation is the diverging part; selecting ideas is the converging part. Doing both at the same time is the most common mistake, because judging kills new ideas before they have a chance.

Start with a clear problem statement: Good ideas need a good question. A problem statement, sometimes called a point of view, combines a user, a need and an insight from research. For example: 'Elderly patients in district towns need to book a doctor's serial without help, because they are afraid of making a mistake in an app and losing their place.' This is specific, rooted in real research, and does not already contain a solution. Compare it with 'We need to add a booking button', which jumps to a solution and leaves nothing to explore.

How might we questions: A popular way to turn a problem statement into an ideation prompt is the 'How might we' question, often written HMW. 'How' assumes there is a solution, 'might' says it is fine if some ideas fail, and 'we' makes it a team effort. From the statement above we could write: How might we make booking feel safe for first-time users? How might we let a relative book on behalf of a patient? How might we confirm a serial without needing the user to read much? A good HMW is not too broad ('How might we fix healthcare?') and not too narrow ('How might we make the button green?'). Writing several HMWs from different angles often opens surprising directions.

Brainstorming: Brainstorming is a group technique for producing many ideas quickly, popularised by the advertising executive Alex Osborn in the mid twentieth century. The core rules are: defer judgement, so nobody criticises ideas during the session; go for quantity, because more ideas means more chances of good ones; welcome wild ideas, since a crazy idea can lead to a practical one; and build on the ideas of others, using 'yes, and' rather than 'no, but'. Design firms often add: stay focused on the topic, have one conversation at a time, and be visual by sketching ideas instead of only talking.

Making brainstorming work: Plain group brainstorming has known weaknesses. Loud people dominate, shy people stay silent, and everyone tends to copy the first ideas. Research has found that people generating ideas alone and then pooling them often produce more ideas than the same people talking together. A practical fix is to start with silent individual idea generation on sticky notes for a few minutes, then share and build together. Set a time limit, write each idea on a separate note, and have a facilitator who keeps the rules. For a team of five, a goal of fifty notes in twenty minutes is reasonable.

Crazy 8s: Crazy 8s is a fast sketching exercise popularised in design sprints. Each person folds a sheet of A4 paper into eight panels and sketches eight different ideas in eight minutes, one minute per panel. The time pressure stops people from perfecting the first idea and pushes them past the obvious ones. The first two or three panels are usually predictable; the interesting ideas often appear in panels five to eight. After the round, everyone presents their sketches briefly and the group discusses them.

SCAMPER: Another way to push beyond the obvious is SCAMPER, a checklist of questions applied to an existing product or idea. The letters stand for Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify (including make bigger or smaller), Put to another use, Eliminate, and Reverse or Rearrange. Applied to booking a serial: Substitute typing with voice; Combine booking with a payment of the fee; Adapt the token-number system from bank counters; Modify by making the date picker show only available days; Put the serial SMS to another use as an entry ticket; Eliminate the registration step for first booking; Reverse the flow so the hospital sends available slots and the patient replies. Not every answer is good, but the checklist reliably produces options.

Other idea sources: Ideas also come from looking around. Analogies ask how other fields solve a similar problem: how does a railway ticket queue, a restaurant waiting list or a bank token machine handle turns? Competitive analysis looks at what similar apps do well or badly. Extreme users, such as someone who cannot read or someone who books for ten family members, reveal needs that ordinary users have in a milder form. Design principles and patterns from earlier lessons, such as Norman's constraints or good feedback, can also be used as idea triggers.

Why sketch: Once ideas exist, sketching makes them concrete enough to discuss. A sketch is a quick, rough drawing that captures an idea. Bill Buxton, in his book Sketching User Experiences, argued that sketching and prototyping are different activities. Sketches are quick, cheap, disposable and plentiful; their purpose is to explore and suggest, not to confirm. They are deliberately ambiguous, which invites others to imagine and contribute. A polished image tells people 'this is decided'; a rough sketch tells them 'this is a question, help me answer it'. That is why designers sketch many options before making even one prototype.

You do not need to draw well: Many students avoid sketching because they think they cannot draw. Interface sketching needs only a small vocabulary. A rectangle is a screen or a container. A rectangle with a label is a button. Lines are text. A box with a cross through it is an image. A circle is an avatar or icon. Arrows show movement between screens or actions. Short labels explain what matters. With these shapes you can sketch any screen in under a minute. Use a thick pen rather than a pencil, so you are not tempted to add fine detail.

Sketching flows, not just screens: Interaction is about sequences, so sketch the flow as well. Draw three to six small screens in a row and connect them with arrows labelled by actions: 'tap Book', 'choose time', 'confirm'. This quickly reveals missing steps, such as what happens if no slot is available, or where the user goes after confirming. A flow sketch is often more useful than a beautiful single screen.

Storyboards: A storyboard is a sequence of sketches, like a comic strip, showing a user in context using the product over time. Unlike a flow of screens, a storyboard includes the person, the place and the situation. Panel one: an elderly man in a village feels chest pain. Panel two: his granddaughter opens DaktarDekhao on her phone. Panel three: they choose the cardiology department at the district hospital. Panel four: an SMS with the serial number arrives. Panel five: next morning he shows the SMS at the hospital counter. Storyboards help the team understand the context, find gaps in the experience, and communicate ideas to stakeholders who do not read wireframes.

Sharing and critiquing sketches: Sketches are meant to be shown. Pin them on a wall or lay them on a table so everyone can see all of them at once. Each person explains their sketch in a minute or two, and others ask questions first, then comment. Useful feedback links back to users: 'Would Rahima, our elderly persona, see this button?' is better than 'I don't like it'. Combining parts of different sketches is encouraged; the best solution is often the header from one idea, the flow from another and the confirmation from a third.

Converging, choosing ideas: After diverging, the team must choose. A simple method is dot voting: everyone gets a few sticky dots, for example three, and places them on the ideas they find most promising. Ideas with many dots move forward. To avoid choosing only what is popular, teams also use an impact-effort matrix: draw two axes, impact on the user's problem and effort to build, and place each idea. Ideas with high impact and low effort are quick wins; high impact and high effort are big bets worth planning; low impact ideas are dropped. Always check the chosen ideas against the problem statement and personas.

A worked session: A team of four spends one hour on 'How might we let a relative book on behalf of a patient?'. Ten minutes of silent note writing produces 46 ideas. After grouping duplicates, 31 remain. A Crazy 8s round on the top themes produces 32 sketches. Dot voting, three dots each, gives 12 dots in total; one idea, 'book for family member with saved patient profiles', gets 4 dots, and 'SMS confirmation sent to both relative and patient' gets 3. On the impact-effort matrix both are high impact and moderate effort, so they go forward to prototyping. Notice how the final ideas came from a pool of more than seventy notes and sketches.

Real-life example 1, a school fee payment: A team designing a school fee payment feature for parents in Bangladesh started with the obvious idea: a form with student ID and amount. Ideation produced alternatives: scanning a QR code printed on the fee slip, choosing the child from a saved list, reminders a few days before the due date, and a receipt sent to both parents. Storyboards revealed that many parents pay from a shop agent, not their own phone, so the slip QR idea became important. None of this appeared in the first idea.

Real-life example 2, the fish market: A start-up wanted to help fish sellers in a Khulna market take orders by phone. Sketching a storyboard of a seller's morning showed wet hands, noise and no time to type. The team's Crazy 8s round produced voice notes, large picture buttons for each fish type and a simple 'ready' tap. The voice-and-picture idea was later tested on paper with real sellers. Sketching the context, not just the screen, changed the whole direction.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: The biggest mistake is falling in love with the first idea. Another is judging during divergence, which shuts down creativity. A third is making sketches too polished, so people only comment on colours. A fourth is skipping the problem statement, so ideas drift away from user needs. Exams ask: state the rules of brainstorming; explain diverge and converge; describe Crazy 8s or SCAMPER; explain the difference between sketching and prototyping; draw a storyboard for a given scenario.

Recap: Ideation generates many options before choosing. Start from a research-based problem statement and turn it into How might we questions. Brainstorm with deferred judgement, quantity, wild ideas and building on others, ideally after silent individual work. Use Crazy 8s and SCAMPER to push past the obvious. Sketch quickly with a simple vocabulary; sketches explore, prototypes test. Sketch flows and storyboards to include context. Converge with dot voting and an impact-effort matrix. Next lesson: turning chosen ideas into prototypes users can try.
key_points: Ideation diverges to generate many ideas, then converges to choose; mixing the two kills new ideas.
A good problem statement combines a user, a need and an insight, without already containing a solution.
How might we questions turn problems into open prompts that are neither too broad nor too narrow.
Brainstorming rules: defer judgement, go for quantity, welcome wild ideas, build on others' ideas.
Crazy 8s (eight sketches in eight minutes) and SCAMPER push thinking past the first obvious ideas.
Sketches are quick, cheap, disposable and ambiguous; they explore ideas, while prototypes test them.
Storyboards show the user, place and situation over time; dot voting and impact-effort matrices help choose ideas.
lessons.tip: Never bring only one design to a discussion. Bring at least three rough sketches. People compare options honestly, but they defend or attack a single design, and you learn far less.
lessons.task: Write one How might we question about a problem you face with any app. Fold an A4 sheet into eight panels and do Crazy 8s: eight different sketched solutions in eight minutes. Then pick the best one and draw a four-panel storyboard showing a real person using it.

quiz.q: Which is a rule of brainstorming?
options: Criticise weak ideas immediately to save time
Only the team leader may suggest ideas
Stop as soon as one good idea appears
Defer judgement and go for quantity
quiz.explain: Brainstorming separates generating from judging. Criticism during the session stops people from sharing new or unusual ideas.

quiz.q: In Crazy 8s, what does each participant do?
options: Sketches eight different ideas in eight minutes
quiz.explain: Eight panels, one minute each. The time pressure pushes people past their first obvious ideas.

quiz.q: According to Bill Buxton, how do sketches differ from prototypes?
options: Sketches explore and suggest; prototypes are for testing and refining
Sketches must be drawn by professional artists
Sketches are used only after the product is released
quiz.explain: Sketches are quick, cheap, disposable and ambiguous, inviting discussion. Prototypes are more refined and used to test ideas.

quiz.q: Which is the best How might we question for a booking problem?
options: How might we fix healthcare in Bangladesh?
How might we let a relative book a serial on behalf of a patient?
How might we make the book button green?
How might we add a booking button?
quiz.explain: It is specific to a real need but open to many solutions. The others are too broad, too narrow or already contain the answer.

quiz.q: On an impact-effort matrix, which ideas are usually picked first as quick wins?
quiz.explain: High impact with low effort gives the most benefit for the least work. High impact, high effort ideas are bigger bets that need planning.

lessons.title: Prototyping and Wireframes
lessons.content:
Before a new building goes up in Dhaka, the architect often makes a small model from cardboard and foam. The owner can walk around it, look into the rooms, and say 'the stairs feel too close to the kitchen'. Moving cardboard stairs costs a few minutes. Moving concrete stairs after the building is finished costs a fortune. Designers of interactive systems do the same thing with prototypes. A prototype lets people experience a design before it is built, so that problems are found while they are still cheap to fix.

What a prototype is: A prototype is an early, incomplete representation of a product that lets people explore, use or evaluate a design idea. It can be a few sheets of paper, a set of linked images on a phone, a clickable mock-up made in a design tool, or partly working code. What makes something a prototype is not the material but the purpose: it exists to answer questions. Will users understand this flow? Is this button findable? Does this layout fit on a small phone? A prototype is a question you can hold in your hand.

Why prototype: Prototypes serve several purposes. They let you test ideas with real users before investing in development. They help the team communicate, because a picture and a click-through explain more than a long document. They help you explore alternatives, since building three cheap versions is possible when each takes an hour. They reveal technical and practical problems early, like a screen that needs too much data. And they support decision making with stakeholders, who often cannot imagine a product from a written requirement but immediately react to something they can tap.

Fidelity: Prototypes differ in fidelity, meaning how closely they resemble the final product. Fidelity has several dimensions. Visual fidelity is how real it looks: hand sketches versus pixel-perfect screens. Content fidelity is whether it uses real text and data or placeholders like 'lorem ipsum'. Interaction fidelity is how much it actually responds: static pictures versus clickable flows versus working features. A prototype can be low in one dimension and high in another, for example rough sketches with real Bangla text, which is useful when the wording itself is being tested.

Low-fidelity prototypes: A low-fidelity prototype is rough and simple, usually made from paper, cards, sticky notes or quick sketches. Each screen is drawn on a card; pop-ups are smaller pieces of paper placed on top; a scrolling list may be a long strip of paper pulled through a slit. Low-fi prototypes are fast, cheap and easy to change, even during a test session. Because they look unfinished, users feel free to criticise them, and the team is not emotionally attached. They are ideal early in the project, when the main questions are about structure, flow and content rather than colour or animation.

Paper prototype testing: In a paper prototype test, one team member plays 'the computer'. A participant is given a task, such as 'Book a serial with a heart specialist for next Tuesday', and touches the paper screen with a finger as if it were a phone. The human computer silently swaps the papers to show the next screen. A facilitator gives the task and asks the participant to think aloud; an observer takes notes on where the participant hesitates or goes wrong. If a problem is obvious, the team can redraw a screen between participants. It feels strange the first time, but people quickly treat the paper as a real interface.

Wizard of Oz prototypes: In a Wizard of Oz prototype, the user believes they are interacting with a working system, but a hidden person is actually producing the system's responses, like the man behind the curtain in the famous story. This is very useful for testing features that are hard to build, such as speech recognition or a chatbot, before investing in the technology. A well-known early example was a study of a 'listening typewriter' in the early 1980s, where a hidden typist typed what users dictated so researchers could learn how people would use speech input. Today a team testing a Bangla voice assistant could have a teammate in another room listen and type the replies. Research ethics require telling participants the truth after the session.

Wireframes: A wireframe is a simple, usually black-and-white layout of a screen that shows structure: where the header, navigation, content blocks, images, buttons and text go, and their relative importance. It deliberately leaves out colours, real images, fonts and decoration, so that discussion focuses on layout and content priorities. Images are often shown as boxes with a cross, text as lines or placeholder words, and buttons as labelled rectangles. Wireframes can be drawn on paper or made in tools; some tools, like Balsamiq, even give them a hand-drawn look on purpose.

Wireframes, a worked example: Consider the DaktarDekhao doctor list screen. A wireframe might show, from top to bottom: a top bar with a back arrow and the title 'Cardiology, Sadar Hospital'; a search field; a filter row with 'Today' and 'This week'; then a list of doctor cards, each with a photo box, the doctor's name in bold, qualifications in smaller text, sitting days, and a 'Book serial' button on the right; and a bottom navigation bar with Home, My serials and Profile. Even in this grey sketch the team can ask: is the button big enough, is the most important information first, do we need the photo at all?

Medium and high fidelity: A medium-fidelity prototype usually has digital wireframes linked together so users can click or tap through the main flow, with real labels and basic layout but little visual styling. A high-fidelity prototype looks and behaves almost like the final product: real colours, fonts, icons, images and transitions, made in a design tool or with code. High-fi prototypes are good for testing details like visual hierarchy, readability, micro-interactions and the overall feel, and for showing stakeholders or investors. They take longer to make and change, and users often comment on colours instead of structure, so they belong later in the process.

Trade-offs between low and high fidelity: Low-fi is cheap, fast and encourages honest feedback about concepts, but cannot test visual details, timing or realistic interaction, and some users find it hard to imagine the real thing. High-fi is realistic and persuasive, tests details and can serve as a specification for developers, but it is slow, expensive to change, may make people think the product is nearly finished, and can lock the team into a design too early. A common path is to go from paper sketches to clickable wireframes to high-fi screens, testing at each step.

Horizontal and vertical prototypes: Another way to classify prototypes is by scope. A horizontal prototype covers many features but shallowly: you can see all the main screens and menus, but nothing works deeply behind them. It is good for testing navigation and overall structure. A vertical prototype covers few features but in depth: one complete flow, such as booking a serial, works fully, perhaps with real data. It is good for testing a critical task end to end. A combination, sometimes called a T-prototype, gives a broad shallow overview plus one deep slice.

Throw-away and evolutionary prototypes: A throw-away prototype is built to learn something and then discarded; the real product is built separately. Paper prototypes and most design-tool mock-ups are throw-away. An evolutionary prototype is built with the intention of gradually improving it into the final product, usually in code. Evolutionary prototyping saves effort if the base is solid, but there is a risk: quick-and-dirty code written for a demo can become the foundation of a real product, carrying hidden weaknesses. Teams should decide which type they are building before they start.

Tools: Most professional teams today design and prototype in tools such as Figma, which runs in a browser, lets several people edit the same file and can link frames into clickable prototypes that run on a phone. Other tools exist for wireframing and prototyping, and front-end frameworks can be used to make coded prototypes. But tools are not the point. A pen, paper and a pair of scissors remain among the best prototyping tools, especially early on, and they work without electricity or internet.

What to prototype, and how much: Prototype just enough to answer your current question. If the question is 'Do users understand that they must choose a department before a doctor?', three paper screens are enough. If it is 'Is the text readable on a cheap phone in sunlight?', you need a real-looking screen on a real phone outside. Building more than needed wastes time; building less than needed gives misleading answers. Write the question at the top of your prototype plan.

Real-life example 1, a bus ticket app: A student team designing an intercity bus ticket app made paper prototypes of six screens in one afternoon and tested them at a bus counter with five travellers. Three of the five did not realise the seat map could be scrolled to see the back of the bus. The team redrew the seat map on a longer strip with a visible 'more seats below' hint and tested two more people the same day. Both found it. The fix cost a sheet of paper and twenty minutes.

Real-life example 2, a Bangla voice helpline: An NGO wanted to know whether farmers would use a voice menu to ask about crop disease. Instead of building speech recognition, the team ran a Wizard of Oz test: farmers called a number, spoke their question, and a hidden agronomist chose a prerecorded answer. The test showed that farmers described problems with local words for diseases and expected a human-like conversation, information that shaped the real system before any recognition model was trained.

Learning from a prototype test: After each session, write down what happened, not what you hoped. Useful notes include where the participant paused for more than a few seconds, what they tapped first on each screen, which words they misunderstood, and whether they finished the task. Patterns across participants matter more than one person's opinion. If one user dislikes a colour, note it; if four of five users miss the same button, fix it before anything else. Then change the prototype and test again; prototyping is a loop, not a single event.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A frequent mistake is jumping straight to high-fi because it looks impressive, then defending it instead of learning from it. Another is prototyping everything instead of what answers the current question. A third is confusing wireframes with prototypes: a wireframe is a layout; it becomes part of a prototype when it is used to simulate interaction. Exams ask: define prototype and its purposes; compare low and high fidelity with advantages and disadvantages; explain horizontal versus vertical and throw-away versus evolutionary prototypes; describe paper prototyping and Wizard of Oz with examples.

Recap: A prototype is an early representation built to answer design questions cheaply. Fidelity has visual, content and interaction dimensions. Low-fi paper prototypes are fast and invite honest feedback; high-fi prototypes test details and feel. Wireframes show structure without decoration. Wizard of Oz fakes hard technology with a hidden human. Horizontal prototypes are broad and shallow, vertical ones narrow and deep. Throw-away prototypes teach and are discarded; evolutionary ones grow into the product. Prototype just enough to answer your question. Next we look at how to organise content and navigation: information architecture.
key_points: A prototype is an early, incomplete representation built to answer design questions before full development.
Fidelity has visual, content and interaction dimensions; a prototype can be low in one and high in another.
Low-fi paper prototypes are cheap, fast and invite honest feedback; high-fi prototypes test details but are slow to change.
A wireframe is a plain layout showing structure and priority without colour or decoration.
In a Wizard of Oz prototype a hidden person simulates hard technology such as speech recognition.
Horizontal prototypes are broad and shallow; vertical prototypes are narrow and deep; T-prototypes combine both.
Throw-away prototypes are discarded after learning; evolutionary prototypes are refined into the final product.
lessons.tip: Write the question your prototype must answer at the top of the page before you draw anything. It stops you from over-building, and it tells you exactly what to watch for when users try it.
lessons.task: Make a paper prototype of four screens for booking a doctor's serial: department, doctor list, time slot, confirmation. Ask a friend to complete the task while you play the computer by swapping papers. Note every hesitation, redraw one screen, and test again.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a prototype?
options: To answer design questions cheaply before full development
quiz.explain: A prototype exists to explore and evaluate ideas, finding problems while they are cheap to fix.

quiz.q: A hidden team member types the replies that users think come from a voice assistant. What kind of prototype is this?
quiz.explain: In a Wizard of Oz prototype a hidden person simulates the system, useful for testing hard-to-build technology.

quiz.q: Which is an advantage of low-fidelity prototypes?
options: They look exactly like the final product
They are fast to change and users feel free to criticise them
They can be released to the app store
quiz.explain: Rough prototypes are cheap and quick, and their unfinished look invites honest feedback about structure and flow.

quiz.q: A prototype in which one complete booking flow works in depth, but other features are missing, is:
quiz.explain: Vertical prototypes go deep on a few features; horizontal ones cover many features shallowly.

quiz.q: What does a wireframe deliberately leave out?
quiz.explain: Wireframes show structure and priority. Leaving out styling keeps the discussion on layout and content.

lessons.title: Information Architecture and Navigation
lessons.content:
Walk into a big supermarket in Dhaka looking for soy sauce. You do not search every shelf. You look up at the hanging signs, find 'Cooking essentials', walk to that aisle, scan for the sauces section and pick the bottle. Somebody decided how to group thousands of products, what to call each group, and how signs would guide you. If they had grouped products by colour of packaging, or labelled the aisle 'Category C-4', you would wander for half an hour. Apps and websites face exactly the same problem with screens, features and content. The discipline that solves it is information architecture.

What information architecture is: Information architecture, or IA, is the practice of organising, structuring and labelling content and features so that people can find what they need and understand where they are. It answers questions like: what are the main sections of this app, what goes inside each one, what do we call them, and how does a user move between them? IA is mostly invisible when done well. Users do not notice a good structure; they just find things. They notice a bad one immediately, as frustration and the feeling of being lost.

The four components: A widely used description of IA comes from Louis Rosenfeld and Peter Morville, whose book on information architecture for the web became a standard text. They describe four main systems. Organisation systems decide how content is grouped and categorised. Labelling systems decide what things are called. Navigation systems decide how users browse and move through the content. Search systems decide how users look for content by typing queries. A good IA designs all four together, because a perfect grouping is useless with confusing labels, and great labels cannot rescue missing navigation.

Organisation schemes, exact: Some ways of grouping are exact, meaning each item belongs clearly in one place. Alphabetical order suits lists people search by name, like a contact list or a medicine index. Chronological order suits things that happen in time, like a news feed, transaction history or a list of past appointments. Geographical order suits location-based content, like hospitals grouped by division and district. Exact schemes are easy to build and easy to understand, but only work when users already know the exact name, date or place they want.

Organisation schemes, ambiguous: Other schemes are ambiguous, meaning an item could belong in more than one group, and grouping needs judgement. Topic or subject groups content by what it is about, like 'Heart', 'Children', 'Skin'. Task-based schemes group by what users want to do, like 'Book a serial', 'See my reports', 'Pay fees'. Audience-based schemes group by type of user, like 'For patients', 'For doctors', 'For hospital staff'. Metaphor-based schemes borrow structure from a familiar thing, like a 'shopping cart'. Ambiguous schemes often match how people think better than exact ones, but they need testing, because the designer's idea of a topic may not be the user's. Many real products use a hybrid, for example task-based main tabs with topic-based lists inside.

Labelling: Labels are the words and icons that represent groups and items. Good labels use the users' language, not the organisation's internal jargon. A hospital may call it 'OPD ticket', patients may call it 'serial'. A bank may say 'fund transfer', customers say 'send money'. Labels should be short, specific, consistent across the app and clearly different from each other. Vague labels like 'Services', 'Resources' or 'More' tell users almost nothing. For a Bangladeshi audience, decide whether labels are in Bangla, English or both, and test the words with real users; a word that seems obvious in an office may be unknown in a village.
