Information scent: Researchers Peter Pirolli and Stuart Card described how people look for information much like animals foraging for food. Users follow information scent: cues in labels, icons and descriptions that suggest the path will lead to their goal. If a user looking for lab results sees a tab called 'Reports', the scent is strong and they tap it. If they see 'Documents', 'Records' and 'Files', the scent is weak and they guess. When scent is weak, users backtrack, give up, or call the helpline. Strong scent comes from clear, specific labels written in the users' words.

Sitemaps: A sitemap, or app map, is a diagram of the IA: a tree showing all main sections, the pages or screens inside them, and how they connect. The top node is the home screen; below are the main sections; below those, the individual screens. Sitemaps help the team agree on the structure before designing screens, spot sections that are too crowded or too empty, and find content that has no clear home. For DaktarDekhao, a simple sitemap might show Home at the top, then Find a doctor, My serials, Reports and Profile, each with its own screens below.

Card sorting: How do you find out how users group things? Card sorting is the classic method. You write each item, such as 'Book serial', 'Cancel serial', 'Blood test report', 'Doctor's fee', 'Change phone number', on a separate card, and ask participants to sort the cards into groups that make sense to them. In an open card sort, participants create and name their own groups, which shows how they think and what words they use. In a closed card sort, the groups are given, and participants place cards into them, which tests whether a proposed structure works. A hybrid sort gives groups but lets participants add new ones. Card sorting can be done with paper cards on a table or with online tools.

Analysing a card sort: With, say, fifteen participants, you look for items that most people put together. A simple way is a similarity count: for each pair of cards, count how many participants placed them in the same group. If 13 of 15 put 'Blood test report' with 'X-ray report', that pair belongs together. If 'Doctor's fee' was split, 7 people putting it with booking and 8 with payments, it is an ambiguous item that might appear in both places or need a clearer label. Also look at the names participants gave their groups; they are a free supply of user-tested labels.

Tree testing: Card sorting helps create a structure; tree testing checks whether people can find things in it. In a tree test, sometimes called a reverse card sort, participants see only the text hierarchy of your IA, with no visual design, and are given tasks such as 'Where would you find your blood test result from last week?'. They click through the tree until they choose a location. You measure whether they ended in the right place, how directly they got there, and where they went wrong first. Because there are no visuals, the test isolates the structure and labels.

Depth versus breadth: A key structural decision is how many items to show at each level versus how many levels to have. Suppose an app has 64 features. You could put all 64 on one screen (broad and flat), use two levels of 8 groups with 8 items each (8 x 8 = 64), or use six levels of 2 choices each (2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 64). Very deep structures force many taps and make users guess at every level, multiplying the chance of a wrong turn. Studies of menu design have generally found that broader, shallower structures perform better than deep ones, as long as items on each level are well grouped and clearly labelled. Extremely broad screens, however, become hard to scan, especially on a small phone. In practice, a moderate number of clear groups with two or three levels works well for most apps.

Navigation systems: Navigation is how the IA appears on screen. Global navigation is available everywhere and leads to the main sections. Local navigation moves within a section. Contextual navigation links related things inline, like 'See other doctors in this department'. Utility navigation holds things like settings, help and language switch. A good navigation system always answers three questions for the user: where am I, where can I go, and how do I get back?

Common navigation patterns on mobile: A bottom navigation bar shows the main sections as icons with labels at the bottom of the screen; platform guidelines generally recommend it for roughly three to five top-level destinations, and it is easy to reach with the thumb. Tabs at the top switch between related views within a section. A navigation drawer, opened by the three-line 'hamburger' icon, can hold many items but hides them; studies and practice have shown that hidden navigation is used less, so important destinations should not live only in a drawer. A stack of screens with a back arrow suits step-by-step flows like booking.

Navigation patterns on the web: Websites commonly use a top navigation bar for global sections, side menus for local navigation, and breadcrumbs. Breadcrumbs show the path from the home page to the current page, such as 'Home > Hospitals > Rajshahi > Cardiology', and each part is a link back. They tell users where they are in a deep structure and give a quick way up. Footer links collect secondary information like contact and policies.

Search: When content is large, search becomes essential. Good search tolerates spelling mistakes, which matters a lot for medicine and doctor names typed in English by Bangla speakers; suggests results while typing; and shows helpful results even for partial queries. Search should complement browsing, not replace it, because many users prefer to browse when they do not know the exact name, and a structure also teaches them what the app contains.

Real-life example 1, a university website: Many university websites are organised by the internal structure of the administration: 'Office of the Registrar', 'Controller of Examinations', 'Directorate of Student Affairs'. A student looking for an exam result does not know which office publishes it. A task-based redesign with sections like 'Admission', 'Exams and results', 'Fees and payments' and 'Notices', checked with an open card sort among students, would match how students think. This is a classic IA lesson: organise around users' tasks, not the organisation chart.

Real-life example 2, DaktarDekhao's restructure: The first version had seven bottom tabs: Home, Doctors, Hospitals, Departments, Serials, Reports, Settings. Users kept mixing up Doctors, Hospitals and Departments, which all led to booking. An open card sort with twelve patients showed they thought in terms of 'find a doctor' and 'my things'. The new IA had four bottom tabs: Home, Find a doctor (with filters by hospital and department inside), My serials and reports, and Profile. A tree test showed the success rate for 'find your blood test report' rose clearly after the change.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Typical mistakes include structuring by the organisation chart, using jargon labels, hiding key destinations in a hamburger menu, making structures too deep, and skipping testing. Exams ask: define IA and its components; explain exact versus ambiguous organisation schemes with examples; describe open and closed card sorting and tree testing; discuss depth versus breadth; describe navigation patterns such as breadcrumbs and bottom navigation.

Recap: Information architecture organises and labels content so people can find it. Rosenfeld and Morville describe organisation, labelling, navigation and search systems. Exact schemes are alphabetical, chronological and geographical; ambiguous ones are topic, task, audience and metaphor. Use users' words and strong information scent. Build sitemaps, discover groupings with card sorting and check them with tree testing. Prefer moderate breadth over great depth. Navigation must show where users are, where they can go and how to get back. Next we look at visual design: layout and hierarchy.
key_points: Information architecture organises, structures and labels content so people can find things and know where they are.
Rosenfeld and Morville describe four systems: organisation, labelling, navigation and search.
Exact schemes: alphabetical, chronological, geographical; ambiguous schemes: topic, task, audience, metaphor.
Labels should use the users' words; strong information scent tells users a path leads to their goal.
Open card sorting reveals users' groupings and words; closed sorting tests a given structure; tree testing checks findability.
Broader, shallower structures generally beat deep ones, provided groups are clear and labelled well.
Navigation must answer: where am I, where can I go, how do I get back (bottom bars, tabs, breadcrumbs, search).
lessons.tip: When you design any app, list every feature on sticky notes before drawing a single screen. Sorting those notes into groups, and asking two friends to sort them too, will teach you more about your structure than hours of drawing.
lessons.task: Pick a website or app you find confusing, such as a university or government site. Write 15 of its features on small paper cards and ask two friends to sort them into groups and name each group (an open card sort). Compare their groups with the real menu and propose a better top-level structure of four to six sections.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Rosenfeld and Morville's four main IA systems?
quiz.explain: The four are organisation, labelling, navigation and search. Rendering is a graphics term, not an IA system.

quiz.q: A transaction history listing payments from newest to oldest uses which organisation scheme?
quiz.explain: Ordering by time is chronological, an exact scheme suitable for things that happen over time.

quiz.q: In an open card sort, participants:
options: Place cards into groups the designer has already named
Find items in a text-only tree
Rate the visual design of each card
Create and name their own groups
quiz.explain: Open sorting reveals how users think and what words they use. Closed sorting uses predefined groups; tree testing checks findability.

quiz.q: What does tree testing mainly evaluate?
options: The colours and fonts of the app
Whether users can find items in the structure and labels, without visual design
quiz.explain: Tree testing shows only the text hierarchy and gives findability tasks, isolating structure and labels.

quiz.q: What do breadcrumbs such as 'Home > Hospitals > Rajshahi > Cardiology' help users with?
options: Knowing where they are and moving back up the hierarchy
quiz.explain: Breadcrumbs show the path to the current page, and each part links back to a higher level.

lessons.title: Visual Design I: Layout and Hierarchy
lessons.content:
Open two restaurant menus at a roadside hotel in Sylhet. The first is a single sheet with forty dishes typed in one long list, same size, same colour, prices scattered at random. The second groups the dishes under clear headings like Rice, Curry and Drinks, puts the prices in a neat column on the right, and prints the house special in a bigger box at the top. Both menus contain exactly the same information. Yet with the first you squint and read every line, and with the second you find your biryani in three seconds. The difference is visual design: layout and hierarchy. This lesson shows that visual design is not decoration. It is a tool that decides how fast and how correctly people find things.

Why visual design is functional: Many beginners think visual design means making a screen pretty at the end. In HCI, visual design has jobs to do. It tells users what is important, what belongs together, what to read first and what they can act on. A screen with poor layout forces users to search, compare and guess, which uses up the limited working memory and attention we studied earlier. A screen with good layout lets the eye do the work almost automatically. Beauty matters too, because people often judge attractive interfaces as easier to use, but the main purpose is communication.

The building blocks: Every screen is made of a few basic elements: text, images, icons, buttons, input fields and empty space. Visual design decides their position, size, colour, weight and grouping. This lesson focuses on layout (where things go) and hierarchy (what stands out). The next lesson covers typography, colour and icons in detail. Both build on the Gestalt principles from the perception lesson, which we now apply to real screens.

Grids, the hidden skeleton: A grid is a set of invisible columns and rows that designers use to place elements. Newspapers have used grids for more than a century. On the web a 12-column grid is common because 12 divides evenly into 2, 3, 4 and 6 equal parts, so you can make two, three or four equal cards in a row. On phones a simpler 4-column grid is often used. Elements snap to grid lines, and the spaces between columns, called gutters, stay the same everywhere. The result is a screen that feels orderly even when users cannot say why.

Spacing systems: Good designs also use consistent spacing values. Many design systems use multiples of 4 or 8 pixels (or density-independent units): 8, 16, 24, 32 and so on. If the gap between a label and its field is 8, between two fields 16, and between two sections 32, users see the structure at a glance: small gaps mean 'these belong together', big gaps mean 'new group'. Random gaps of 7, 13 and 22 make a screen look messy and make groups unclear.

Alignment: Alignment means lining elements up along a common edge or centre. When the left edges of labels, fields and buttons all sit on the same vertical line, the eye can scan down smoothly. Every element that is slightly out of line creates a small visual bump that the brain notices. A common rule is to choose one main alignment, usually left alignment for text in left-to-right languages like English and Bangla, and stick to it. Centred text works for short titles but is hard to read in long paragraphs, because each line starts at a different place.

White space: White space, also called negative space, is the empty area between and around elements. It does not have to be white; it is simply space without content. Beginners often try to fill every corner, thinking empty space is wasted. In fact white space is what makes groups visible (the Gestalt principle of proximity), gives important elements room to stand out, and makes text easier to read. A crowded screen feels stressful and slow. Adding space around the main button of a screen often does more for it than making it bigger.

Visual hierarchy, the idea: Visual hierarchy is the order in which the eye notices things. A good hierarchy matches the importance of information: the most important thing is noticed first, the next most important second, and so on. If everything shouts, nothing is heard. The designer's job is to decide the order of importance first, then use visual tools to express it.

Tools of hierarchy, size and weight: Bigger elements are noticed before smaller ones, so headings are larger than body text, and the main number on a dashboard, such as the account balance, is the largest text. Weight means thickness: bold text stands out from regular text. A simple type scale, such as body text 16, subheading 20, heading 24 and page title 32, creates a clear hierarchy without needing many colours.

Tools of hierarchy, colour, contrast and position: High contrast draws attention: a dark button on a light background, or one coloured element among grey ones. That is why most screens have one primary button in a strong brand colour, while secondary actions are outlined or plain text. Position also matters: elements at the top of a screen are usually seen first, and in left-to-right reading cultures the top left is a strong starting point. Placing the main action where the thumb naturally rests at the bottom of a phone screen makes it easier to reach, even if it is not the first thing read.

A quick test for hierarchy, the squint test: Designers often use a simple trick: step back or squint at the screen until the text becomes blurry. What do you still see? The shapes that remain visible are the top of your hierarchy. If you see one clear heading, one main block of content and one primary button, the hierarchy is working. If you see ten equal grey blocks, or the most visible thing is an advertisement banner, the hierarchy is broken.

Gestalt in layout: The Gestalt principles turn into practical layout rules. Proximity: put a label close to its own field and farther from the next field, so nobody wonders which label belongs to which box. Similarity: make all tappable links the same colour, so users learn the pattern. Common region: put related items in a card or box with a border or background, like a doctor's name, specialty and fees inside one card. Continuity: items in a straight line or a list are read as a sequence. Figure-ground: a dialog sits on top of a dimmed background, so it is clearly in front.

Reading patterns, F and Z: Eye-tracking studies by the Nielsen Norman Group found that on text-heavy web pages people often scan in an F-shaped pattern: they read across the top, then across a bit lower, then scan down the left side. This means the first words of headings and paragraphs carry the most weight, so start them with the important words. On simpler pages with little text, such as a landing page, the eye tends to move in a Z shape: top left to top right, diagonally down to the bottom left, then across to the bottom right. Designers place the logo at the top left, key message across the top, and the main button at the end of the Z. These patterns are tendencies, not laws, and good hierarchy can guide the eye in other ways.

Consistency: Consistency means the same kind of element looks and behaves the same everywhere. If primary buttons are blue and rounded on one screen, they should be blue and rounded on all screens. If the screen title is at the top left on the home page, it should be there on every page. Consistency lowers the learning effort, because users learn a pattern once and reuse it. It also has an external side: following platform conventions, such as the back arrow on the top left in Android apps, so users can use what they learned in other apps.

Mobile layout: Phones bring special limits. The screen is small, so one main column is usual, and content is stacked vertically. Thumbs are bigger than mouse pointers, so touch targets must be large enough, around 44 to 48 points or density-independent pixels in common platform guidelines, with space between them. The bottom of the screen is easier to reach with the thumb than the top, which is one reason for bottom navigation bars. Designs should also handle different screen sizes, from small budget phones common in Bangladesh to large tablets, by letting content reflow rather than placing everything at fixed positions.

Worked redesign, a cluttered screen: Take the first version of the DaktarDekhao doctor profile screen. It showed, all in the same size and grey colour: the hospital logo, a news ticker, the doctor's name, degrees, a long biography, fees, chamber times, a map, a share button, a rate button, a report button and, at the very bottom, 'Book serial'. Testing showed users took a long time to find how to book. The redesign started with a priority list: who is this doctor, when is the doctor available, how much does it cost, book now. Then the layout followed: the name in large bold text at the top with a photo; specialty and degrees on the next line in smaller text; a card grouping fees and chamber times; the biography collapsed behind 'Read more'; the news ticker removed; share and report moved into a menu; and 'Book serial' as the only strongly coloured button, fixed at the bottom within thumb reach. Spacing used steps of 8, 16 and 32. In the next round of testing, users found the booking button almost immediately.

Real-life example 1, a news portal: Many Bangladeshi news websites have a home page packed with dozens of headlines, advertisements, a stock ticker and pop-ups. Readers looking for one story struggle. A better layout uses a clear grid, one large lead story at the top, sections with headings, consistent spacing, and fewer competing elements. The information is the same, but the hierarchy tells readers where to look first.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet home screen: A good mobile wallet home screen shows the balance at the top, usually hidden until tapped for privacy, then a grid of large icons for the most common actions such as Send Money, Cash Out, Mobile Recharge and Payment, each with a label, and offers or ads lower down. Notice the hierarchy: the most frequent actions are large and near the top, the grid aligns them neatly, and the equal spacing shows they are a group of similar choices.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes are filling every space, using too many sizes and colours so nothing stands out, making several buttons equally strong so users do not know which is primary, misaligned elements, and labels placed equally close to two fields. Exams often ask you to explain visual hierarchy and the tools that create it, to describe grids and white space and why they matter, to explain the F-pattern and Z-pattern, to apply Gestalt principles to a given screen, and to critique and redesign a cluttered layout with a sketch.

Recap: Visual design is functional: it tells users what matters, what belongs together and what to do. Grids and consistent spacing give structure. Alignment creates smooth scanning lines. White space separates groups and lets important items breathe. Visual hierarchy, built with size, weight, colour, contrast and position, decides what is seen first; the squint test checks it. Gestalt principles become layout rules. F and Z patterns describe common scanning habits. Consistency inside the app and with platform conventions reduces learning. Next lesson: typography, colour and icons.
key_points: Visual design is functional: it shows what is important, what belongs together and what can be acted on.
Grids (often 12 columns on the web, 4 on phones) and spacing in multiples of 4 or 8 give an orderly structure.
Consistent alignment, usually left for English and Bangla text, creates smooth scanning lines.
White space makes groups visible and lets important elements stand out.
Visual hierarchy uses size, weight, colour, contrast and position; the squint test checks it.
Eye-tracking shows F-shaped scanning on text-heavy pages and Z-shaped scanning on simple pages.
Consistency within the app and with platform conventions lowers the learning effort.
lessons.tip: Before you add colour or images to any screen, write a numbered list of what the user should notice first, second and third. Then design the layout to match that list. Hierarchy decided on paper is much easier than hierarchy fixed after the screen is full.
lessons.task: Take a screenshot of a crowded screen from any app or website you use. Squint at it or blur it and note what stands out. Then redraw the screen on paper using a simple 4-column grid, spacing steps of 8, 16 and 32, and only one primary button. Compare the two versions with a friend.

quiz.q: Why is a 12-column grid popular on the web?
options: Because screens are always 12 inches wide
Because browsers can only display 12 columns
Because 12 divides evenly into 2, 3, 4 and 6 equal parts
quiz.explain: Twelve columns can be split into halves, thirds, quarters or sixths, so many card layouts fit neatly.

quiz.q: A label sits exactly halfway between two input fields, and users are unsure which field it describes. Which principle should fix this?
quiz.explain: Proximity says close items are seen as a group. Put the label close to its own field and farther from the next one.

quiz.q: What is the squint test used for?
options: Checking visual hierarchy by seeing what still stands out when blurred
Testing whether text is spelled correctly
quiz.explain: When details blur, only the strongest elements remain visible. Those should be the most important items on the screen.

quiz.q: On text-heavy web pages, eye-tracking research found people often scan in which pattern?
options: A circle from the centre outward
quiz.explain: People read across the top, then a bit lower, then scan down the left side, so first words of headings matter most.

quiz.q: A screen has five buttons, all large and in the same bright colour. What is the main problem?
options: The buttons use too little white space only
The grid has too many columns
There is no clear hierarchy, so users cannot tell which action is primary
quiz.explain: If everything shouts, nothing stands out. One primary button with secondary actions styled more quietly creates a clear hierarchy.

lessons.title: Visual Design II: Typography, Colour and Icons
lessons.content:
Imagine a wedding invitation card printed in a thin, curly font, pale yellow text on a white background, with tiny Bangla letters where the vowel signs crash into the line above. Your uncle holds it at arm's length, then close to his nose, then hands it to you: 'What time is the reception?' The card has all the information, but the typography and colour hide it. Screens have the same problem a thousand times a day. In the last lesson we arranged elements with layout and hierarchy. In this lesson we look at the materials those elements are made of: letters, colours and icons.

Why typography matters: Most of what users do on screens is read: labels, buttons, messages, prices, names. Typography is the craft of choosing and arranging type so that text is readable, clear and fits the purpose. Good typography is invisible; people simply read. Poor typography makes people slow down, misread numbers or give up. Typography also carries tone: a banking app and a children's game should not look the same.

Typefaces and fonts: A typeface is a family design, such as Roboto or Noto Sans Bengali. A font, strictly speaking, is one particular style and weight of that typeface, such as Roboto Bold. In everyday talk people use the two words loosely. The two big groups are serif typefaces, which have small strokes or 'feet' at the ends of letters (like Times New Roman), and sans serif typefaces, which do not (like Arial, Roboto or Helvetica). On screens, sans serif typefaces are very common for interface text because they stay clear at small sizes, while serif faces are often used for long reading or headings. Decorative and script typefaces should be kept for logos or special titles, never for body text or buttons.

Legibility and readability: Two related words. Legibility is how easily individual letters can be told apart: can you distinguish 1, l and I, or 0 and O? This matters a lot for passwords, codes and phone numbers. Readability is how easily blocks of text can be read and understood, which depends on size, spacing, line length and contrast as well as on the typeface. A legible typeface can still produce unreadable text if the lines are too long or too tightly packed.

Size: Text that is too small is the most common typography problem. For phones, body text around 16 density-independent pixels (or points) is a widely used starting point, and platform guidelines suggest not going much below about 12 for even the smallest captions. Users can also increase system font size in accessibility settings, so a good app must not break when text grows: buttons should expand, and text should wrap instead of being cut off.

Line length: Line length is the number of characters per line. If lines are very long, the eye struggles to find the start of the next line; if they are very short, reading becomes choppy. Typographers commonly recommend around 50 to 75 characters per line for comfortable reading of body text in English. On phones this happens almost naturally; on wide desktop screens, designers limit the width of text columns instead of letting a paragraph stretch across the whole monitor.

Line height and spacing: Line height (also called leading) is the vertical distance between lines. Too tight and lines blur together; too loose and they fall apart. For body text, a line height of about 1.4 to 1.6 times the font size is a common choice, and WCAG's text spacing guidance uses 1.5 as a reference. Spacing between paragraphs should be larger than between lines, so paragraphs read as groups, which is the Gestalt principle of proximity again.

Bangla typography: Bangla text has its own needs. Bangla letters hang from a horizontal headstroke called the matra, many vowel signs sit above or below the letters, and conjuncts (juktakkhor) such as ক্ষ or ন্ত্র combine several letters into one shape. This means Bangla usually needs more line height than English, so vowel signs above one line do not touch those below the previous line. It also means Bangla text at the same nominal size often looks smaller or more crowded than English, so designers frequently use a slightly larger size for Bangla. Most importantly, the text must be stored in Unicode and rendered with a proper Unicode font, such as Noto Sans Bengali, SolaimanLipi, Kalpurush or Hind Siliguri, and a text engine that handles conjunct shaping correctly. Older non-Unicode encodings, used with some legacy Bangla typing tools, show garbage characters when the matching font is missing, which still causes broken text in some documents and websites.

Mixing Bangla and English: Many Bangladeshi interfaces mix the two scripts, for example a Bangla label with an English medicine name. Choose a Bangla typeface and a Latin typeface that look balanced together in size and weight, or a family designed to cover both scripts. Test with real content, including long words and numbers, and decide consistently whether numbers appear as Bangla digits or Western digits on each screen.

Colour basics: Colour can be described with three properties. Hue is the colour family: red, green, blue. Saturation is how intense or grey the colour is. Lightness (or value) is how light or dark it is. Two colours with the same hue but different lightness, like dark green and light green, are good for building a calm palette. The colour wheel helps find combinations: complementary colours sit opposite each other (blue and orange) and create strong contrast; analogous colours sit next to each other (blue, blue-green, green) and feel harmonious.

Colour in interfaces, roles not decoration: In interface design, colour is given roles. A primary colour, often the brand colour, marks the main actions and key highlights. Neutral colours, greys and off-whites, make up backgrounds and most text. Semantic colours carry meaning: red or similar for errors and destructive actions, green for success, amber or yellow for warnings, blue for information or links. Keeping these roles consistent means users learn them once. If red means error on one screen and 'special offer' on another, users get confused.

The 60-30-10 idea: A popular rule of thumb, borrowed from interior design, is to use a dominant colour for about 60 percent of the area, a secondary colour for about 30 percent and an accent colour for about 10 percent. In an app this often means a neutral background as the 60, a secondary surface colour for cards or bars as the 30, and the brand accent for buttons and highlights as the 10. It is a guideline for balance, not a scientific law, but it stops beginners from painting every element a different bright colour.

Colour and contrast: Text must have enough contrast with its background. Light grey text on white may look elegant on a designer's expensive monitor but becomes invisible on a budget phone in Dhaka sunlight. The accessibility lesson covers the exact contrast ratio rules from WCAG; here remember the habit: check contrast early, especially for small text and for text on top of images.

Never rely on colour alone: About 1 in 12 men and about 1 in 200 women have some form of colour vision deficiency, most commonly difficulty separating red and green. If a form shows wrong fields only by turning their border red, some users will not see it. Always pair colour with a second signal: an icon, a text message, an underline, or a pattern. A chart with red and green lines should also use different line styles or direct labels.

Colour and culture: Colours carry cultural meanings. In Bangladesh red is strongly linked with weddings and celebrations, as in a bride's red sari, and also with danger and the red of the national flag; white is often associated with mourning; green is linked with the flag and with nature. Meanings also depend on context: red can mean a loss in a finance app. Designers should check meanings with their actual users rather than copying palettes from foreign apps without thought.

Icons: Icons are small pictures that represent actions or objects. They save space and can be recognised quickly, but only if users already know them. A small set of icons is widely understood, such as a magnifying glass for search, a house for home, a bell for notifications and a trash can for delete. Many others are ambiguous: is a heart 'like', 'save' or 'health'? Is a star 'favourite' or 'rate'? Usability research has repeatedly found that icons without text labels are often misunderstood. The safe rule is to show icons together with short text labels, especially in navigation bars and for less common actions.

Designing good icons: Good icons are simple, use one consistent style (all outlined or all filled, same line thickness), are large enough to tap, and match the user's world. An icon of a floppy disk for 'save' is a convention many young users have never seen as an object but have learned as a symbol. For low-literacy users, familiar real-world pictures, such as a taka note for payments or a phone handset for calling, can help, but they still need testing with real people.

Design systems and platform guidelines: A design system is a collection of reusable components, rules and styles: colours, type scale, spacing, buttons, cards, icons and how to use them. Big platforms publish their own: Google's Material Design for Android and the web, and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines for iPhone, iPad and Mac. They specify things like minimum touch target sizes (48 dp in Material, 44 points in Apple's guidelines), type scales, and standard component behaviour. Following them makes your app feel familiar to users of that platform and saves design time. Companies also build their own design systems so dozens of designers and developers produce consistent screens.

Real-life example 1, DaktarDekhao's typography fix: Early testing showed elderly patients struggled to read appointment times. The team increased body text to a larger size, increased Bangla line height so vowel signs no longer touched, switched the time display to a bold weight with clear digits, and replaced pale grey text with dark grey. They also made sure the app respected the phone's large-text setting. Complaints about 'small writing' disappeared from feedback.

Real-life example 2, a status colour mistake: A delivery app showed order status only by colour: a green dot for delivered, a red dot for cancelled, an orange dot for on the way. Some users with colour vision deficiency could not tell the dots apart, and in sunlight nobody could. The fix was to add words next to each dot: 'Delivered', 'Cancelled', 'On the way', and a small icon for each. Colour became a helper, not the only messenger.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes include too many typefaces on one screen (two families are usually enough), tiny or low-contrast text, decorative fonts for body text, cramped Bangla line height, a rainbow of colours with no roles, and icons without labels. Exams ask you to distinguish serif and sans serif, legibility and readability, to state recommended line lengths, to explain why colour must not be the only signal, to describe the 60-30-10 guideline, and to explain what a design system is with examples.

Recap: Typography makes text readable: choose clear typefaces, adequate size, 50 to 75 characters per line and line height around 1.5. Bangla needs Unicode fonts, correct conjunct shaping and extra line height. Colour has hue, saturation and lightness; give colours roles, keep them consistent, check contrast and never rely on colour alone. Colour meanings depend on culture. Icons work best when familiar, consistent and labelled. Design systems such as Material Design and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines package these decisions for reuse.
key_points: Typography is about readable, clear text; serif faces have small strokes at letter ends, sans serif faces do not.
Legibility is telling letters apart; readability is how easily blocks of text are read and understood.
Common guidance: body text around 16 on phones, 50 to 75 characters per line, line height about 1.4 to 1.6.
Bangla needs Unicode fonts, correct conjunct shaping and more line height for vowel signs above and below.
Give colours roles (primary, neutral, semantic) and keep them consistent; 60-30-10 is a balance rule of thumb.
Never rely on colour alone: about 1 in 12 men have a colour vision deficiency.
Icons should be familiar, consistent and labelled; design systems like Material Design and Apple's HIG package these rules.
lessons.tip: Keep a small personal 'type and colour card': one Bangla font, one Latin font, a type scale of four sizes, one primary colour, neutrals and four semantic colours. Starting every project from a tiny fixed set like this stops you from making the rainbow-and-ten-fonts mistake.
lessons.task: Open an app in Bangla on your phone and screenshot a text-heavy screen. Check: do vowel signs touch between lines, are numbers easy to read, are any icons unlabelled? Then increase your phone's font size to the largest setting and see whether the app breaks. Write down three problems you found.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between serif and sans serif typefaces?
options: Serif typefaces have small strokes at the ends of letters; sans serif do not
Sans serif typefaces cannot show numbers
Serif typefaces are only for Bangla
quiz.explain: Serifs are the small 'feet' at letter ends. Sans serif means without serifs, and these are common for interface text.

quiz.q: Why does Bangla text usually need more line height than English text?
options: Vowel signs and conjuncts extend above and below the letters, so lines can collide
Bangla is read from right to left
quiz.explain: Signs above and below letters need extra vertical space so they do not touch the line above or below.

quiz.q: A form marks invalid fields only by turning their border red. What is the main problem?
options: Some users with colour vision deficiency may not notice it, so a second signal is needed
Red is too expensive to display
Borders cannot be coloured on phones
quiz.explain: Colour should never be the only signal. Add an icon and a text message next to the field.

quiz.q: Which statement about icons is best supported by usability research?
options: Icons are always understood faster than words
Every icon has one universal meaning
Icons without text labels are often misunderstood, so labels help
Icons should change style on every screen
quiz.explain: Only a few icons are widely understood. Short labels remove ambiguity, especially for less common actions.

quiz.q: What is a design system?
options: A collection of reusable components, styles and rules for building consistent interfaces
quiz.explain: Design systems such as Material Design or Apple's Human Interface Guidelines define colours, type, spacing and components so screens stay consistent.

lessons.title: Heuristic Evaluation
lessons.content:
Before a big cricket match, a coach does not wait for the opponents to expose every weakness on the field. He sits with two or three experienced players, watches the practice session with a checklist in mind: footwork, shot selection, running between the wickets, and writes down what is going wrong. It is quick, cheap and catches most obvious problems before the real test. Heuristic evaluation is that coach's checklist for interfaces. A few evaluators look at a design against a short list of proven principles and report where it breaks them. It is one of the most used evaluation methods in HCI because it is fast, cheap and needs no users at all.

Inspection methods: HCI evaluation methods fall into two big groups. In user testing, real users try the system and we observe them; the next lessons cover this. In inspection methods, experts examine the interface themselves, without users, looking for problems using principles, guidelines or a step-by-step procedure. Heuristic evaluation and the cognitive walkthrough are the two most famous inspection methods. Inspections are sometimes called 'discount usability' because they cost little and can be used early, even on paper sketches or wireframes.

What a heuristic is: A heuristic is a rule of thumb: a general principle that usually leads to good results, but is not an exact law. 'Show users what is happening' is a heuristic. It does not tell you exactly which progress bar to use, but it tells you what to look for. Jakob Nielsen developed heuristic evaluation with Rolf Molich around 1990, and in 1994 Nielsen published a refined list of ten usability heuristics based on an analysis of many usability problems. That list is still the standard reference and is what exams expect you to know.

Heuristic 1, visibility of system status: The system should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time. Example violation: after tapping 'Pay', nothing changes for five seconds. Good practice: a loading indicator immediately, then a clear success screen. Others: showing which tab is selected, how many steps remain in a form, whether a message was sent, delivered or read.

Heuristic 2, match between system and the real world: The system should speak the users' language, with words, phrases and concepts familiar to them, rather than system-oriented terms, and follow real-world conventions so information appears in a natural and logical order. Violation: a hospital app shows 'Entity not found (code 404)' instead of 'No doctor found with this name'. Good practice: using 'Serial' because that is what Bangladeshi patients say, showing taka with the ৳ sign, and ordering dates in a familiar day-month-year form.

Heuristic 3, user control and freedom: Users often choose functions by mistake and need a clearly marked 'emergency exit' to leave the unwanted state without going through an extended dialog. Support undo and redo. Violation: a multi-step booking flow with no back button and no way to cancel except closing the app. Good practice: a visible back arrow, a cancel option, undo after deleting a message.

Heuristic 4, consistency and standards: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions. Violation: the confirm button is on the right on one screen and on the left on another; one screen says 'Remove', another says 'Delete' for the same action. Good practice: one name and one style per action, and platform conventions such as the Android back behaviour. Nielsen distinguishes internal consistency (within your product) and external consistency (with other products and conventions).

Heuristic 5, error prevention: Good error messages are important, but even better is a careful design that prevents a problem from occurring in the first place. Either eliminate error-prone conditions or check for them and ask users to confirm before they commit. Violation: a free text field for dates that accepts anything. Good practice: a date picker that only allows valid dates, disabling 'Send' until the number is complete, showing the receiver's name before sending money. This links directly to the slips and mistakes lesson.

Heuristic 6, recognition rather than recall: Minimise the user's memory load by making objects, actions and options visible. The user should not have to remember information from one part of the interface to another. Violation: a screen that asks for a 'transaction ID from the previous screen' that is no longer shown. Good practice: recent contacts list instead of typing numbers, search suggestions, showing the selected doctor's name on the payment screen. This rests on the memory lesson: recognising is easier than recalling.

Heuristic 7, flexibility and efficiency of use: Shortcuts, hidden from novice users, may speed up interaction for experts, so the system can serve both inexperienced and experienced users. Allow users to tailor frequent actions. Violation: an expert pharmacist must go through five menus every time to record the same common sale. Good practice: keyboard shortcuts, 'repeat last order', favourites, saved payment details, while beginners still have the plain step-by-step path.

Heuristic 8, aesthetic and minimalist design: Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed. Every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units and reduces their visibility. Violation: a home screen with twelve banners, a news ticker and pop-ups covering the main actions. Good practice: show the most needed items, move the rest into secondary screens. Note that minimalist does not mean 'flat and empty'; it means focused on what matters.

Heuristic 9, help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors: Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution. Violation: 'Transaction failed. Error 0x8001.' Good practice: 'Payment failed because your balance (৳120) is less than the fee (৳300). Add money or choose another payment method.' Also keep the user's input so they do not have to retype everything.

Heuristic 10, help and documentation: It is best if the system does not need any extra explanation, but it may be necessary to provide documentation to help users understand how to complete their tasks. Help should be easy to search, focused on the user's task, list concrete steps and not be too long. Good practice: short tips at the point of need, a searchable FAQ, a short video showing how to book a serial, and contact details for human help.

Running a heuristic evaluation, the process: A typical evaluation has a few stages. First, a briefing: evaluators learn the purpose of the system, the typical users and the main tasks, and agree on the heuristic list. Second, independent evaluation: each evaluator goes through the interface alone, usually at least twice, first to get a feel for the flow and second to examine each screen and element. They note every problem, where it occurs and which heuristic it violates. Working independently matters, because evaluators influence each other if they work together. Third, a debriefing: evaluators merge their lists, remove duplicates and discuss problems and possible fixes. Fourth, severity rating and a report.

How many evaluators: Nielsen's studies found that a single evaluator typically finds only about a third of the usability problems, because different people notice different things. Adding evaluators finds more, with diminishing returns; three to five evaluators usually find a large majority of the problems at reasonable cost. Evaluators who know both usability and the domain, such as someone who understands both HCI and hospital workflows, find more problems than novices.

Severity ratings: Not all problems are equally serious, and teams have limited time, so each problem gets a severity rating. Nielsen's widely used scale is: 0, not a usability problem at all; 1, cosmetic problem only, fix if extra time is available; 2, minor usability problem, low priority; 3, major usability problem, important to fix, high priority; 4, usability catastrophe, imperative to fix before release. Severity depends on the frequency of the problem (how often it occurs), its impact (how hard it is to overcome) and its persistence (whether users can learn to work around it or it keeps bothering them). Ratings are best made by each evaluator independently and then averaged.

Writing good findings: Each finding should state where the problem is, what the problem is, which heuristic it violates, the severity, and a suggested fix, ideally with a screenshot. Example: 'Payment screen. After entering the PIN there is no feedback for 4 to 6 seconds; users may tap again and pay twice. Heuristic 1, visibility of system status. Severity 3. Fix: show a processing indicator immediately and disable the button until the result appears.' A list of good findings is something developers can act on directly.

Worked mini-evaluation, DaktarDekhao: Three evaluators inspected the booking flow. Merged findings included: 'Serial confirmed' message shows no date or doctor name (heuristic 1, severity 3); the word 'Slot' is used, but patients say 'Serial' (heuristic 2, severity 2); no way to cancel a booking inside the app (heuristic 3, severity 3); the confirm button changes position between screens (heuristic 4, severity 2); the phone number field accepts letters (heuristic 5, severity 2); a hospital logo is slightly blurry (heuristic 8, severity 1). The team fixed the severity 3 items first, then planned the rest.

Strengths and limits: Heuristic evaluation is quick, cheap, needs no users, can be done early on sketches and finds many problems, including small ones. But it has limits. Evaluators are not real users and may miss problems caused by users' real context, knowledge or language, such as a rural user not understanding an English term. It can also produce 'false alarms', problems that real users never actually experience. Results depend heavily on the evaluators' skill. That is why heuristic evaluation is usually combined with usability testing: inspect first to remove obvious problems cheaply, then test with real users to find what experts cannot predict.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students sometimes list heuristics without being able to give an example of a violation; always pair each heuristic with a concrete example. Another mistake is evaluating as a group from the start, which reduces the number of distinct problems found. Some confuse severity with how annoying a problem feels to the evaluator; severity should consider frequency, impact and persistence. Exams often ask you to list and explain Nielsen's ten heuristics, describe the evaluation process, explain severity ratings, discuss how many evaluators to use, compare heuristic evaluation with user testing, and evaluate a given screen.

Recap: Heuristic evaluation is an inspection method where a few evaluators examine an interface against Nielsen's ten heuristics: visibility of system status; match with the real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recover from errors; help and documentation. Evaluators work independently, then merge findings and rate severity from 0 to 4 using frequency, impact and persistence. Three to five evaluators find most problems. It is cheap and early but does not replace testing with real users.
key_points: Heuristic evaluation is an inspection method: experts check an interface against principles, without users.
Nielsen (with Molich) developed it around 1990; the ten heuristics were refined in 1994.
The ten heuristics: system status, real-world match, user control, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall, flexibility, minimalist design, error recovery, help.
Evaluators first work independently, usually going through the interface at least twice, then merge findings.
A single evaluator finds only about a third of problems; three to five evaluators find most of them.
Severity ratings 0 to 4 consider frequency, impact and persistence.
It is cheap and early but can miss real-context problems and raise false alarms, so combine it with user testing.
lessons.tip: Learn each heuristic as a pair: its name plus one Bangladeshi app example of a violation you have personally seen. In an exam, examples earn the marks; a bare list of names rarely does.
lessons.task: Choose one app you use, such as a ticket, food delivery or wallet app. Go through one main task twice, noting every problem with the heuristic it violates and a severity from 0 to 4. Ask a friend to do the same alone, then merge your lists and count how many problems only one of you found.

quiz.q: A payment app shows nothing for five seconds after the user taps Pay. Which heuristic is violated most directly?
quiz.explain: Users should always be informed about what is going on through timely feedback, such as a processing indicator.

quiz.q: Why should evaluators work independently before merging results?
options: Because group work is not allowed in HCI
Because it makes the report shorter
Because evaluators influence each other in groups and find fewer different problems
quiz.explain: Different people notice different problems. Working alone first maximises the variety of problems found.

quiz.q: On Nielsen's severity scale, what does a rating of 4 mean?
options: Usability catastrophe that must be fixed before release
quiz.explain: The scale runs 0 (not a problem), 1 (cosmetic), 2 (minor), 3 (major), 4 (catastrophe).

quiz.q: A screen asks users to type an ID shown on the previous screen, which is no longer visible. Which heuristic is violated?
options: Match between system and the real world
quiz.explain: Users should not need to remember information from one part of the interface to another; keep it visible.

quiz.q: Which is a real limitation of heuristic evaluation?
options: It can miss problems that come from real users' context and can raise false alarms
It always needs at least 50 users
It can only be done after the app is released
It cannot find any problems in early sketches
quiz.explain: Evaluators are not real users, so some problems are missed and some reported problems never bother real users. Combine it with user testing.

lessons.title: Cognitive Walkthrough and Other Inspections
lessons.content:
Imagine your cousin has just arrived in Dhaka from a village and wants to buy an intercity bus ticket on an app for the first time. She has never used this app. Nobody is there to help her. At every screen she has to guess: what should I tap now? Is this the right button? Did it work? A cognitive walkthrough is a way for designers to put themselves in her shoes, step by step, and ask those exact questions before she ever meets the app. In the last lesson heuristic evaluation looked at the whole interface against general principles. The cognitive walkthrough looks at one task at a time, through the eyes of a new user.

What a cognitive walkthrough is: A cognitive walkthrough is an inspection method in which evaluators step through the actions needed to complete a task and, at each step, ask whether a typical new user would know what to do and would understand the result. It was developed in the early 1990s by researchers including Clayton Lewis, Peter Polson, Cathleen Wharton and John Rieman, based on a theory of how people learn by exploring a new system. Its main focus is learnability: can someone use the system successfully the first time, without training or a manual?

Why exploration matters: Most people do not read manuals. They learn an app by trying things: looking at the screen, choosing what seems closest to their goal, and checking whether it worked. The cognitive walkthrough simulates this exploring behaviour. If at any step the right action is hidden, badly labelled, or gives confusing feedback, an exploring user gets lost. These are exactly the problems the walkthrough is designed to find.

What you need before starting: A walkthrough needs four inputs. First, a description of the users: who they are, what they already know, what devices and apps they have used. 'First-time smartphone app users aged 40 to 60, comfortable with phone calls and mobile recharge, little English' is a useful profile. Second, a task, written as the user would understand it: 'Buy one bus ticket from Dhaka to Rajshahi for tomorrow morning'. Third, the correct action sequence: the list of every action needed to complete the task with the current design. Fourth, the interface itself, as a prototype, wireframes or a working app.

The four questions: At every step in the action sequence, evaluators ask four questions. One: will the user try to achieve the right effect? In other words, does the user's goal at this moment match what the system needs? Two: will the user notice that the correct action is available? Is the button, menu or gesture visible? Three: will the user associate the correct action with the effect they are trying to achieve? Does the label or icon clearly match what they want? Four: if the correct action is performed, will the user see that progress is being made toward the task? Is there clear feedback?

The four questions and Norman's gulfs: Notice how these questions map to ideas you already know. Questions one to three are about the gulf of execution: having the right goal, finding the action and recognising it as right. Question four is about the gulf of evaluation: seeing and understanding the result. The walkthrough is a structured way of checking both gulfs at every single step of a task.

Recording the answers: For each step, evaluators write a short success or failure story. If the answer to any question is 'no' or 'maybe not', they explain why, from the user's point of view, and note the problem and an idea for a fix. A simple table works: step number, action, answers to the four questions, problem, suggested fix. The method is slow, but the result is very concrete: you know exactly at which step and why a new user will fail.

Worked example, the bus ticket app, steps 1 to 3: Task: buy one ticket from Dhaka to Rajshahi for tomorrow morning. Step 1: tap the 'From' field on the home screen. Q1, will she try this? Yes, she wants to choose where she leaves from. Q2, will she notice it? The field shows grey text 'Leaving from' in a large box: yes. Q3, will she connect it with her goal? Yes. Q4, will she see progress? A list of cities appears: yes. Step 2: type 'Dha' and pick 'Dhaka'. All four questions answered yes. Step 3: the app then requires choosing a specific counter such as Gabtoli or Mohakhali, on a second list with no explanation. Q1: maybe not; she thinks she has already chosen her city and may not expect to choose a counter. Q3: the heading 'Boarding point' is unfamiliar to her. Problem: an unexpected extra step with an unfamiliar term. Fix: label it 'Where will you get on the bus?' and show counters with area names.

Worked example, steps 4 to 7: Step 4: choose the date. The calendar opens with today highlighted. Q2 and Q3 are fine, but there is a small 'Tomorrow' shortcut chip that many would like; adding it would help. Step 5: choose a bus from the list. The list shows times in 24-hour format, such as 07:30 and 21:30, with operator names. Q3: maybe; some users read 21:30 with difficulty. Fix: show 'Morning 7:30' and 'Night 9:30' with am or pm. Step 6: choose a seat on the seat map. Q2: the seat map is visible, but Q4 is a problem: after tapping a seat, it changes only from grey to a slightly darker grey. She cannot see that it is selected and taps again, unselecting it. Fix: strong colour plus a tick, and a summary 'Seat B2 selected'. Step 7: tap 'Proceed'. Q2: the button is below the seat map, off screen on small phones. Fix: a fixed button at the bottom showing the price.

What the example shows: In a few steps the walkthrough found several problems that the design team, who knew the app by heart, had never noticed: an unexpected step, unfamiliar words, a time format, weak feedback on the seat map and a hidden button. None of these is a bug in the code. They are all learnability problems for a first-time user, which is the walkthrough's speciality.

Strengths of the cognitive walkthrough: It is cheap and needs no users, so it can be done early, even on paper prototypes. It is focused on tasks, so the problems found are directly related to what users actually need to do. It produces precise explanations of why a problem happens, which helps designers fix the cause. It is especially good for walk-up-and-use systems such as kiosks, ticket machines, ATMs and public service apps, where users get no training.

Weaknesses: It is slow and can feel repetitive, because the four questions are asked at every step. It covers only the tasks you choose, so problems elsewhere are missed. It focuses on new users, so it says little about efficiency for experts or about satisfaction. And the evaluators still have to imagine the user; if their user profile is wrong, their answers will be wrong. For these reasons a streamlined version was later proposed that uses just two questions per step: will the user know what to do at this step, and if they do the right thing, will they know that they did the right thing and are making progress?

Pluralistic walkthrough: A pluralistic walkthrough brings together three kinds of people in one session: representative users, developers and usability experts. They all look at printed screens or a prototype for a task, one screen at a time. Each person first writes down, alone, what action they would take on that screen. Then the group discusses, with users speaking first so that experts do not dominate. Developers hear users' confusion directly, which often convinces them more than any report. It is slower to organise but mixes inspection with real user input.

Guideline review and standards inspection: In a guideline review, evaluators check the interface against a list of detailed design guidelines, such as an organisation's style guide, platform guidelines like Material Design or Apple's Human Interface Guidelines, or accessibility guidelines like WCAG. A standards inspection checks that the interface follows a specific formal standard, for example a government web standard. These are thorough but can involve hundreds of items, and passing every guideline does not guarantee that real users can complete their tasks.

Consistency inspection: In a consistency inspection, designers from different teams of the same product, or from a family of products, compare their screens to make sure terminology, colours, layouts, icons and behaviours are consistent. For example, a bank with a mobile app, a website and ATMs might check that 'Fund transfer' is called the same thing and works the same way everywhere. It directly supports Nielsen's consistency heuristic.

Comparing inspection with user testing: Inspection methods are cheaper, faster and possible early, without recruiting users. They find many problems, especially obvious and rule-based ones. But they rely on experts predicting users, so they can miss problems that come from users' real knowledge, culture and environment, and they can report problems that do not bother real users. User testing finds the real problems real people have, but costs more and needs a working prototype. Good practice is to combine them: inspect early to clean up the obvious issues, then test with users so the testing time is spent on the problems experts could not predict.

Real-life example, a government service kiosk: Imagine a self-service kiosk at a district office where citizens can check the status of an application by entering a tracking number. A cognitive walkthrough for the task 'check my application status' with a profile of first-time, low-literacy users might find: the start screen only says 'Touch to begin' in English (Q2 problem), the tracking number field does not show where on the receipt to find the number (Q3 problem), and after submission the result shows a code like 'STAT-04' rather than 'Your application is approved, collect it from counter 3' (Q4 problem). Each fix is cheap, but without the walkthrough the kiosk might stand unused in the corner.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A common mistake is answering the questions as yourself, an expert, instead of as the described new user. Another is skipping the correct action sequence and walking through vaguely. Some students confuse the cognitive walkthrough with heuristic evaluation; remember: heuristic evaluation is principle-based and looks at the whole interface, the cognitive walkthrough is task-based, step-by-step and focused on learnability. Exams ask: list the inputs and the four questions, perform a walkthrough on a given task, compare cognitive walkthrough with heuristic evaluation, and describe the pluralistic walkthrough.

Recap: The cognitive walkthrough is a task-based inspection method focused on learnability for new users who learn by exploring. Inputs: user profile, task, correct action sequence and interface. At each step ask: will the user try to achieve the right effect, notice the correct action, associate it with their goal, and see progress? The first three questions check the gulf of execution, the fourth the gulf of evaluation. Other inspections include the pluralistic walkthrough, guideline and standards reviews and consistency inspections. Inspections are cheap and early, but should be combined with testing on real users.
key_points: A cognitive walkthrough steps through a task action by action, from the viewpoint of a new user learning by exploration.
It was developed in the early 1990s by Lewis, Polson, Wharton, Rieman and colleagues, and focuses on learnability.
Inputs: user profile, a realistic task, the correct action sequence, and the interface or prototype.
Four questions per step: right effect, notice the action, associate action with goal, see progress.
Questions one to three check the gulf of execution; question four checks the gulf of evaluation.
A pluralistic walkthrough brings users, developers and usability experts together, with users speaking first.
Guideline reviews, standards inspections and consistency inspections complement walkthroughs; all inspections should be combined with user testing.
lessons.tip: When you do a walkthrough, write the user profile on a sticky note and stick it beside the screen. Every time you answer a question, glance at the note and ask whether that person, not you, would answer the same way.
lessons.task: Pick a task such as 'recharge 20 taka to a friend's number' on an app you know. Write a user profile for a first-time elderly user, list every action step, then answer the four questions for each step in a small table. Find at least two steps where an answer is 'no' and suggest a fix.

quiz.q: What is the main focus of a cognitive walkthrough?
options: Learnability for new users who explore the system
quiz.explain: The walkthrough simulates a first-time user learning by exploring, step by step through a task.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the inputs needed before a cognitive walkthrough?
options: The correct action sequence for the task
The source code of the app
quiz.explain: You need a user profile, a task, the correct action sequence and the interface. Code is not needed; walkthroughs can be done on paper.

quiz.q: After tapping a seat, it changes only slightly in colour and users cannot tell it is selected. Which walkthrough question fails?
options: Will the user try to achieve the right effect?
Will the user notice the correct action is available?
Will the user see that progress is being made?
Will the user associate the action with the effect?
quiz.explain: The action was done correctly, but feedback is too weak. That is the fourth question, about seeing progress, which relates to the gulf of evaluation.

quiz.q: How does a cognitive walkthrough differ from heuristic evaluation?
options: The walkthrough is task-based and step-by-step; heuristic evaluation checks the whole interface against general principles
The walkthrough always needs 30 real users
Heuristic evaluation can only be done after release
They are exactly the same method
quiz.explain: Both are inspections, but the walkthrough follows specific tasks through a new user's eyes, while heuristic evaluation uses a list of principles.

quiz.q: In a pluralistic walkthrough, why do users usually speak first in each discussion?
options: Because users must approve the budget
Because developers are not allowed to speak
So that experts and developers do not dominate and users' real reactions are heard
quiz.explain: Letting users speak first keeps their honest reactions from being overshadowed by experts and developers.

lessons.title: Usability Testing
lessons.content:
A cook can taste her own biryani a hundred times and think it is perfect. The real test comes when guests eat it: one finds it too salty, another cannot find the meat under the rice, a child refuses it because it is too spicy. The cook learns more in ten minutes of watching guests eat than in a week of tasting alone. Usability testing is the same idea for interfaces. Instead of asking experts what they think, we put the design in front of real users, give them real tasks, and watch what happens. It is the most direct and convincing way to find out whether people can actually use what we built.

What usability testing is: Usability testing is an evaluation method where representative users try to complete realistic tasks with a product or prototype while observers watch, listen and measure. The aim is to find usability problems and to measure how well the design supports users' goals. It is different from asking opinions in a survey or a focus group. We do not ask 'Do you like this app?'; we watch whether people can book a serial, send money or find a bus, and where they struggle.

Goals of a test: Tests have two broad goals. Formative testing happens during design, often with prototypes, to find and fix problems; it is mostly qualitative: what goes wrong and why. Summative testing happens on a nearly finished or finished product to measure its usability, such as success rates and task times, maybe to compare with a competitor or a previous version or check against a target. Before any test, write down what you want to learn, for example: 'Can first-time users book a serial in under two minutes without help?'

Participants and recruiting: Participants should represent the real users, not your classmates or the development team, who know too much. For DaktarDekhao that means patients and family members of different ages, including older people and people with little smartphone experience. Recruit through clinics, community groups or relatives of friends, with a short screening questionnaire to check they fit the profile. Small gifts such as mobile recharge are a common thank-you. Avoid testing only with people who are very comfortable with technology; they will hide the problems that matter most.

Writing tasks: Tasks should be realistic, specific and written in the user's language, without giving away the answer. A bad task: 'Tap the Book Serial button on Dr. Rahman's profile.' It tells the user exactly what to press. A good task: 'Your mother has knee pain. Find an orthopaedic doctor at the district hospital and get a serial for this Thursday.' Each task should have a clear end point so you know whether it was completed. Five to eight tasks fill a session of about 45 to 60 minutes.

The think-aloud protocol: The most common technique in usability testing is think-aloud. Participants are asked to say what they are thinking while they work: what they are looking for, what they expect, what confuses them. 'I want to choose the date, I am looking for a calendar, hmm, is this the date? No, this is the time...' These spoken thoughts reveal the reasons behind actions, which pure observation cannot show. Moderators gently remind silent participants with neutral prompts such as 'What are you thinking now?', never with hints like 'Have you tried the menu?'.

Concurrent and retrospective think-aloud: In concurrent think-aloud the participant speaks while doing the task, as above. It gives rich, immediate thoughts but can slow people down and change their behaviour slightly. In retrospective think-aloud the participant first completes the task silently, then watches a recording of the session and explains what they were thinking at each point. It keeps task times more natural but relies on memory. Concurrent is more common for formative testing; retrospective is useful when you also want accurate timings.

Moderated and unmoderated, lab and remote: In a moderated test a facilitator is present, in person or by video call, to give tasks, prompt thinking aloud and ask follow-up questions. In an unmoderated test participants complete tasks on their own using an online testing tool that records the screen and their voice. Unmoderated tests are cheaper and faster for many participants but you cannot ask 'why?' in the moment. Tests can happen in a usability lab, with a one-way mirror or cameras, or remotely in the participant's own home or workplace, which shows real devices and real network conditions. For Bangladeshi users, testing on their own budget phones and mobile data can reveal problems that a fast office Wi-Fi never would.

The moderator's behaviour: The moderator must stay neutral. Before starting, explain that you are testing the design, not the person, that there are no wrong answers, and that they can stop at any time. Get informed consent, especially if recording. During the test, do not help, do not explain the interface and do not show disappointment. If a participant asks 'Should I press this?', return the question: 'What would you do if I were not here?'. Only step in if the person is completely stuck and upset, then note the task as failed.

Metrics, effectiveness: The most basic measure is task success: did the participant complete the task correctly? The success rate is the number of successful participants divided by the total. If 6 out of 8 participants book the serial correctly, the success rate is 6 / 8 = 75 percent. Some teams also record partial success. Errors are another effectiveness measure: count wrong taps, wrong paths and mistakes, and note which are serious, such as booking the wrong date.

Metrics, efficiency: Time on task measures how long participants take to finish a task, usually counted only for successful attempts. Task times are often skewed by one slow person, so the median is a better summary than the mean for small samples. Example: five participants take 45, 50, 52, 60 and 180 seconds. The mean is 387 / 5 = 77.4 seconds, pulled up by the one slow user, while the median is 52 seconds, closer to the typical experience. Other efficiency measures include the number of steps or taps compared with the shortest path.

Metrics, satisfaction and the SUS: Satisfaction is measured with questionnaires after tasks or at the end. The best-known is the System Usability Scale (SUS), created by John Brooke in the 1980s. It has ten statements, each rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Odd-numbered statements are positive, such as 'I thought the system was easy to use', and even-numbered ones are negative, such as 'I found the system unnecessarily complex'. The alternation stops people from ticking the same column without reading.

SUS scoring, worked: Scoring has three steps. For each odd item (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) subtract 1 from the response. For each even item (2, 4, 6, 8, 10) subtract the response from 5. Add the ten results and multiply by 2.5. Example responses for items 1 to 10: 4, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, 5, 1. Odd items: 4-1=3, 5-1=4, 4-1=3, 4-1=3, 5-1=4, total 17. Even items: 5-2=3, 5-1=4, 5-2=3, 5-2=3, 5-1=4, total 17. Sum 34, times 2.5 gives a SUS score of 85. The score ranges from 0 to 100, but it is not a percentage. Studies of many products have found an average SUS score of about 68, so 85 is well above average, while a score in the 50s suggests serious usability problems. A participant who answers 3 to every item gets exactly 50.

How many participants, the five-user idea: Jakob Nielsen and Tom Landauer modelled how many problems a test finds. If one participant reveals on average a proportion L of the problems, then n participants reveal about 1 - (1 - L) to the power n. In their data L was about 0.31. With 1 user: 31 percent. With 3 users: 1 - 0.69 cubed, about 67 percent. With 5 users: 1 - 0.69 to the fifth, about 84 percent. With 15 users almost all. The practical lesson is that for formative testing, it is better to run several small rounds of about five users, fixing problems between rounds, than one big test with 15 users. This rule applies to one fairly uniform user group; with very different groups, such as young urban users and elderly rural users, test about five from each. Summative measurement with statistics needs larger samples.

Analysing and reporting: After the sessions, list every observed problem, how many participants hit it, and its severity, using a scale like the one from heuristic evaluation. Support each problem with evidence: a quote, a video clip, a task time. Prioritise by severity and frequency, and propose fixes. A short highlight video of real users struggling often persuades managers and developers more than any slide. Then fix and test again; usability testing is part of the iterative design cycle, not a one-time exam.

A/B testing in brief: For live products with many users, A/B testing compares two versions of a design by showing version A to one random group of users and version B to another, then measuring a behaviour such as how many complete a booking. Because the groups are random and large, a statistically significant difference can be attributed to the design change. A/B testing tells you which version performs better, but not why; usability testing tells you why. They complement each other.

Real-life example 1, DaktarDekhao round one: Five participants, aged 22 to 64, were given four tasks on a clickable prototype. Task 'book a serial for Thursday' had 3 of 5 successes. Think-aloud revealed that two older users did not realise the doctor card was tappable and that the word 'Slot' confused them. Median time for successful users was 95 seconds. The average SUS score was 61, below the benchmark. After fixes, a second round of five new participants achieved 5 of 5 successes, median 48 seconds, and an average SUS of 79.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet in a village: A team tested a new cash-out flow with five agent customers at a village market, on the customers' own phones. Concurrent think-aloud in Bangla showed that people expected to enter the agent's number before the amount, the opposite of the app's order. Nobody in the Dhaka office had noticed, because they all knew the flow. Changing the order to match people's habit raised success sharply in the next round.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes are leading tasks that reveal the answer, helping participants, testing with colleagues instead of real users, relying only on what people say rather than what they do, treating SUS as a percentage, and testing once at the end. Exams ask you to explain the steps of a usability test, think-aloud and its variants, effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction metrics, to compute a SUS score, to explain the five-user rule with its formula, and to compare usability testing with heuristic evaluation and A/B testing.

Recap: Usability testing puts real users in front of realistic tasks and watches what happens. Plan goals, recruit representative participants and write realistic, non-leading tasks.
