Use think-aloud, concurrent or retrospective, and stay neutral as a moderator. Measure effectiveness (success rate, errors), efficiency (time on task, preferably median) and satisfaction (for example SUS: odd items minus 1, 5 minus even items, sum times 2.5; average about 68). About five users per round find most problems in one user group, by 1 - (1 - 0.31) to the n. Report with evidence, fix, and test again.
key_points: Usability testing: representative users try realistic tasks while observers watch, listen and measure.
Formative testing finds problems during design; summative testing measures a nearly finished product.
Think-aloud reveals why users act; concurrent is spoken during tasks, retrospective while watching a recording.
Metrics: effectiveness (success rate, errors), efficiency (time on task, median preferred), satisfaction (questionnaires).
SUS: odd items minus 1, 5 minus even items, sum times 2.5; range 0 to 100, average about 68, not a percentage.
Five-user idea: 1 - (1 - 0.31)^5 is about 84 percent, so run several small rounds and fix between them.
A/B testing compares versions on large random groups and shows which is better; usability testing shows why.
lessons.tip: During a test, keep your hands in your lap and your mouth closed. Write down exact quotes, not your interpretation. 'Where is the date? Is this the date?' is far more useful to the team than 'user was confused'.
lessons.task: Run a mini test of any app with two family members. Give each the same realistic task without saying which button to press, ask them to think aloud, time them with your phone and note every hesitation. Then give them the ten SUS statements and calculate both SUS scores.

quiz.q: Which task wording is best for a usability test?
options: Tap the blue Book Serial button on the second card
Open the menu and choose Appointments
Do you like the booking feature?
Your father needs a heart doctor; get him a serial for Sunday
quiz.explain: A good task is realistic, written in the user's terms and does not reveal which button to press.

quiz.q: Five users take 45, 50, 52, 60 and 180 seconds. Which value best summarises the typical time?
quiz.explain: One slow participant pulls the mean up. The median, 52 seconds, better reflects the typical user in small samples.

quiz.q: A participant answers the SUS items 4, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, 5, 1. What is the score?
quiz.explain: Odd items give 3+4+3+3+4 = 17, even items give 3+4+3+3+4 = 17, total 34, and 34 x 2.5 = 85.

quiz.q: Using 1 - (1 - 0.31)^n, about what share of problems do five users from one group reveal?
quiz.explain: 0.69 to the fifth power is about 0.156, so 1 - 0.156 is about 0.84, roughly 84 to 85 percent.

quiz.q: What does A/B testing tell you that usability testing usually does not?
options: Which of two live versions performs better with large random user groups
Exactly why each user was confused
What users are thinking while they work
How to write a good task
quiz.explain: A/B testing measures behaviour across many users to show which version wins; think-aloud usability tests explain why.

lessons.title: Predictive Models: Fitts' Law, Hick's Law and the Keystroke-Level Model
lessons.content:
Imagine two designers arguing about a payment screen. One says the Pay button should be big and at the bottom where the thumb rests. The other says a small button at the top looks cleaner. They could argue for an hour, or they could test with users for a week. There is a third option: use a model that predicts, with a few numbers and a calculator, which design will be faster. HCI has a small set of such predictive models, borrowed from experimental psychology. They do not replace user testing, but they let you compare designs on paper in minutes. In this lesson we learn the three most famous ones: Fitts' law, Hick's law and the keystroke-level model.

What a predictive model is: Most evaluation methods we have studied, like usability testing and heuristic evaluation, look at a design and find problems. Predictive models are different. They are formulas that estimate how a skilled user will perform, usually how long a task will take, without needing real users in the room. They work because some parts of human behaviour are surprisingly regular. Moving a hand to a target, choosing from a list and pressing keys follow patterns that scientists measured in thousands of trials. The models capture those patterns in simple equations.

Fitts' law, the idea: In 1954 the psychologist Paul Fitts studied how long it takes to move a hand or a pointer to a target. He found two things matter: the distance to the target and the size of the target. Far targets take longer to reach. Small targets take longer too, because you must slow down at the end to land precisely. Your intuition already knows this: tapping a huge button next to your thumb is fast, tapping a tiny link on the far corner of the screen is slow and error-prone.

Fitts' law, the formula: The version most used in HCI today, often called the Shannon formulation, is MT = a + b log2(D/W + 1). MT is the movement time. D is the distance from the start point to the centre of the target. W is the width of the target measured along the direction of movement. The term log2(D/W + 1) is called the index of difficulty, ID, measured in bits. The constants a and b are found by experiment for a particular device and person; a is a fixed start-up time and b says how much each bit of difficulty costs. Because of the logarithm, doubling the distance does not double the time; it only adds roughly one bit of difficulty.

Fitts' law, a worked example: Let us use a = 0.1 seconds and b = 0.15 seconds per bit, values chosen only for illustration. A button is 300 pixels away and 30 pixels wide. D/W = 300/30 = 10, so ID = log2(10 + 1) = log2(11), which is about 3.459 bits. MT = 0.1 + 0.15 x 3.459, which is about 0.619 seconds. Now make the button twice as wide, 60 pixels. D/W = 5, ID = log2(6), about 2.585 bits, and MT = 0.1 + 0.15 x 2.585, about 0.488 seconds. The wider button saves about 0.13 seconds per tap. That sounds tiny, but on a button pressed millions of times a day it adds up, and wider targets also reduce mis-taps. Interestingly, keeping the width at 30 but halving the distance to 150 pixels gives exactly the same ID, 2.585 bits, because only the ratio D/W matters.

Fitts' law in design: Several famous design rules come straight from Fitts' law. Make frequently used targets big. Put them close to where the pointer or thumb already is. Screen edges and corners are special on a desktop: the pointer stops at the edge, so a target there behaves as if it were infinitely deep, which is why menus at the very top of the screen and buttons in corners are quick to hit. Pop-up menus that open at the pointer position have distance close to zero. On phones, keep primary buttons in the easy thumb zone and make tap targets large; platform guidelines recommend roughly 44 points on iOS and 48 dp on Android. Also keep dangerous buttons small and far from common ones, since Fitts' law works in both directions.

Hick's law, the idea: The second model is about decisions rather than movement. In the early 1950s William Hick and Ray Hyman studied how long people take to react when they must choose among several equally likely options. They found the reaction time grows with the number of choices, but logarithmically, not linearly. Going from 2 to 4 options costs as much extra time as going from 4 to 8. This is called Hick's law or the Hick-Hyman law.

Hick's law, the formula: A common form is RT = a + b log2(n + 1), where RT is the reaction or decision time, n is the number of equally likely choices, and a and b are constants found by experiment. The +1 is often explained as including the choice of not responding. Take a = 0.2 seconds and b = 0.15 seconds per bit for illustration. With n = 7 options, log2(8) = 3, so RT = 0.2 + 0.15 x 3 = 0.65 seconds. With n = 15 options, log2(16) = 4, so RT = 0.2 + 0.15 x 4 = 0.8 seconds. Doubling the options from 7 to 15 adds only 0.15 seconds, not double the time.

Hick's law in design, and its limits: The practical lesson is that more choices cost time, so remove options people do not need, group related ones and highlight the most common choice. But be careful: Hick's law applies to simple choices among equally likely, well-known options. It does not apply when people must read and search through unfamiliar items; scanning a list of unfamiliar items takes roughly linear time, one item after another. It also does not mean every menu must be tiny. One flat menu with 16 clear options can be faster than four nested menus of 4, because each extra level adds movement and another decision. Use Hick's law as a warning against clutter, not as a rule to hide everything.

GOMS, the bigger family: In 1983 Stuart Card, Thomas Moran and Allen Newell published a family of models called GOMS. The letters stand for Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules. Goals are what the user wants to achieve, such as 'send a message'. Operators are the basic actions the user can perform, such as pressing a key or moving the mouse. Methods are learned sequences of operators that achieve a goal, such as 'select the text with the mouse, then press Delete'. Selection rules decide which method to use when there are several, such as 'if the text is short, use backspace; otherwise select and delete'. GOMS describes skilled, error-free behaviour on routine tasks.

The keystroke-level model: The simplest member of the GOMS family is the keystroke-level model, KLM. You write down the sequence of low-level operators a skilled user performs, look up a standard time for each, and add them. The commonly used values from Card, Moran and Newell are: K, pressing a key, about 0.2 seconds for an average skilled typist (faster for experts, slower for beginners); P, pointing with the mouse to a target, about 1.1 seconds on average; B, pressing or releasing a mouse button, 0.1 seconds, so a click (press and release, BB) is 0.2 seconds; H, homing the hand between keyboard and mouse, 0.4 seconds; and M, mental preparation, about 1.35 seconds, the pause to think or decide before an action. A system response time R can be added when the user must wait.

KLM, a worked example: Consider a desktop web form where a user enters an 11-digit phone number and clicks Send, starting with the hand on the keyboard. The sequence is: H (move hand to mouse) 0.4, M (decide where to click) 1.35, P (point to the field) 1.1, BB (click) 0.2; that part is 3.05 seconds. Then H (back to keyboard) 0.4, M (recall the number) 1.35, and 11K (type the digits) 11 x 0.2 = 2.2; that part is 3.95 seconds, total 7.0 so far. Finally H (to the mouse) 0.4, M 1.35, P (point to Send) 1.1, BB 0.2, another 3.05. The total is 10.05 seconds.

KLM, comparing designs: Now suppose the form offers the saved number as an autofill suggestion. The sequence becomes H, M, P, BB to click the field (3.05 seconds), then M, P, BB to click the suggestion (1.35 + 1.1 + 0.2 = 2.65 seconds), total 5.7 seconds, if Send is pressed automatically or counted separately. Comparing the two typing-and-clicking parts, the suggestion removes two homing moves and eleven keystrokes. Even if you add one more P and BB to press Send, the new design is clearly faster, and it also removes the chance of mistyping a digit. That is the real power of KLM: comparing two designs before building either.

Where to put M: The trickiest part of KLM is placing the mental operator M. Card, Moran and Newell gave heuristic rules. Roughly: put an M before each new chunk of action, like before pointing to a new target or before starting to type a word, but not inside a well-practised unit, such as between the letters of a familiar word or between pointing and clicking on the same target. Different analysts may place M slightly differently, which is one reason KLM gives estimates, not exact truths.

What these models can and cannot do: Predictive models are cheap, fast and repeatable. They are good for comparing alternatives, for optimising highly repeated tasks such as call-centre screens or cashier systems, and for explaining why a design is slow. But they assume skilled users doing routine tasks without errors. They say nothing about whether the design is easy to learn, whether people understand the labels, whether they enjoy it, or whether they make mistakes. The constants vary between people, devices and contexts; a thumb on a bumpy bus is not a lab mouse. So use models to compare and to guide, and use real usability testing to confirm.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet home screen: A wallet app's home screen has 20 small icons in a grid, and testing shows people hesitate. Hick's law suggests that reducing the visible choices to the six most used services, with a 'More' button for the rest, will speed decisions. Fitts' law suggests making those six icons larger and placing Send Money, the most frequent action, in the lower part of the screen where thumbs reach easily. Both models point in the same direction, and a quick usability test can confirm it.

Real-life example 2, a hospital registration desk: At a busy hospital in Dhaka, a clerk registers hundreds of patients a day. A KLM analysis of the old screen shows each registration involves switching between keyboard and mouse six times. Redesigning the form so the clerk can move between fields with the Tab key and submit with Enter removes those homing operators and pointing actions. If each registration saves even 5 seconds and the clerk registers 300 patients, that is 1,500 seconds, 25 minutes a day, saved for one clerk, and shorter queues for patients. For DaktarDekhao, the same thinking would apply to the reception staff who confirm serials.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students often forget that in Fitts' law W is measured along the direction of movement, or they use D/W without the +1 in the Shannon form. Another mistake is to apply Hick's law to searching through unfamiliar lists. In KLM, people often forget the H operators when switching devices, or count a click as 0.1 instead of 0.2 seconds. Exams usually ask you to state Fitts' law and calculate ID and MT, to explain how target size and distance affect design, to state Hick's law with an example, to expand GOMS, and to compute a KLM estimate for a given task and compare two designs.

Recap: Predictive models estimate skilled performance without users. Fitts' law, MT = a + b log2(D/W + 1), says movement time grows with distance and shrinks with target width; only the ratio matters. Hick's law, RT = a + b log2(n + 1), says decision time grows logarithmically with the number of equally likely choices. GOMS breaks tasks into goals, operators, methods and selection rules; its simplest form, KLM, adds up operator times K, P, B, H and M to compare designs. With our numbers: 0.619 versus 0.488 seconds for a wider button, 0.65 versus 0.8 seconds for 7 versus 15 choices, and 10.05 versus 5.7 seconds for typing versus autofill. Models guide; testing confirms.
key_points: Predictive models estimate skilled users' performance with formulas, without running a user study.
Fitts' law (Shannon form): MT = a + b log2(D/W + 1); bigger and closer targets are faster to hit.
With a = 0.1, b = 0.15: D = 300, W = 30 gives ID about 3.459 bits and MT about 0.619 s; W = 60 gives about 0.488 s.
Hick's law: RT = a + b log2(n + 1); decision time grows logarithmically with equally likely choices (7 options 0.65 s, 15 options 0.8 s in our example).
GOMS stands for Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules (Card, Moran and Newell, 1983).
KLM operators: K 0.2 s, P 1.1 s, B 0.1 s (click 0.2 s), H 0.4 s, M 1.35 s; add them to estimate task time.
Models assume skilled, error-free routine use; they compare designs but do not replace usability testing.
lessons.tip: Memorise the five KLM numbers as a little rhyme or table and practise one full calculation by hand. Exams love a two-design KLM comparison, and the marks are in writing every operator in order, including the H moves people forget.
lessons.task: Choose a task you do often on a computer, such as renaming a file or logging into a website. Write its operator sequence using K, P, B, H and M, add up the time, then design a faster method (for example a keyboard shortcut) and calculate how many seconds it would save over 100 repetitions.

quiz.q: In Fitts' law MT = a + b log2(D/W + 1), what happens to the index of difficulty if you double the target width while keeping distance the same?
options: It decreases, so the target becomes faster to hit
It increases by exactly one second
quiz.explain: A wider target lowers D/W, so log2(D/W + 1) gets smaller and movement time drops. In our example 3.459 bits became 2.585 bits.

quiz.q: Using Hick's law with a = 0.2 s and b = 0.15 s, what is the decision time for 7 equally likely options?
What do the letters GOMS stand for?
quiz.explain: GOMS, from Card, Moran and Newell, describes goals, the operators used, methods built from operators, and rules to select among methods.

quiz.q: In the keystroke-level model, which operator represents moving the hand between keyboard and mouse, and how long does it take?
quiz.explain: H is homing, about 0.4 seconds. P is pointing, M is mental preparation and K is a keystroke.

quiz.q: Which is a real limitation of predictive models like KLM?
options: They assume skilled, error-free users and say little about learnability or satisfaction
They can only be used after the product is released
They work only for voice interfaces
quiz.explain: KLM and Fitts' law model routine expert performance. They cannot tell you whether novices understand the design or enjoy it, so testing is still needed.

lessons.title: Accessibility: Designing for Everyone
lessons.content:
Close your eyes and try to send a message to a friend on your phone. Hard, right? Now imagine doing it every day. Millions of blind people do exactly that, quickly and confidently, because their phones read the screen aloud and let them navigate by gestures. That works only when app designers and developers did their part: labelled the buttons, ordered the content sensibly and avoided relying on sight alone. When they did not, a blind user hits a wall of buttons announced as 'button, button, unlabelled image'. Accessibility is the practice of making sure that wall is never built.

What accessibility is: Accessibility means designing products so that people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with them. It is part of usability, not a separate decoration. A design that is easy for most people but impossible for someone who cannot see, hear, use a mouse or read long text is not finished. The World Health Organization estimates that about 1.3 billion people, roughly one in six people worldwide, experience a significant disability. Add older people whose eyesight, hearing and hand control decline with age, and accessibility becomes a design concern for a very large part of any user base.

Disability as a mismatch: Modern thinking describes disability not only as a property of a person but as a mismatch between a person and their environment. A wheelchair user is not disabled by the wheelchair; they are disabled by stairs without a ramp. In the same way, a blind user is disabled by an app whose buttons have no labels, not by the phone. This view is powerful for designers because it puts the solution in our hands: change the design and the mismatch shrinks.

Types of disability: Designers usually think in four broad groups. Visual: blindness, low vision and colour vision deficiency. Hearing: deafness and hearing loss. Motor: difficulty with fine movement, tremor, paralysis or missing limbs, which make small targets, mouse use or fast gestures hard. Cognitive and learning: difficulties with memory, attention, reading (such as dyslexia) or understanding complex information. Some people have more than one. Speech disabilities also matter for voice interfaces.

Permanent, temporary and situational: Microsoft's inclusive design guidance popularised a useful idea: the same limitation can be permanent, temporary or situational. Having one arm is permanent; a broken arm in plaster is temporary; holding a baby or a bag of shopping in one arm is situational. Being blind is permanent; an eye infection is temporary; bright sunlight on your phone screen is situational. Being deaf is permanent; an ear infection is temporary; a noisy bus terminal is situational. Designing for the permanent case helps a much larger group in temporary and situational cases.

The curb-cut effect: When cities cut slopes into pavement kerbs for wheelchair users, it turned out that people with prams, suitcases, bicycles and delivery trolleys all benefited. This is called the curb-cut effect: features designed for disabled people often help everyone. Captions on videos help deaf viewers, but also people watching on a silent bus. High-contrast text helps low-vision users, but also everyone in bright sunlight. Large tap targets help people with tremor, and also anyone walking while using the phone.

WCAG and POUR: The main international guideline for web accessibility is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG, published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). WCAG 2.0 came in 2008, 2.1 in 2018 and 2.2 in 2023. Though written for the web, its ideas are widely applied to mobile apps too. WCAG is organised around four principles, remembered as POUR. Perceivable: information must be presentable in ways users can perceive, for example text alternatives for images and captions for video. Operable: users must be able to operate the interface, for example by keyboard, with enough time and without content that causes seizures. Understandable: information and operation must be understandable, for example readable text, predictable behaviour and help with input errors. Robust: content must work with current and future assistive technologies, which mainly means using correct, standard code.

Conformance levels: Each WCAG success criterion has a level: A, AA or AAA. Level A is the minimum; failing it blocks some users completely, for example images with no text alternative. Level AA addresses the biggest and most common barriers and is the level most laws and organisations aim for. Level AAA is the highest and is not usually required for whole sites, because some criteria cannot be met for all content. When a project says 'we meet WCAG 2.2 AA', it means it satisfies all level A and AA criteria.

Colour contrast, the rule: Text must stand out from its background. WCAG defines a contrast ratio from 1:1 (no contrast, same colour) to 21:1 (black on white). For level AA, normal text needs at least 4.5:1, and large text (roughly 18 point, or 14 point bold) needs at least 3:1. For AAA, normal text needs 7:1 and large text 4.5:1. WCAG 2.1 also requires 3:1 for important non-text elements such as input borders and icons that carry meaning.

Colour contrast, how it is calculated: Each colour is converted to a relative luminance L between 0 (black) and 1 (white), using a formula that accounts for how our eyes perceive red, green and blue differently. The ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the lighter colour. Black on white: (1 + 0.05) / (0 + 0.05) = 21. Grey #777777 has a luminance of about 0.1845, so on white the ratio is 1.05 / 0.2345, about 4.48:1. That just fails AA for normal text. A very slightly darker grey, #767676, gives about 4.54:1 and passes. A darker grey, #595959, gives about 7.0:1 and passes even AAA. This shows why designers should check with a contrast tool instead of trusting their eyes: #777777 and #767676 look identical, yet one passes and one fails.

Do not rely on colour alone: Roughly 1 in 12 men and about 1 in 200 women have some form of colour vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green. If a form marks errors only by turning a field red, or a chart separates lines only by colour, these users miss the information. Always add another cue: an icon, a text message, a pattern or a label. 'Payment failed' in red with a warning icon works for everyone.

Text alternatives: Every meaningful image needs a text alternative, called alt text on the web and a content description or accessibility label in apps. Screen readers read it aloud. Good alt text describes the purpose, not every pixel: for a doctor's photo, 'Dr. Nasrin Akter, child specialist' is better than 'image of a woman smiling'. An icon button needs a label describing its action, such as 'Search' or 'Call doctor', not 'magnifier icon'. Purely decorative images should be marked so screen readers skip them.

Screen readers: A screen reader is software that reads the content of the screen aloud or sends it to a braille display, and lets users navigate with gestures or keys. TalkBack comes with Android, VoiceOver with iPhones and Macs, and NVDA is a free screen reader for Windows; JAWS is a widely used commercial one. Users often move element by element with swipes, or jump between headings. For this to work, elements need correct names and roles (this is a button, this is a heading), a logical reading order, and visible focus. Testing your app with TalkBack switched on for ten minutes teaches more than any checklist.

Keyboard access and focus: Many users cannot use a mouse or touchscreen and rely on a keyboard, switch devices or voice control. Every function must be reachable and usable with the keyboard alone, in a sensible tab order, with a clearly visible focus indicator showing where you are. A custom drop-down that opens only on mouse hover locks these users out. Avoid keyboard traps where focus enters a component and cannot leave.

Structure and form labels: Screen reader users often skim a page by jumping from heading to heading, just as sighted users skim by looking at bold titles. So real headings must be marked as headings in the code, not just made big and bold. Every form field needs a label that is programmatically tied to it, so the screen reader says 'Mobile number, edit text' instead of just 'edit text'. A placeholder inside the field is not enough, because it disappears when typing starts. Error messages should be announced and should name the field that needs fixing.

Touch target size: Small targets are hard for people with tremor, older users and anyone on the move. WCAG 2.2 added a level AA minimum target size of 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with some exceptions, and AAA asks for 44 by 44. Platform guidelines go further for touch: around 44 by 44 points on iOS and 48 by 48 dp on Android. Spacing between targets matters too, so a slightly shaky finger does not hit the neighbour.

Time, motion and captions: Give users enough time; a payment page that times out in 60 seconds can lock out a screen reader user or someone who types slowly, so warn before timeout and allow extension. Avoid flashing content, which can trigger seizures, and let users reduce animation. Provide captions for video and transcripts for audio, so deaf and hard-of-hearing users get the same information. Use simple, clear language and consistent navigation, which helps users with cognitive disabilities and everyone else.

Real-life example 1, DaktarDekhao with TalkBack: A blind user tries to book a serial in DaktarDekhao. In the first version, the doctor cards are images without labels, the time slots are coloured boxes where green means free and red means full, and the Book button is an icon only. TalkBack reads 'image, image, button'. The fix: each card gets a label like 'Dr. Rahman, medicine, Tuesday and Thursday', each slot is read as '10:30 am, available' or '11:00 am, full', and the button says 'Book serial with Dr. Rahman'. The same changes help a sighted user who cannot tell red from green.

Real-life example 2, a government form in sunlight: A farmer fills an online subsidy form on a cheap phone outdoors at noon. The form uses light grey text on white, about 2.85:1 for #999999, and tiny checkboxes. In sunlight he can barely read it, a situational visual limitation. Raising the text to a darker colour with at least 4.5:1, enlarging checkboxes and labels so the whole label is tappable, and adding Bangla text with clear error messages make the form usable for him, for an elderly user with low vision, and for everyone else.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A common mistake is treating accessibility as a final checklist instead of designing for it from the start. Another is thinking only of blind users and forgetting motor, hearing and cognitive needs. Some designers trust their eyes on contrast or use colour as the only signal. Exams ask: define accessibility and explain the social or mismatch view of disability; explain POUR with examples; state WCAG contrast requirements and calculate or interpret a ratio; describe screen readers and alt text; explain permanent, temporary and situational disabilities and the curb-cut effect.

Recap: Accessibility makes products usable by people with disabilities and helps everyone through the curb-cut effect. Disability is a mismatch between a person and a design, and it can be permanent, temporary or situational. WCAG, now version 2.2, follows POUR: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust, with levels A, AA and AAA. Normal text needs 4.5:1 contrast at AA; #777777 on white at 4.48:1 fails while #767676 at 4.54:1 passes. Do not rely on colour alone, give images and icons text alternatives, support screen readers and keyboards, make targets big enough, give enough time, and caption media.
key_points: Accessibility means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with a product; it is part of usability.
Disability can be seen as a mismatch between person and design; limitations can be permanent, temporary or situational.
The curb-cut effect: features designed for disabled people often help everyone.
WCAG (W3C, version 2.2 in 2023) is built on POUR: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust, with levels A, AA and AAA.
AA contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text; ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). #777777 on white is 4.48:1 and fails; #767676 is 4.54:1 and passes.
Never use colour as the only signal; add icons, text or patterns.
Give images and icon buttons text labels, support screen readers (TalkBack, VoiceOver, NVDA) and full keyboard access, and use large touch targets.
lessons.tip: Turn on your phone's screen reader (TalkBack or VoiceOver) for ten minutes and try to use your favourite app with your eyes closed. Learn how to turn it off first! Nothing teaches accessibility faster than experiencing the barriers yourself.
lessons.task: Pick three colour pairs from an app or website you use, such as body text on background and a button label on its button. Use any free online contrast checker to measure their ratios, write down whether each passes WCAG AA for normal text (4.5:1), and suggest a darker or lighter colour for any that fail.

quiz.q: What does the 'O' in WCAG's POUR principles stand for?
quiz.explain: POUR is Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust. Operable means users can operate the interface, for example with a keyboard and with enough time.

quiz.q: Grey text #777777 on a white background has a contrast ratio of about 4.48:1. For normal-size text at WCAG level AA, this:
options: Is irrelevant because contrast rules apply only to images
Just fails, since AA needs at least 4.5:1
quiz.explain: Normal text at AA needs 4.5:1. 4.48 is just below; the nearly identical #767676 gives about 4.54:1 and passes.

quiz.q: A delivery rider cannot hear a notification sound in a noisy market. This is an example of a:
quiz.explain: The limitation comes from the situation, not the person. Designing for deaf users, such as visual and vibration alerts, also helps here.

quiz.q: Which is the best text alternative for an icon button that opens the search screen?
options: An empty label so the screen reader skips it
quiz.explain: Alt text and labels should describe the purpose or action, not the picture. Leaving it empty hides a working control from screen reader users.

quiz.q: A form shows errors only by turning the field border red. What is the main accessibility problem?
options: Red is too bright for screens
It relies on colour alone, so people with colour vision deficiency may miss it
Borders cannot be read by keyboards
Error messages are not allowed in forms
quiz.explain: About 1 in 12 men have some colour vision deficiency. Add a text message and an icon so the error does not depend on colour.

lessons.title: Designing for Bangladesh: Bangla, Low Literacy and Low Bandwidth
lessons.content:
Picture two users of the same health app. Tanvir is a university student in Dhaka with a new smartphone, fast Wi-Fi and English-medium schooling. Rahima Khatun is a 55-year-old woman in a village in Rangpur. She uses her son's old Android phone, shared with the whole family, on a slow and expensive mobile data pack. She reads Bangla slowly and does not read English. Most HCI textbooks are written with Tanvir in mind. But if you build software for Bangladesh, Rahima is just as much your user, and often the one who needs the service most. This lesson applies everything we have learned to the real context of Bangladeshi users.

Why local context matters: User-centred design says: know your users, their tasks and their context. Context includes language, script, literacy, devices, network, money, culture and trust. A design that tests well in a Silicon Valley lab can fail completely in a Bangladeshi village, not because the users are less capable, but because the design assumed things that are not true there: unlimited data, a personal phone, fluent English, and comfort with abstract icons. Designing for Bangladesh means checking each of those assumptions.

The Bangla script: Bangla is written in its own script, read left to right like English. Unlike English, consonants combine into conjuncts, called juktakkhor, such as ক্ষ or ন্ত, formed in Unicode by joining letters with the hasanta sign. Vowel signs can appear before, after, above or below a consonant: in কি the sign for i is drawn before the consonant even though it is typed after it. Most letters hang from a horizontal headline called the matra. All of this means Bangla text needs a proper text-shaping engine to display correctly. Modern Android, iOS and browsers handle it well, but custom game engines, some PDF generators, old printers and badly configured fonts can show broken conjuncts or vowel signs in the wrong place. Always test real Bangla text on real devices, including receipts and SMS.

Unicode and fonts: Bangla has its own Unicode block, and all modern software should store and exchange Bangla as Unicode text. In the past, much Bangla publishing used non-Unicode fonts with keyboard systems like Bijoy, where Bangla letters were stored as English character codes; text copied from such documents appears as gibberish in other software. If your system imports old data, plan for conversion. For display, choose a well-made Unicode Bangla font, such as Noto Sans Bengali, SolaimanLipi or Kalpurush, test its readability at small sizes, and make sure Bangla and English text look balanced when mixed.

Typography for Bangla: Bangla letters have more vertical detail than Latin letters: vowel signs above the matra and below the baseline. If you copy line-height settings designed for English, the vowel signs of one line can collide with the next, or get clipped inside buttons with fixed heights. Give Bangla text a bit more line height and avoid tight fixed-height containers. Bangla at the same point size often looks smaller than English, so body text may need a slightly larger size. Avoid fake bold and italic styles that the font does not support; slanted Bangla is rarely readable.

Input methods: Typing Bangla is a real effort for many users. Common methods include phonetic typing, where you type in Latin letters and software converts them (Avro made this popular; 'ami' becomes আমি), fixed layouts like Bijoy and the national standard layout, and on-screen phone keyboards such as Gboard that offer Bangla. Many people, especially young users, chat in Banglish, Bangla words written in English letters. A search box in a Bangladeshi app should therefore cope with Bangla script, English and Banglish: a user looking for 'daktar', 'ডাক্তার' or 'doctor' wants the same thing. Prefer selection over typing wherever you can.

Which language for labels: Should the interface be in Bangla, English or both? The answer comes from user research, not taste. Many Bangladeshi apps offer a language switch, which is good, but it must be easy to find, ideally on the first screen, with each option written in its own language ('বাংলা' and 'English'), not 'Bengali' written in English. Some terms are better known in English even among Bangla speakers, such as 'mobile recharge' or 'OTP', and forcing a pure-Bangla translation can confuse. Write natural, everyday Bangla, not heavy formal words. A label like 'টাকা পাঠান' beats a stiff official phrase that users never say aloud.

Numbers, dates and money: Bangla has its own digits, ০ to ৯. In a Bangla interface showing Bangla digits is natural, but phone numbers, OTPs and amounts are often typed with English digits, so input fields should accept both and convert. Dates are usually written day first, such as 14/04/2025, never month first as in the US. Many people also follow the Bangla calendar for festivals such as Pohela Boishakh, and the Hijri calendar for religious events. The taka sign is ৳, and large numbers are often grouped in lakh and crore in everyday speech. Display formats should match what your users actually read and say.

Low literacy, the challenge: Some users read slowly or not at all, and many more are not comfortable reading long text. This is not a lack of intelligence; these users manage money, businesses and families every day. The design challenge is to reduce dependence on reading. Long paragraphs, dense menus and text-only instructions shut them out, and so do flows that require typing names or addresses.

Low literacy, techniques: Research and field projects suggest several helpful patterns. Pair icons with short labels; icons alone are often misunderstood, while labels alone need reading. Use photos of real, familiar objects, such as a picture of a medicine strip, rather than abstract symbols. Offer voice: audio instructions in Bangla and voice input. Use short videos to explain a process. Keep flows linear and short, one decision per screen. Use numbers and colours consistently so people can memorise paths. And test with actual low-literacy users, because designers who read fluently cannot easily imagine the experience.

Low bandwidth and older phones: Many Bangladeshi users have slow or unreliable connections and pay for data by the megabyte or by the pack, often on older or low-cost phones with small storage. Design consequences: keep app size small, since a huge download may never be installed; compress images and load them only when needed; show useful content while loading; cache data so the app works offline or on a poor connection, and sync later; avoid auto-playing video; and let users choose low-data modes. Lite versions of big apps exist precisely because of such users worldwide. Every extra megabyte is real money for Rahima.

USSD and SMS: Not everyone has a smartphone or data. USSD lets users dial a short code on any basic phone and navigate numbered text menus, without internet. Mobile financial services in Bangladesh are widely used through such menus. USSD design has its own HCI rules: screens are tiny and text-only, sessions time out quickly, and users must remember where they are. Good USSD design keeps menus short, puts the most common option first, uses the same numbers for the same actions, confirms details before money moves, and sends an SMS receipt.

Shared phones and privacy: In many families one phone is shared among several people. That breaks assumptions like 'the device belongs to one user'. An app that stays logged in may reveal one person's messages or balance to another; notifications showing amounts may expose private information. Design for this with easy account switching, PIN protection for sensitive actions, and discreet notifications. Privacy expectations also differ by gender and family structure, which is another reason to research with real users.

Trust and culture: Trust is a major design factor. Many shoppers in Bangladesh prefer cash on delivery because they worry about paying for goods that never arrive. Interfaces build trust with clear prices including delivery charges, real photos, recognisable payment methods, visible helpline numbers, and confirmation messages in Bangla. Culture also shapes icons and colours: an owl or a particular hand gesture may carry different meanings, and religious and festival seasons change behaviour, with big spikes in shopping and travel before Eid. Respect for elders, formal address and modesty in images all matter.

Flexible layouts for two languages: When an interface switches between Bangla and English, the length of every label changes. 'Send Money' and 'টাকা পাঠান' happen to be similar, but many translations are longer, and some English words have no short Bangla equivalent. A button with fixed width will then cut text off or squeeze it into an unreadable size. Design layouts that grow with their content, allow labels to wrap onto two lines, and test every screen in both languages, at the largest font size the phone allows, because many older users increase the system font. Sorting is another detail: a list of names in Bangla must follow Bangla alphabetical order, which software handles correctly only if it uses the right locale settings.

Researching in the field: Most of these lessons cannot be learned from a desk in Dhaka. Visit the places where people will use the product: a union health complex, a village bazar, a garment factory gate. Watch people use their own phones, note the network bars, the cracked screens, the shared handsets, and the noise. Recruit test participants who match the real users in age, literacy and location, and run tests in Bangla. Simple paper prototypes and short sessions work well and respect people's time.

Real-life example 1, DaktarDekhao for Rahima: The DaktarDekhao team visited a union health complex and watched elderly patients try the app. Changes followed. The first screen offers বাংলা and English as two big buttons. Doctor specialities are shown as photo icons with short Bangla labels, such as a child for শিশু and a heart for হৃদরোগ. A speaker button reads each screen aloud in Bangla. The booking flow has one choice per screen and ends with a large serial number and an SMS. The app works offline for browsing doctors and syncs when the network returns. A USSD option lets people with basic phones book by dialling a short code.

Real-life example 2, a farmer's market price service: A service sends crop prices to farmers. The first version used long English SMS messages. Uptake was low. The redesign used short Bangla SMS with Bangla digits, a fixed format like 'ধান ১,২০০৳/মণ, আলু ২৫৳/কেজি', and an option to call and hear prices as a voice message. Farmers who read slowly could memorise the format and find their crop quickly, and the voice option reached those who could not read at all.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Common mistakes include translating an English interface word for word into formal Bangla, testing only on new phones with fast Wi-Fi, using icons without labels, assuming every user can type in Bangla script, and ignoring Bangla rendering on receipts and PDFs. Exams may ask how you would localise an app for Bangladesh, design for low-literacy users, design for low bandwidth, or compare app, USSD and SMS channels. Answer with specific techniques and always mention testing with real local users.

Recap: Designing for Bangladesh means questioning assumptions about language, literacy, devices, network, money and trust. Bangla script needs proper Unicode, good fonts, extra line height and testing everywhere text appears. Support Bangla, English and Banglish input, accept both digit sets, and use local date and money formats. For low-literacy users, combine icons with labels, photos, voice and short linear flows. For low bandwidth, keep apps small, cache and work offline. Remember USSD and SMS for basic phones, design for shared phones, and build trust with clarity. Above all, test with real users like Rahima, not only users like Tanvir.
key_points: Design for the real Bangladeshi context: language, literacy, devices, network, cost, sharing and trust.
Bangla script uses conjuncts, vowel signs around consonants and the matra; it needs Unicode, a good font and proper text shaping, tested everywhere.
Give Bangla text more line height and avoid fixed-height containers that clip vowel signs.
Support Bangla, English and Banglish input, accept both Bangla and English digits, and use day-first dates and the ৳ sign.
For low-literacy users: icons with short labels, real photos, voice, short videos and one decision per screen.
For low bandwidth and older phones: small app size, compressed images, caching, offline use and low-data modes; USSD and SMS for basic phones.
Shared phones and trust shape design: discreet notifications, PIN for sensitive actions, clear prices and visible help.
lessons.tip: Whenever you design something, imagine two users side by side: a fast urban user and an older rural user on a shared, slow phone. If your design works for the second, it almost always works for the first too.
lessons.task: Take one app you use and switch it to Bangla, if it supports it. Write down three places where the Bangla text is unnatural, clipped, mixed with English awkwardly or uses formal words people do not say. Rewrite those labels in everyday Bangla, and estimate how much data the app's home screen uses by checking your phone's data usage settings.

quiz.q: Text copied from an old Bijoy-typed document appears as random English letters in a modern app. What is the most likely reason?
options: The old document stored Bangla with a non-Unicode font encoding
The modern app does not support left-to-right text
Bangla cannot be stored on computers
The text was written in Banglish
quiz.explain: Older Bangla publishing often used non-Unicode fonts where Bangla letters were stored as English character codes; it needs conversion to Unicode.

quiz.q: Why should a search box in a Bangladeshi app accept 'daktar', 'ডাক্তার' and 'doctor'?
options: Because users search in Bangla script, Banglish and English for the same thing
Because search engines need three spellings
Because Bangla script cannot be searched
quiz.explain: Users type in different ways depending on keyboard and habit. Matching all common forms reduces failed searches.

quiz.q: Which design best supports users with low literacy?
options: Long written instructions in formal Bangla
Icons only, with no text, to avoid reading
Icons paired with short labels, voice prompts and one decision per screen
A dense menu with all options on one screen
quiz.explain: Icons alone are often misunderstood and long text excludes slow readers. Combining pictures, short labels, voice and simple flows works best.

quiz.q: What is a key HCI constraint of USSD menus on basic phones?
options: Screens are tiny and text-only and sessions time out quickly
quiz.explain: USSD works without internet on any phone, but its short text screens and time limits require short menus, consistent numbering and confirmations.

quiz.q: On a shared family phone, which design choice best protects privacy?
options: Stay logged in forever and show full balances in notifications
Discreet notifications and a PIN for sensitive actions
Remove all notifications from the app
Ask users to buy a second phone
quiz.explain: Shared phones break the one-device-one-user assumption. Discreet notifications and PIN protection keep private data private without hurting usability.

lessons.title: Dark Patterns and the Ethics of Design
lessons.content:
You try to cancel a monthly subscription. Signing up took one tap. Cancelling takes you through five screens: 'Are you sure?', 'You will lose all your benefits!', a special offer, a survey, and finally a tiny grey link that says 'continue to cancel', placed under a big bright button that says 'Keep my plan'. Nothing here is a bug. Every step was designed, tested and measured, and it works: many people give up and keep paying. This lesson is about the dark side of everything you have learned in this course. The same knowledge of perception, memory, attention and habit that lets you make interfaces easy can be used to trick people. HCI must also teach where the line is.

Persuasion is not always bad: Every design persuades a little. Putting the most useful button first, reminding someone to take their medicine, or showing a progress bar that encourages finishing a health course are all forms of persuasion. The researcher B. J. Fogg at Stanford studied this field, called persuasive technology. Persuasion is acceptable when it helps users reach their own goals, is transparent, and leaves them free to choose. It turns into manipulation when it works against the user's interests, hides what is happening, or exploits weaknesses so that people make choices they would not make if they understood clearly.

What dark patterns are: The term 'dark patterns' was coined in 2010 by the UX designer Harry Brignull for interface designs crafted to trick users into doing things they did not mean to do, such as buying, signing up or sharing data. He later began using the term 'deceptive patterns', which many people now prefer because it describes what the design does. Dark patterns are not accidents of bad design. They are deliberate uses of design knowledge against the user.

Why they work: Dark patterns exploit exactly the human traits we studied. Limited attention means people skim, so small print is missed. Habits mean people click the big coloured button without reading. Loss aversion means 'you will lose your benefits' feels stronger than an equal gain. Social pressure means 'everyone else bought this' influences us. Time pressure reduces careful thinking. Default effects mean most people keep whatever was pre-selected. A designer who understands these can make interfaces kinder, or can turn them into traps.

Confirmshaming: Confirmshaming means wording the option to decline so that it makes the user feel guilty or foolish. A pop-up offers a discount and the decline link says 'No thanks, I don't like saving money'. Or a health app's opt-out says 'No, I don't care about my family's health'. The honest version is simply 'No thanks'.

Roach motel and hard to cancel: The roach motel is a design where getting in is easy but getting out is hard, named after insect traps. Signing up for a subscription takes one screen, but cancelling requires a phone call during office hours, hidden settings or many screens of discouragement, like the example at the start. Closely related is forced continuity: a free trial asks for card details and then silently starts charging when the trial ends, without a clear reminder.

Sneak into basket and hidden costs: In sneak into basket, the site adds an extra item to your cart, such as insurance or a donation, through a pre-ticked box you may not notice. Hidden costs appear at the last step of checkout: the price looked cheap, but a 'service charge', 'convenience fee' or high delivery charge appears only after you have invested time filling in details, when you are less likely to give up. The honest design shows the total price, including all fees, from the start.

Trick questions and preselection: Trick questions use confusing wording, often double negatives, so that users choose the opposite of what they intend. For example, a checkbox that says 'Uncheck this box if you do not wish to not receive offers'. Preselection makes the option the business wants the default, such as a ticked box agreeing to share data with partners. Because most people accept defaults, preselection quietly decides for them.

Disguised ads and misdirection: Disguised ads are advertisements designed to look like content or controls, the most famous being fake 'Download' buttons on file-sharing sites that lead to unrelated software. Misdirection draws attention to one thing to distract from another: a bright 'Accept all' button next to a pale, text-only 'Manage settings' link. Remember Norman's signifiers? Here they are used to lie.

Nagging, fake urgency and fake social proof: Nagging means repeatedly interrupting the user with the same request, such as asking to turn on notifications every time the app opens, until they give in. Fake urgency uses countdown timers that reset when the page reloads, or 'offer ends in 10 minutes' messages that are not true. Fake scarcity claims 'only 2 left' when stock is plentiful. Fake social proof shows invented messages like 'Rahim from Khulna just bought this' or made-up reviews. All of these pressure the user to act before thinking.

Privacy dark patterns: Some patterns target personal data. Interfaces may push users to share more than they want, bury privacy settings deep in menus, make the privacy-friendly choice take many more steps than 'Accept all', or ask for permissions such as contacts or location that the app does not need. Brignull called one version 'privacy zuckering', tricking people into publicly sharing more information than they intended.

The attention economy: A wider ethical issue is the attention economy. Many free apps earn money from advertising, so their business depends on how much time and attention users give. Features like infinite scroll, autoplay of the next video, streaks that punish breaks, and unpredictable rewards (the pull-to-refresh that sometimes shows something exciting, like a slot machine) can keep people using an app longer than they want. Not every such feature is a dark pattern, but designers should ask whether the product serves the user's goals or only the time-spent metric.

Consent and regulation: Ethics is also becoming law. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), applied from 2018, requires consent for data processing to be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and European regulators and courts have treated pre-ticked boxes as not valid consent. Regulators in the United States and other countries have also started acting against deceptive designs, especially hard-to-cancel subscriptions. Good practice everywhere: ask clearly, explain why, make refusing as easy as accepting, and let people change their minds later.

Privacy by design: Privacy by design is the idea, associated with Ann Cavoukian, that privacy should be built into systems from the beginning, not added later. In practice: collect only the data you need (data minimisation), make privacy-protective settings the default, explain data use in plain language at the moment it matters, protect data with security measures, and let users see, download and delete their data. For DaktarDekhao, health data is sensitive: the app should not ask for contacts or location unless needed, and should never share patient information with advertisers.

The designer's responsibility: Designers and developers often say 'the business asked for it'. But professional ethics says individuals are responsible for what they build. The ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct, updated in 2018, asks computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being, avoid harm, be honest and trustworthy, and respect privacy. Practical steps: raise concerns with data, such as showing that dark patterns increase complaints, refunds and loss of trust; propose honest alternatives that still meet business goals; and refuse clearly harmful designs.

Ethics beyond dark patterns: HCI ethics also includes research ethics (informed consent, voluntary participation, protecting participants' data, as discussed in user research), inclusion (not excluding people through inaccessible design), and fairness in automated systems (an AI feature that works poorly for darker skin tones or for Bangla speakers excludes people). The guiding question is simple: who could be harmed by this design, and have we listened to them?

Honest alternatives: For almost every dark pattern there is an honest design that still serves the business. Instead of confirmshaming, use neutral 'Yes' and 'No thanks' options of equal weight. Instead of a roach motel, put 'Cancel subscription' in the account settings, and if you want to keep the customer, offer a pause option or a discount once, politely. Instead of forced continuity, send a reminder a few days before the trial ends. Instead of hidden costs, show the full price early. Instead of fake urgency, show real deadlines only. Honest designs often convert a little less in the very short term but earn repeat customers, fewer refunds and a better reputation.

A quick ethics check: Before shipping a design, a team can ask a few simple questions. Would we be comfortable explaining this design to the user face to face? Would we be happy if our parents or younger siblings were treated this way? Is the choice we want them to make as easy to reverse as it was to make? Are we measuring success only by clicks and time spent, or also by complaints, cancellations and user satisfaction? If any answer makes the team uncomfortable, the design needs another look.

Real-life example 1, an e-commerce checkout: An online shop in Bangladesh shows a phone at 15,000 taka. At the final step, a 'platform fee' of 300 taka and a pre-ticked 'extended warranty' of 1,200 taka appear, and a timer says 'Price valid for 5 minutes'. The customer pays 16,500 instead of 15,000 plus delivery. Later they discover the warranty, feel cheated and leave a one-star review. The honest redesign shows all fees on the product page, makes the warranty an unticked option with clear terms, and removes the fake timer. Short-term revenue per order may drop slightly, but returns and complaints drop and trust grows.

Real-life example 2, a mobile loan app: Imagine a lending app that shows a big 'Get money now' button, hides the true yearly interest and fees in long English text, asks for access to the user's contact list, and later uses it to pressure borrowers by messaging their contacts. This combines hidden costs, privacy abuse and coercion, and can cause real harm to vulnerable people. An ethical design shows the total amount to repay in Bangla in large text before acceptance, asks only for necessary permissions, and offers a cooling-off period.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students sometimes call every persuasive design a dark pattern; the test is whether it works against the user's interest through deception or pressure. Others think dark patterns are only a legal topic; they are a design responsibility. Exams ask: define dark patterns and who coined the term; explain and give examples of types such as confirmshaming, roach motel, hidden costs, sneak into basket, trick questions and disguised ads; discuss ethics in HCI and privacy by design; and redesign a given deceptive interface honestly.

Recap: Persuasion that helps users reach their own goals transparently is acceptable; manipulation that works against them is not. Dark or deceptive patterns, named by Harry Brignull in 2010, exploit attention, habit, defaults, loss aversion and social pressure. Common types include confirmshaming, roach motel, forced continuity, sneak into basket, hidden costs, trick questions, preselection, disguised ads, nagging, fake urgency and privacy tricks. Laws such as GDPR increasingly demand honest consent. Privacy by design, honest defaults and professional codes like ACM's guide designers. Your skill in HCI is power; use it for users, not against them.
key_points: Persuasion is acceptable when it helps users' own goals transparently; manipulation works against their interests.
Harry Brignull coined 'dark patterns' in 2010; many now say 'deceptive patterns'.
Dark patterns exploit attention limits, habits, defaults, loss aversion, time pressure and social proof.
Common types: confirmshaming, roach motel, forced continuity, sneak into basket, hidden costs, trick questions, preselection, disguised ads, nagging, fake urgency.
The attention economy can push designs that maximise time spent rather than user goals.
GDPR requires freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous consent; refusing should be as easy as accepting.
Privacy by design and the ACM Code of Ethics (avoid harm, be honest, respect privacy) guide responsible designers.
lessons.tip: Keep a list of dark patterns you meet in real apps, with screenshots and the pattern's name. It sharpens your eye, gives you strong exam examples, and one day it will help you argue for an honest alternative in a real team meeting.
lessons.task: Try to cancel or unsubscribe from something you signed up for, such as a newsletter, a trial or an app notification setting. Count the steps to sign up versus the steps to leave, and note any confirmshaming, hidden links or nagging. Sketch an honest cancel flow in no more than three screens.

quiz.q: A pop-up's decline link reads 'No thanks, I prefer paying full price'. Which dark pattern is this?
quiz.explain: Confirmshaming words the decline option to make users feel guilty or foolish. The honest version is simply 'No thanks'.

quiz.q: Who coined the term 'dark patterns' in 2010?
quiz.explain: UX designer Harry Brignull coined the term for designs that trick users; he later used 'deceptive patterns'.

quiz.q: Signing up takes one tap, but cancelling requires a phone call during office hours. This is called:
quiz.explain: Easy to get in, hard to get out: the roach motel pattern, also described as hard to cancel.

quiz.q: Under GDPR, which is NOT valid consent for data processing?
options: An unticked box the user ticks after reading a clear explanation
A pre-ticked box the user does not change
A clear 'Allow' button next to an equally clear 'Don't allow' button
A specific request explaining what data is used and why
quiz.explain: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; European regulators and courts have treated pre-ticked boxes as not valid consent.

quiz.q: Which practice best reflects privacy by design?
options: Collect all possible data in case it is useful later
Hide privacy settings to keep the interface simple
Collect only needed data and make privacy-protective settings the default
Share health data with advertisers if the terms mention it
quiz.explain: Privacy by design builds privacy in from the start: data minimisation, protective defaults, clear explanations and user control.

lessons.title: Emerging Interfaces and Course Wrap-up
lessons.content:
Your grandmother may never learn to use a laptop, but she can say 'Call Shafiq' to a phone and it dials. A garment worker can follow a training video on a VR headset that shows exactly where to place her hands on a machine. A watch on a rickshaw puller's wrist can count his steps and warn of a high heart rate on a hot afternoon. The screens, mice and keyboards we studied are being joined by voices, headsets, watches, gestures and AI assistants. The technology changes fast, but the human side changes slowly. In this final lesson we look at emerging interfaces through the lens of everything you learned, and then pull the whole course together.

Why old principles still apply: Every new interface must still answer Norman's questions: can people discover what is possible, do they know what to do, do they understand what happened? The human still has limited memory and attention, still makes slips and mistakes, still needs feedback within about a second, and still comes in all abilities and contexts. New devices often fail exactly where they ignore these old lessons. So as you study each new interface, ask: what makes the gulfs of execution and evaluation wider or narrower here?

Voice user interfaces: A voice user interface (VUI) lets people interact by speaking and listening. Smartphone assistants became widely known with Apple's Siri in 2011, and smart speakers such as Amazon's Echo with Alexa followed from 2014. Voice is natural, hands-free and eyes-free, which helps while driving or cooking, for people with visual or motor disabilities, and for people who find reading hard. It is also fast for short commands like setting an alarm.

Voice, the design challenges: Voice has a serious discoverability problem: there are no visible buttons or menus, so users do not know what they can say. Speech is linear and fleeting, so long lists are hard to remember; reading out ten options overloads working memory. Recognition errors happen, especially with accents, background noise and languages with less training data, so the system must confirm important actions ('Send 500 taka to Karim, right?') and make correction easy. Voice is also public: people may not want to say private things aloud on a bus. Good VUI design keeps prompts short, offers two or three choices at a time, tells users what they can say, confirms risky actions, and provides a fallback to touch or a human.

Chatbots and conversational interfaces: Text chatbots in messaging apps and websites share many voice issues. Users expect them to understand like a person, and disappointment comes quickly when they do not. Good chatbot design states clearly what the bot can help with, offers quick-reply buttons so users do not have to guess wording, handles 'I don't understand' gracefully, remembers context within the conversation, and hands over to a human when stuck. A bot that pretends to be a human, or traps users in loops, breaks trust.

Virtual reality: Virtual reality (VR) places the user inside a fully computer-generated world, usually through a head-mounted display that tracks head movement. The idea is old: Ivan Sutherland built a head-mounted display in 1968. VR is used for games, training (surgery, flight, machine operation), architecture walkthroughs and therapy. Its key quality is presence, the feeling of being there. Its HCI challenges include cybersickness, a kind of motion sickness caused when what the eyes see does not match what the body feels; text that is hard to read; input without a visible keyboard; and safety, since the user cannot see the real room.

Augmented and mixed reality: Augmented reality (AR) overlays digital information on the real world, usually through a phone camera or see-through glasses. Examples include camera translation apps that replace a sign's text with your language, furniture apps that place a virtual sofa in your room, and games that put characters on the street. Mixed reality usually describes systems where virtual objects are anchored to and interact with the real environment. AR design must handle cluttered, changing real backgrounds, keep overlays readable in sunlight, avoid hiding real dangers such as traffic, and respect the privacy of people captured by the camera.

Wearables: Wearables are computers worn on the body: smartwatches, fitness bands, smart glasses and earbuds with sensors. Their screens are tiny or absent, and use happens in short bursts, so interaction must be glanceable, lasting a few seconds. Notifications must be prioritised, or the watch becomes a constant buzzing distraction. Haptic feedback, such as a tap on the wrist, communicates without sound. Fitts' law reminds us that tiny watch targets are slow and error-prone, so watches favour large buttons, swipes, voice and automatic sensing. Health wearables also raise serious privacy questions about who sees the data.

Gesture and tangible interfaces: Gesture interfaces track body or hand movements with cameras or sensors, as in game consoles or touchless controls. They feel futuristic, but gestures lack signifiers and are tiring when held in the air for long, sometimes called the gorilla arm problem. Tangible user interfaces, explored by Hiroshi Ishii and colleagues at the MIT Media Lab, let people control digital information by handling physical objects, such as blocks on a table that represent buildings in a city simulation. They use the natural affordances of physical objects, which is Norman's idea applied to the digital world.

Multimodal interaction: Many new systems combine several channels at once: you speak a request, see the answer on a screen, confirm with a tap and feel a vibration when it is done. This is called multimodal interaction. It is powerful because each channel covers the weaknesses of another: voice is fast but fleeting, the screen is persistent but needs eyes, touch is precise but needs hands, haptics work in a pocket. It also helps accessibility, because a person who cannot use one channel can use another. The design rule is consistency: the same action should mean the same thing in every channel, and the user should always be able to switch channel when one fails, for example from voice to touch in a noisy place.

Ubiquitous computing: In 1991 Mark Weiser of Xerox PARC wrote 'The Computer for the 21st Century', describing ubiquitous computing: computers embedded everywhere in the environment, so many and so well integrated that they fade into the background. Smart homes, sensors in buildings, contactless payments and connected cars are steps toward that vision. Weiser and his colleague John Seely Brown also described calm technology, which informs without demanding attention, moving between the periphery and the centre of attention as needed. In an age of constant notifications, calm technology is an ideal worth remembering.

AI-powered interfaces: Large language models and other AI systems now power assistants, writing tools, image generators and recommendation feeds. They create new HCI challenges. AI output is probabilistic and can be wrong while sounding confident, so users may over-trust it. Users need to know what the system can and cannot do, how reliable it is, and why it gave a particular answer. Researchers at Microsoft published guidelines for human-AI interaction in 2019, including ideas such as making clear what the system can do and how well, supporting efficient correction when it is wrong, and showing why it did what it did. These apply our old principles: conceptual models, feedback, error recovery and user control.

AI, trust and fairness: The goal is calibrated trust: users trust the AI when it is reliable and check it when it is not. Design patterns that help include showing sources, highlighting uncertainty, making it easy to edit or undo AI suggestions, and keeping humans in control of important decisions such as medical or financial ones. AI systems can also perform worse for some groups, for example for Bangla speech or for accents underrepresented in training data, so testing with diverse users matters even more.

Real-life example 1, a voice feature for DaktarDekhao: The team adds a Bangla voice option so patients can say 'আমি কাল শিশু ডাক্তার দেখাতে চাই'. Research shows the recognition sometimes mishears names and dates in noisy clinic corridors. Design response: the app repeats what it understood on screen and aloud, asks for confirmation before booking, shows two or three possible slots instead of reading a long list, and offers a button to switch to touch at any time. Voice lowers the barrier for low-literacy users, while confirmation protects against recognition errors.

Real-life example 2, AR for field workers: An agriculture extension project could let farmers point a phone camera at a diseased leaf and see an overlay suggesting what the disease might be and what to do. HCI questions decide whether it helps or harms: does the app say how confident it is, does it show a clear 'ask an officer' option, does it work offline in the field, is the text readable in sunlight, and is it in Bangla? An overconfident wrong answer could make a farmer spray the wrong chemical, so calibrated trust is a safety issue, not a nicety.

Course recap, the human and the principles: Let us pull the course together. We began with HCI as the study of the human, the computer and the interaction loop. We studied the human: perception and Gestalt, memory limits, attention and mental models. We studied the computer: input and output devices and interaction styles. We learned Norman's principles: affordances, signifiers, mapping, constraints, feedback, conceptual models, the seven stages and the two gulfs, and how to design for error.

Course recap, the process and evaluation: Then we learned the user-centred design process: usability and UX goals, user research by asking and watching, personas and scenarios, task analysis, ideation and sketching, prototyping, information architecture and visual design. We evaluated designs with heuristic evaluation, cognitive walkthrough and usability testing with SUS, and predicted performance with Fitts' law, Hick's law and KLM. Finally we widened the circle with accessibility, design for Bangladesh, ethics and emerging interfaces.

What to learn next: To go further, practise: redesign apps you use and test with real people. Learn a design tool such as Figma to build prototypes. Read Norman's The Design of Everyday Things and articles from usability research groups. If you build software, combine this course with Mobile App Development and front-end development, and learn platform guidelines such as Material Design and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines. If research interests you, look at the proceedings of the ACM CHI conference to see current HCI work. Building a small portfolio of case studies, showing research, sketches, prototypes, test results and iterations, is the best way to show employers your HCI skills.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: A common mistake is to treat new technology as automatically better; voice or VR is good only when it fits the user, task and context. Another is to forget that old principles still apply. Exams ask you to compare AR and VR, explain the design challenges of voice interfaces, describe ubiquitous computing and Weiser's vision, discuss wearable design, and explain trust and transparency in AI interfaces. Strong answers link each new interface back to principles from the course.

Recap: Emerging interfaces include voice, chatbots, VR, AR and mixed reality, wearables, gesture, tangible interfaces, ubiquitous computing and AI. Each brings benefits, such as hands-free use, immersion and glanceability, and new challenges, such as discoverability, recognition errors, cybersickness, tiny targets, privacy and over-trust. The tools to handle them are the ones you already have: know your users, apply Norman's principles, design for error and accessibility, prototype, and test with real people. Technology changes; people stay human. That is why HCI will matter for the rest of your career.
key_points: Old HCI principles still apply to new interfaces: discoverability, feedback, error handling, memory limits and accessibility.
Voice interfaces are hands-free and natural but lack discoverability, overload memory with long lists and need confirmations for recognition errors.
VR immerses users in a virtual world (presence, cybersickness risk); AR overlays information on the real world.
Wearables need glanceable interactions, prioritised notifications and large targets; they raise privacy issues for health data.
Mark Weiser (1991) described ubiquitous computing, where computers fade into the background, and calm technology.
AI interfaces need calibrated trust: show capabilities, uncertainty and sources, support correction, keep humans in control.
The course path: the human, the computer, Norman's principles, the user-centred process, evaluation, accessibility, local context and ethics.
lessons.tip: Pick one emerging technology you are excited about and write a one-page critique using only course vocabulary: gulfs, signifiers, feedback, mental models, accessibility. If you can do that, you have truly learned HCI, because you can apply it to things the textbook never covered.
lessons.task: Use your phone's voice assistant to complete three tasks, such as setting an alarm, calling a contact and asking for the weather, once in English and once in Bangla if supported. Note every time you did not know what to say, it misunderstood you, or the feedback was unclear. Suggest one design improvement for each problem.

quiz.q: What is a major discoverability problem of voice user interfaces?
options: They respond too slowly to commands
They need a keyboard to work
There are no visible menus, so users do not know what they can say
They cannot be used while driving
quiz.explain: Without visible options, users must guess commands. Good VUIs tell users what they can say and offer a few choices at a time.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes AR from VR?
options: AR replaces the real world completely; VR adds labels to it
AR and VR are two names for the same technology
AR overlays digital information on the real world; VR places the user in a fully virtual world
VR works only on phones; AR needs a headset
quiz.explain: Augmented reality adds to what you see of the real world, while virtual reality replaces it with a computer-generated environment.

quiz.q: Who described ubiquitous computing in the 1991 article 'The Computer for the 21st Century'?
quiz.explain: Mark Weiser of Xerox PARC described computers embedded everywhere and fading into the background, along with the idea of calm technology.

quiz.q: Why must smartwatch interfaces use large targets and glanceable screens?
options: Because watches have more processing power than phones
Because small screens and short bursts of use make tiny targets slow and error-prone
Because users never look at watches
quiz.explain: Fitts' law shows tiny targets take longer and cause errors, and watch use happens in seconds, so interactions must be quick and big.

quiz.q: What does calibrated trust in an AI interface mean?
options: Users always trust the AI completely
The AI hides its uncertainty to look reliable
Users trust the AI when it is reliable and check it when it is not, helped by shown uncertainty and sources
quiz.explain: Calibrated trust matches trust to actual reliability. Showing confidence, sources and easy correction helps users neither over-trust nor under-trust.
